3846: The petitioner, a woman, filed an application under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for maintenance from her husband. She claimed that she was married to the respondent on 2nd December, 1980 and that she had lived as husband and wife for a long spell. The trial court rejected the said application holding that the evidence produced by the petitioner did not establish that she was legally married to the petitioner. The High Court confirmed the order of the trial court. Dismissing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The presumption is rebuttable, a heavy burden lies on him who seeks to deprive the relationship of legal origin. Law leans in favour of legitimacy and frowns upon bastardy. In this view, the contention deserves no consideration. [811C] 2. The presumption arises in favour of wedlock between the two, by eye witness evidence that they were validly married, few will succeed. The contention deserves to be negatived and it is accordingly rejected. [812D]

6169: The petitioner, a member of the State Legislature (State) of Jammu & Kashmir, was appointed as Chairman of the Board on October 1, 1966. He was removed from the office by an order dated November 30, 1969. The petitioner challenged his removal before the High Court in Writ Petition No. 818 of 1970. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had not been able to show sufficient cause for his absence and that he could not be allowed to continue beyond the period of six weeks. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The petitioner has failed to show sufficient reason for his absence. [819B] The petitioner is entitled to have his name included in the panel prepared by the State Government under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. [820C] The petitioner cannot claim any right to be included in the said panel. [821D] The petitioner has no vested right to get his name included within the panel. [882E] The petitioner was not entitled to be included within the said panel because he did not satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3) of the , which provides that the State Government shall constitute a Committee consisting of three persons who are or have been members of the State Legislative Assembly and one person nominated by the State government. The petitioner was also not qualified to be a member of this Committee. [884F] The petitioner had not shown sufficient cause for absence. [885A] The petitioner 's removal from the office of Chairman of the State Council was illegal because he was not a member of any of the State Councils. [886B] The State Government should indicate the names of the persons who were or have been the members of the Council. [887C]

1848: The appellant, a zamindar of Simlapal in the State of West Bengal entered into a contract with the respondent for cutting trees in certain demarcated areas of certain forests of the Zamindari on payment of a sum of Rs. 7,131/8/ . Under the terms of the said document the period during which the appellant was given this right to cut trees was to end on April 14, 1955. The appellant 's case was that the forest had been taken over by the Government under section 4(1) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 and that the respondent had no right to cut the trees. Held, that the forest land belonged to the Zamindar and the respondent had acquired the right to cut it under the provisions of the Act. The forest land was not a private property but was a private property of the Zamindar. The forest was not a public property within the meaning of section 5 of the Act and the respondent was entitled to cut the same. The forest is a private property and the respondent has no right to do so.
903: The assessee was a shareholder in a company which had its registered office at Bombay. He was a shareholder, holding shares of Mafatlal Gagalbhai & Co., Ltd., and also a private limited company with its registered office in Bombay. In the year 1949, he was assessed to income tax on a total income of Rs. 1,50,765 which included a grossed up dividend income of Rs, 1,47,026. In the latter case, the assessee claimed that the dividends declared by him were not taxable as income under section 4(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, but as a result of the decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay City vs Camco Colour Co.(P) Ltd. ; , it was held that the dividends were not taxable because they were received by the assessee in British India. Held, that the assessee was entitled to claim exemption from taxation under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income Tax Act. The assessee was not a resident in British India and was not liable to tax in respect of his income. The assessee did not bring these dividends into British India. The assessee could not be said to have been a resident in India within the meaning of section 4(3) (xi) of the Act. The dividend income was not taxable as an income of the assessee.
1748: The petitioners and respondent No. 2, their mother, are members of a joint Hindu family governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law. Under a family custom which was prevailing in this family for centuries, the Raj as well as the Zamindari properties belonging to the family were held by a single individual and the other members of the family were entitled to maintenance according to the status of the family with the right to succession to the Raj as and when they became members of the Ruling Deb Barman family. In consequence, at the time of regency of the Rituals of the Rhena, the maintenance allowance paid to the maintenance holders was fixed arbitrarily without any regard to their status and their hereditary needs and that led to the appointment of another Committee to go into the matter, but the Committee could never function with the result that the condition of the majority of the maintenance holders grew midway between the Rhenas and the Rinidhi. The petitioners contended that the provisions of section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure were not applicable to the case and that the impugned order was invalid. Held: (i) Section 87B of Code of Civil procedure is not applicable to proceedings under section 87B because the Act does not apply to proceedings before the High Court or the Supreme Court. The provisions of section 8(1)(b), 8(2) and 8(3) of the Code are not applicable to such proceedings. (ii)The provisions of section 88B of the Indian Succession Act are not applicable in the present case because the Act applies only to cases where the parties have agreed to the terms of the will. (iii)Section 87B of Indian Succession Act is not applicable because the Act has no application to proceedings under sections 8(1) (b), 8 (2) and (3). (iv)The Act does not provide for the payment of maintenance allowance to the maintenance holder. (v)The Act is not intended to apply to proceedings under the Act. (vi)The Act applies to proceedings under Chapter VIII of the Code and not to proceedings under chapter VIII of the Act.
1946: The plaintiff, the eider sister of the first defendant instituted a suit for possession of half share in the properties described in the schedule to the plaint and for partition and separate possession of half the property. The defendants pleaded that they had no right to the suit properties as their possession over the properties was adverse to them and as they were in adverse possession for over the statutory period, the suit was barred. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff was entitled to half share in all the properties described as 'Gowramma ' and that the defendants were not entitled to any relief against them. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court held that the plaintiff had lost her right to the half share in these properties because she did not want to join her as coplaintiff in the suit and that the plaintiff could not claim a decree against the other defendants. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant had acquired only a life interest in the properties and that the respondents had acquired only an absolute interest in the property and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant has lost her right of claiming a decree against her. [875C] 2. The appellant is entitled to succeed to her share in the property. [876D] 3. The appellant cannot be said to have acquired only a limited interest in the joint family properties. The appellant had acquired a limited interest only in the properties which were the subject matter of the suit. The appellant was not entitled to the benefits of Section 51. [877E] 4. The appellant could not claim any right to the property. She had acquired only the life interest in her property. [887B] 5. The appellant can not claim a right to the share of her father in the properties. [885F] 6. The appellant would be entitled to the share in the suit properties. [892A]

In the view of the Tribunal 's opinion, the business in the shares and the sale of shares was one of a number of commodities in which the Company dealt in the ordinary course of business. The Tribunal observed that there was complete unity of control and shares were one of a series of commodities in the ordinary business. The question whether the various activities carried on by the assessee constituted one business or separate businesses was not decided by the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the petition filed by the appellant company. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the business of the appellant was not one of a kind of business but of a different nature. [384 D] (ii) The High Courts had taken the view that the business was one of an individual business and that the profits earned by the appellant could not be said to form part of the business of a person carrying on a trade. [385 B C] (iii) The High court was wrong in saying that the business did not constitute one business. The business was one in which the company dealing in shares and other commodities was one of the several commodities in which a company dealing in the ordinary and special business. The company
1201: The respondent was granted a village in 1901 by the Nizam. In 1917, the respondent 's case was that the village had been granted to his ancestor and that the grant was not permanent. On the death of Raja Nemiwant Bahadur, the village was conferred on him by the Nizam and the respondent was only entitled to the pan mukta of the village and no more. The respondent 's suit for possession of the village as well as for recovery of the lease money was decreed and the plaintiff was held entitled to recover possession of the land as well as to recover mesne profits at the rate of Rs. 931 12 0 0 per year. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The respondent ' s case was that he was a bilmaktdar and that the village was granted as bilmakhtar to the respondent. The respondent was not a bilamkatta holder but was a bazardar. The respondent could not claim to be a bilomaktadar. [1927 D] (2) The respondent was a bhoomidar and was not a mere bhooms or a pujari. He was merely a bhoofan. The respondent had no right to the land which was granted to him as bilomkatta. [1928 A B] (3) The respondent had not claimed any title adverse to the respondent in respect of the village. The respondent did not claim any title adverse against the respondent. [1929 C] (4) The respondent could claim to be the owner of the village only if he was a Bahnavi pujari and was a bhaya. [1930 E]
5094: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to wealth tax as a registered firm and the two partners were separately assessed in respect of their share of income. The assessment order included the amount of interest accruing on account of interest accrued on the credit balance standing to the credit of Rangi Lal in his accounts. The assessee filed a return of his net wealth on July 17, 1965. The Wealth Tax Officer held that the sum of Rs.1,85,043 which had been credited to the account of Rangi lal in the books of the firm was not liable to be included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld this view. On further appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the amount of Rs.23,330 was not liable for deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the reference holding that the sum was not deductible from the net wealth. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the amount was not liable, because, the assessee had not received any interest on the amount of the credit balance in his account and that the amount should have been treated as an asset of the assessee 's family. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The amount of interest is not an asset of an individual. It is a payment made by the assessee to a member of his family or to a person who has no legal right to receive it. [801C] 2. The amount must be regarded as a capital receipt. [802D] 3. The amount cannot be said to be a capital receipt in the hands of the assessee merely because it is paid to him. [803E] 4. The amount is not an item of property within the meaning of section 2(e) of the Wealth Tax Act. The amount can only be regarded as an asset for the purposes of the Act. [805F] 5. The amount could not be regarded as income of the assessee unless it was received by him. [885G] 6. The amount was not an asset for purposes of the Wealth tax Act. [894A] 7. The amount did not come within the purview
4507: The appellant, a tenant in respect of the land in question, filed a return under section 21 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961. The respondent No. 1, the State Government, issued a notification dated January 26, 1962 declaring that the surplus area of the land held by him was to be excluded from the holding of the appellant and that the surplus land would be allotted to the appellant. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the proceedings commenced with the filing of a return under the Act were dropped as the appellant had not been given an opportunity of being heard; that the proceedings were not in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the Act; that the order of the Collector was without jurisdiction and that the proceedings could not be continued after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed by the statute. HELD: The provisions of sections 3 to 7 of the Act are mandatory and they do not confer any right upon the person affected thereby. [866 D] The provisions of section 5 of the Act have no application to the facts of the case. Section 5(1)(a) provides that where the Collector has made an order under section 3, he shall cause a notice thereof to be served on the person concerned requiring him within such time as may be specified therein to show cause why the order should not be passed. The appellant did not file any objections against the proposed action. He did not appear at the hearing. The proceedings were therefore not in accordance. [867 C E] The proceedings were not vitiated because the appellant had failed to comply with the requirements of the Act. [868 A B] The proceedings must be deemed to have been initiated under section 5(2) of the Act and the proceedings must be treated as having abated. [869 F] The proceedings cannot be continued after a period of one year from the date of the commencement of the Act or the date of making the declaration under section 6. [871 G]
886: The appellant and his mother in law entered into an agreement with the owners of certain lands in village Mohammadpur Munirka to purchase certain lands at Rs. 5 per sq. Earnest money. The vendor was to pay the vendor 's share of the sale proceeds to the vendors. The vendor executed a deed on June 12, 1957, in favour of the vendees. The vendees paid the amount to the vendors and the vendees were given possession of the land. The vendee filed a suit for specific performance of the agreement. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the suit was barred under section 17(1) of the Acquisition Act as the suit was not for the purpose of obtaining compensation for the acquisition of the land but only for the purpose for which it was being acquired; that the suit having been instituted after the expiry of the period prescribed by section 17(2), the suit was within time; that the High Court erred in holding that the suit had been filed beyond the period of limitation; that the appellant had no right to file the suit within the period of three years from the date of the execution of the agreement and that the suit should have been dismissed as barred by limitation. HELD : (i) The suit was not barred by limitation because the suit was filed after the expiry prescribed by section 4 of the Acquisition act. [504 A] (ii) The suit is not barred by section 17 of the Acquisition. It is not barred under section 19 of the Limitation Act. [505 D] (iii) The suit must be held to be within time. [506 B] (iv) The suit could not be said to be barred by limitation if the suit was for the purpose mentioned in section 17(3). [505 C] (v) The suit cannot be said to have been filed beyond three years from June 12,1957. [508 F] (vi) The suit has been instituted beyond three years of the date of execution of the contract. [509 G]
4973: The appellant, a Hindu, adopted by Asharfi Devi, widow of one Purushottam Lal, the first respondent, and the properties belonging to the idol. The respondents filed a suit for recovery of possession of the idol and temple of Gopalji described in the plaint and the money lying in deposit with the Punjab National Bank at Vrindavan, the zamindari abolition compensation and rehabilitation grant bonds specified in the plaint. The trial court decreed the suit except as regards items to 25 and 37 to 41 of list I of Schedule "Ba" and the sum of Rs. 1004.97. The appellant filed an appeal in the District Court and the respondents filed a cross objection in that appeal in regard to the money claim disallowed by the trial court. The learned Second Additional District Judge, Mathura allowed the appeal and dismissed the cross objection. The respondents ' case was that the idol of Gopalji was installed by Purushottambhai Lal in his house at Vrindawan which later became the temple of the deity. Purushottaman died on 20 11 1956 leaving behind him his wife Asharfali and two sons. The appellant instituted a suit for possession of the said idol and the property described in the schedule to the plaint. In the plaint it was stated that the idols were installed by Purshottam Lal in his own house at Vrsindavan and that the appellant had no right to do so. The trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree of the trial Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not gone into the question of the adoption of the second respondent by Asharffi Devi. The High court has not gone through the evidence adduced by the parties and the judgment of the courts below in regard to item No. 25 and 37 of list I. The High Courts have not gone into this question of the validity of the adoption. [626E] 2. The High courts are not competent to decide whether the adoption is valid or not. The question of the legality of the adoption can be decided only after the parties adduce their respective evidence. The question whether the adoption was valid or not will depend upon the facts of
6636: The detenu made a representation to the appropriate Government. By then the Advisory Board was already constituted and it was scheduled to meet to consider the case of the detenu. The Government forwarded the detenu 's representation to the Advisory Board. The Advisory Board considered the matter and after considering the representation, confirmed the detention order. The detention order came to be passed on 9 March 1989. The detenus filed Writ Petition No. 845 of 1989 in this Court challenging the validity of the detention order and for quashing the same. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The detention order is invalid because the representation of the detenus was not considered before confirming the detention order without the consideration of the representation. [943C] 2.1 The detenu 's right to make a representation under Article 22(5) of the Constitution is a constitutional right. It is a constitutional obligation of the detaining authority to consider the representation of an accused person expeditiously and pass orders thereon. If the representation is not disposed of within a reasonable time, the detention order would stand vitiated. [944E F] 3.1 The detaining authority has to consider the grounds of detention as early as possible before making the order of detention. The detaining authority must consider all the relevant facts and circumstances before passing any order. If no such considerations are given, the detention orders will become illegal. [946A B] 4.1 The order of detention cannot be sustained if the detaining authority did not apply its mind to the relevant material before arriving at the subjective satisfaction that there were sufficient cause for the detention of the detenue. [947D E] 4.2 The detaining authority should have considered the representation of a detenu along with other materials before passing the order of preventive detention. [948F] 4.3 The detenu ''s right to be released on bail is a valuable right. He can make an application for release on bail pending investigation or trial. The detaining Authority must consider the representation independently of the judicial opinion. [949B C] 4.4 The detaining authority shall forward the detenu ' s representation together with the record of the proceedings held against him to the Advisory board for their consideration. The Advisory board shall thereafter decide whether the detention of
5255: The appellant was a public servant and was holding the post of a Judge or Magistrate. He filed a complaint under Section 120(b) read with Sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code against the respondent, who was working as a clerk in the bank. After summons were issued to him he raised objection regarding the maintainability of this prosecution for want of sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The Metropolitan Magistrate held that Section 197 is attracted only when a public servant is not removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government and therefore the view taken by the Courts below is not correct. The High Court dismissed the Revision Petition. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after the nationalisation of the bank, the appellant will fall within the definition of public servant and therefore Sec. 197 would be attracted. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The expression 'public servant ' has been defined in Section 2(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 which reads as follows: "Public servant" means any person who is deemed to be a public servant in terms of Section 2(a)(i) of the Act. [447C] 1.2. The expression "public servant" has been defined under Section 2(e) of the 1988 Act to mean a person who holds office as such during the period of office tenure of a member of the armed forces of the Union or as the case may be, any other class of such service in connection with the affairs of the Union. The word 'public servant' has been defined to mean any person who holds an office connected with the defence or any other country outside India. [448D E] 1.3. The expression public servant has been defined by Section 2(d) to mean a member of any of the Armed Forces of the Union while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty. [449E] 1.4. The expression is defined in Section 3(c) to include any company or association or body of individuals whether incorporated or not. [450F] 1.5. The expression means any person whose services are temporarily lent or let out by the Government to the Board or
3607: The first appellant is an association of manufacturers of Mangalore pattern roofing tiles in south Gujarat area. The other appellant, a partnership firm, is a member of the association. The question that falls to be determined in this appeal by special leave is whether entry 22 added by the Gujarat Government by notification dated March 27, to Part of the Schedule to the cover of employment in agriculture only as included in the schedule to the cover, or any process or blanch of work forming part of such employment, is an amendment to the Schedule so as to bring it in conformity with the provisions of section 2(g) of the Minimum Wages Act. The appellants contended that entry 22 was not applicable to them because the notification did not specify the rate of wages and that the notification merely provided for the fixation of minimum rates of wages. HELD: (1) The notification does not make any reference to the minimum rates of wage fixed under the Act. It merely provides for the revision of minimum rates. The notification does nothing more than adds to the minimum rate of wages fixed under the Rules framed under the Act and the rules made thereunder. [560 D E] (2) The notification merely makes it clear that the appropriate Government has to fix minimum rates of pay in respect of any scheduled Section 5. The notification also makes it clear beyond doubt that the notification is intended to apply to all persons employed in any industry. The notification therefore clearly applies to all persons who are employed in any scheduled Section. [561 G H; 552 A B] (3) The notification is not intended to apply only to persons employed in a factory or establishment. The notification merely clarifies the position and makes it clear there from that the notification applies to all employees in factories or establishments. [552 C] (4) The notification cannot be construed to mean that the notification must be confined to the persons employed in the factory or establishment in which the factory or the establishment is situated. The notification can only have prospective effect. [553 F] (5) The notification makes no mention of the minimum rates. It merely says that the minimum rates would be applicable to all persons irrespective of the fact whether they were employed in any factory or establishment or in any other establishment. [551 G]
891: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of certain properties in Ahmedabad. The three widows were named as 'individuals " in one case and ' association of persons " in the other. The income from these properties was assessed separately in the hands of the three widows. The Income tax Officer issued notices to the legal heirs of the deceased, under section 9(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, for assessment years 1950 51 and 1951 52 (the corresponding account years being the Sambat years 2005 and 2006). The assessments were completed on the basis that the shares of the three wives were liable to be assessed separately in their hands. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the point (a), but accepted the point (b). Then the Tribunal held that the entire estate of the deceased was inherited by the three widows and that in any event the income from property ought to have been assessed separately in its hands in the hands 'of the three widows by reason of the provisions in section 9(1)(i) of the Act. The Tribunal also held that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was wrong in holding that the shares were definite and determinable and section 9(2) was applicable. The High Court answered the question against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to decide whether the shares of a Hindu undivided Hindu family were definite and determined in the hands or not. [417D] 2. The Tribunal has rightly held that the shares are definite and determinate and section 9 (3) is applicable. [418E] 3. The Tribunal was right in holding that in the instant case the shares were indeterminate and determinable. [419C] 4. The Tribunal rightly held that in the present case the shares of three widows were liable to assessment in their hands in the status of an association of persons. [420B C] 5. The Tribunal erred in holding that there was no evidence to show that the three widows were members of the Hindu undivided family. [421A] 6. The Tribunal did not consider the evidence in its proper perspective. The Tribunal should have considered the evidence in the light of the facts and circumstances of each case. [422F]
3853: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. for causing the death of one Nainsukh and for causing injuries to him with a gun. The High Court acquitted the appellant but convicted him on the ground that the prosecution had failed to prove the motive for the murder. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable as they were interested in the success of the case and that the evidence was not trustworthy. HELD: (1) There is no reason why the evidence of an injured witness should be discarded only because he is interested in the outcome of the cross examination. [980 D] (2) The evidence of the injured witness cannot be rejected merely because he is related to the deceased or is otherwise interested in the deceased. It is for the court to consider whether his testimony inspires confidence and if it is found to be reliable, conviction can be based on such evidence. [981 C D] (3) The evidence given by the injured witness is admissible under section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act. The statement made by the injured person is admissible under Section 32(1). [982 E]
4259: The petitioner was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a term of two years under section 376 I.P.C. and a fine of Rs. 500/, in default simple imprisonment for one month. On appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment of three months. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction is not vitiated merely because there is absence of corroboration of the testimony of the prosecutrix. [405D E] 2. The evidence of the prosecutrix does not suffer from any infirmity. [408A B] 3. The mere fact that the victim has been examined by the doctor does not mean that she must have been tutored or swayed by someone who could be said to be an eye witness. It is only when the doctor has given such a certificate that it can be accepted as a valid piece of evidence. [403B C] 4. The court may look for some corroboration if the circumstances of the case so demand. But where the medical evidence does not support the ocular testimony, the court cannot base its conviction on the sole testimony of the victim. [402E F] 5. In the instant case, the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of the petitioner beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction was therefore unsustainable. [406G H]
273: The respondent, Ram Narain, acting on behalf of his firm, Ram Narain Joginder Nath, carrying on business at Mailsi in Multan District, was allowed cash credit limit of rupees three lakhs by the appellant Bank. On 15th August 1947, when the bank 's godown keeper at MailsI left Mailia branch in September, 1947, and the cashier, who was left in charge, also was forced to leave that place in October, 1947. On inquiry he found that cotton bales pledged with the bank had disappeared. On enquiry he found that the goods were stolen from Mailia Branch and that they were not stolen. He therefore applied under section 188, Criminal Procedure Code, to the East Punjab Government for sanction for the prosecution of the respondent. The sanction was granted by the Central Government. The respondent thereupon filed a complaint before the Magistrate against the appellant for offences under sections 379, 411 and 412 I.P.C., and the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence. The appellant contended that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the case as the offence was committed outside India and that the Magistrate could not take cognizance of it without the consent of the Central Government and that the appellant was entitled to be tried by the Court of Session. Held, that the Magistrate was competent to take cognizance and try the accused person. The Magistrate had jurisdiction to take action under section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, and the Magistrate had jurisdiction under section 190(1)(b) of the Code to take cognizance. The Magistrate could not proceed to take cognizance unless the accused was produced before him. The Magistrate did not have any power to take cognizance if he was not so produced. The Magistrate was competent under section 190 (1)(a), Cr. P. C., to take cognizance even though he was not actually present when the offence was alleged to have been committed.

4400: The appellant was a recognised dealer under the Gujarat Sales Tax Act, 1969. For the purpose of manufacturing the goods, the appellant which was also a recognised dealer was registered as dealer under the provisions of the Gujarat Sales tax Act, 1969 and the appellant purchased raw materials from the respondent for its factory at Gujarat. The respondent issued a certificate in Form No. 19 to the appellant on the basis that the raw materials purchased by it were used in the manufacture of taxable goods which would be sold by it in the State of Gujarat. The appellant filed an appeal before the Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax and the Gujarat Sales Taxes Tribunal against the levy of purchase tax under section 16 of the Act on the ground that certain electric goods manufactured out of raw materials etc. purchased against declaration in Form No 19 had been violated. The appeals filed by the appellant before the Tribunal were unsuccessful. Thereafter at the instance of the appellant the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court of Gujarat under section 69 of the Act: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case and on a correct interpretation of sub section (33) of section 2 of the Gujarat State Sales Tax Act 1969 the Tribunal was right in deciding that the applicant was liable to pay purchase tax under Section 16 of the Gujarat sales Tax Act, 1968 on the ground of contravention of the conditions of registration of the dealer under the Act ?" The High Court answered the questions in favour of the appellant holding that the appellant was not liable to pay the purchase tax under the Act on account of the fact that the undertaking given in Form No, 19 had been contravened. In Civil Appeal No. 1185 of 1979, the appellant was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The appellant purchased raw material from the respondent in the State for its factory in Gujarat. The raw material was used in the factory of the appellant for generation and distribution of electrical energy. The appellant claimed exemption from payment of tax under the Gujarat sales tax Act, 1968. The Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes rejected the claim of exemption. The Appellate Authority held that the appellant had failed to prove that the undertaking was violated and that the appellant could not be said to have committed any breach of the condition of registration. The appellant preferred a revision application before the Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the revision
347: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The provisions of section 439(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure are not applicable in India. Section 439(6), however, does not apply to a case where an appeal is pending before the High Court. [999 G] (2) The right of appeal by a convict against his conviction is a statutory right and it cannot be exercised except on the ground that the sentence imposed upon him has been reduced or enhanced by the High Court under section 423(1). [999 D E] (3) The right to appeal by a person who had been convicted by the High court is a statutory one and its exercise by the High Courts is subject to the limitations prescribed by section 439(1). If the High Court finds that the accused has been wrongly convicted by the trial court, it can direct the release of the accused on bail. [998 F H]
3616: The respondent was a minor on 1 1 1970. He had two sons, one of whom was minors on 1 1 1971 and the other a daughter, who was a major on 1 1 1 1970, and the ceiling area allowed under section 82(1) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act 2964 for a family consisting of himself, his wife and children. The respondent executed three deeds of gift transferring a total extent of 12.83 acres to his three children. To the eldest daughter who was a minor she transferred 3.84 acres and to her son who became a major in 1971. On 28 March, 1974 the respondent executed three documents of gift transferring the total extent of 8.78 acres to his daughters. To the second daughter who became a minor in 1971 he transferred 5.14 acres and to his son who became major in 1973 he transferred 5,14 acres and the respondent 's son who became minors on the date of the gift. The respondent filed an objection on 5 April, 1974 stating that he and his wife were not entitled to have the excess land surrendered by them. The Land Board recog ssed the gift to the eldest of them a daughter, whose daughter was a major, on 1 January, 1970. The respondent 's contention was accepted by the High Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The respondent ' s father had two sons and the daughter were minors on that date. The respondent was the only son and the daughter was a minor. The respondent could not be said to be a member of the family on the date when the gift deed was executed. [880C] (2) The respondent was not a member of a family on 1 1.1970. His wife was a minor and the respondent was not entitled to claim any excess land. [881D] (3) The respondent had no right to transfer the excess land. The respondent had only a right to retain the excess land if he wanted to surrender it. [882E] (4) The respondent could have claimed the excess land only if he had surrendered the excess land to the Government. [886F]
4503: The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death on the charge that he had committed the murder of his mother 's brother also called Muniappan. The conviction for murder and the sentence of death were confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the trial court overlooked the provision contained in section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 which provides that when the accused is asked on the question of sentence, he does not say anything, the accused has committed the crime and therefore no sympathy can be shown to him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 354(3), Cr. P.C., is a rule, not an exception nor a rule of law. It is a rule of prudence and not of law. [272B] 2. The learned Sessions Judge did not make any serious effort to elicit from the accused what he wanted to say on the question whether he should be hanged by the neck or should be sent to the police station. He made no attempt to elicit any information as to why he should be sent. The fact that he was asked on the point of sentence would not render the sentence of life imprisonment illegal. [271D E] 3. The learned Judge must make a genuine effort to eress from the accused whatever he wants to say on that question of sentence. If he makes some kind of statement, he must explain the same. [274E] 4. The learned judge must give due consideration to the fact that the accused is a young man of 22 years of age and is a menace to society and there are no criminal antecedents of his own. [275F] 5. The learned sessions Judge was right in convicting the appellant under section 302 I.P.C. and sentencing him to death. [276A]
2861: The appellants in these appeals are the mortgagees of the suit properties. The respondents in both the appeals claim to represent the interest of the mortgagors. The appellants in the other appeal claimed that they were insane at the time he sold the suit properties to the respondents. The trial court dismissed both the suits except as regards the mortgage executed on April 26, 1912. In second appeal, the High Court confirmed the decision of the courts below. In second appeals, the appellants contended that the claim for redemption was barred by limitation. The respondents contended that the suit was not barred by limitation and that the suit should have been dismissed. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The question whether a particular transaction is voidable under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, has to be decided on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case. [901 G] (2) The question of limitation does not depend upon the proof of the fact that the parties to the transaction intended to defeat or delay the creditors. It depends upon the intention of the parties to be gathered from the surrounding circumstances. [902 B C] (3) The question as to whether the suit is barred by limitation depends upon the question whether the suit was filed within three years from the date of the sale deed. [903 D E] (4) The question about the validity of the sale deeds cannot be decided in this case because the sale deeds do not contain any recital regarding the date of execution of the sale documents. [904 F] (5) The question regarding the validity of a document which is voidable can only arise when it is shown that the document is voidable. [905 A] (6) The question relating to the validity of an agreement to sell the property involved in the suit must be determined on the basis that the transaction is void. [906 B] (7) The question is not whether the transaction is valid or not but whether the transaction was lawful. [907 C] (8) The question arises as to what is the effect of the sale transactions. 3961: The respondent was appointed as a Sub Inspector of Police in 1955. He was discharged from service on July 13, 1957. On March 13, 1957, he instituted a suit for declaration that the order dated January 21, 1956 was illegal and void and that he continued as Sub Inspector of police in the Uttar Pradesh Police Service. It was alleged that on a false complaint made against him in respect of the custody and detention of one Smt. Phoolmati, an enquiry had been held in consequence of which the appellant had been arbitrarily and illegally terminated his services. The suit was contested by the appellant who maintained that the termination of the respondent 's services was not by way of punishment because it attached a stigma or amounted to a reflection on the competence of the government servant and affected his future career. The suit also was decreed by the trial court. In appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, the appellant contended that the finding recorded during the enquiry on the original complaint against the respondent was not binding upon the Government servant and that the termination was not by itself a punitive discharge. Held: (i) The order terminating the respondent ' s service was not by virtue of any stigma nor was it a stigmatization simpliciter. The order merely stated that the respondent 'S officer was guilty of misconduct. There was no stigma attached to the respondent. [880 D] (ii)The order of termination of the services of the respondent was bad because it did not contain any stigmatisecti on. The order was therefore liable to be set aside. The order could not be said to have been passed in accordance with the rules applicable to temporary government servants.
468: The petitioners were prosecuted for offences under sections 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. They were convicted by the Special Judge on a charge that they accepted illegal gratification for showing official favour to one Panna Lal. The High Court set aside their conviction and directed their acquittal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the sanction given by the competent authority was invalid as the prosecution had not been sanctioned by the competent authorities; (ii) the sanction granted by the Inspector General of Police was invalid because the sanction was not valid in law; (iii) the sanction accorded by the Inspector of Police was bad in law; and (iv) the trial was vitiated by reason of the fact that the sanction was obtained by fraud. HELD : (i) The sanction was valid in law. It is well settled that if a public servant who has been dismissed from service before he could be tried again for the same offence, the question whether or not sanction should have been given by the authority competent to dismiss him earlier would depend upon the nature of the offence and the particular facts and circumstances of each case. [880 E F] (ii)The sanction was valid only when it was passed by the competent officer. The order of dismissal was made by the Inspector-General of Police after he had taken over charge of the office of the Superintendent of Police. The order was not passed by the Inspector general of Police. [881 G H] (iii)The sanction given by an Inspector General of police was valid in all respects. [882 A B]
3421: The respondent company was a small scale industry in the country. It had a Distribution Office at Nicholson Road, Delhi. There were 30 employees at the relevant time. The workmen were not given their wages or compensation for the period of lay off. An industrial dispute was raised and referred by the Delhi Administration on the 17th April 1968 to the Labour Court. The Labour Court held that the workmen were not entitled to any lay off compensation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the management had a right to lay off its workmen under section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that the action of the management to lay off the workmen with effect from 5th February 1968 was illegal and/or unjustified. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The management has a right to close down its business. [372B] 2. The lay off of the workmen is not prohibited by section 25F. The lay-off is not an automatic closure but is only a temporary one. [373C] 3. The layoff is not a permanent or temporary one. The question whether the management has a legal right to close the business or not depends upon the facts of each case. [374D] 4. The lay Off is not a mere stoppage of work without anything more. The layover is a temporary one and the employer can lay off the workman if he so desires. [375E] 5. The lay over is a temporary measure. The lay out is a permanent one. The lay should be closed down immediately after the closure of the undertaking. [376A]
1910: The appellant was a landholder in the district of Kamrup. He holds a hat or market on his land since 1936 and this market is known as Kharmahat. 6607: The respondents filed a suit against the appellant for grant of leave to institute a suit as required under section 92 of the Code. 472: The appellant along with one Qudrat Ullah was tried for the murder of one Sabir. The prosecution case was that there was an exchange of abuses between the deceased and the appellant near the shop of the First Informant, Qudrat ullah. The appellant was acquitted by the Sessions Judge but the High Court reversed it and convicted him under section 302 read with section 114 I.P.C. The appellant contended that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable as they were interested in the occurrence and that the statement made by them to the police was not admissible in evidence because they had no previous enmity with the accused. Held, that the evidence given by the eye witnesses could be used only to corroborate the statements of the eye witness or to contradict them. The evidence of the witnesses was admissible under section 157 of the Evidence Act. The statement made by the eye witness to the police did not amount to a substantive piece of evidence and therefore, the statement made to the police would not be admissible in evidence. The statement of the eye-witnesses to the police cannot be used to corroborate their statements. The statement is admissible in evidence if it contains some facts which are inconsistent with those stated in the evidence. The mere fact that the statement of the witness recorded by the police does not amount to any substantive evidence is not sufficient to vitiate its evidentiary value. The statement must be such as can be relied on for convicting the accused. The statement may be used to contradict the person who deposed to the incident or to contradict him in material particulars. But the statement should be such as to make the witness understand the questions put to him and give him a fair opportunity to explain them. If he gives a false answer to the questions put, his evidence will be excluded from consideration.

Subsequently, the respondents demanded possession of the building from the appellants and despite several notices given by them, the respondents failed to give possession of the premises. The appellants claimed that they required the building in order to extend their business by running a hotel there itself; secondly, as the lease had expired by efflux of time, the respondents were legally bound to surrender possession. Thirdly, it was averred that the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) was wholly inapplicable to the premises in dispute, because the yearly income of the respondents was Rs. 20,000 and that running a hotel did not fall within the purview of section 2(3) of the Act. The suit was resisted by the respondents contending that the appellants had no personal necessity and had filed the suit merely for the purpose of getting a higher rent. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellants were entitled to a decree of ejectment against the respondents. The High Courts decision is correct. [412D] 3. Section 2(3)(a) of the Rent Control Act defines "house" to mean any building or part of a building let separately for residential or nonresidential purposes. It includes a room in a building used for residence. [413E] 4. The definition of the word "house" in section 2(1)(b) does not include a room

2337: The appellant was a member of the State Medical Service. He was posted at the Civil Hospital, Ahmedabad and on February 18, 1950, one Nabimhomed complained to Mr. Rathod that he had been falsely implicated by the Anti Corruption Branch of the Police and asked him to consider his representation before giving sanction for prosecution against him. On March 16, 1950, the Government issued an order under section 161(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure directing the Civil Surgeon, Ahmedabad to place the appellant under suspension pending further orders from the date of the receipt of the memorandum. In pursuance of this order the Surgeon General sent a report dated April 19, 1950, to the Government recommending that the appellant should be placed under suspension pending enquiry into the charges framed against him. The Government also directed that the appellant shall be paid in addition Rs. 35/ per mensem as dearness allowance during the entire period of suspension. On August 21, 1950, Mr. R. S. Patel, Deputy Secretary to the Government wrote to the Surgeon General stating that the Government had decided to suspend the appellant pending further orders. On September 2, 1950, he wrote to the Government that the Government should not pass any order with regard to the appellant until the Government had approved the recommendation made by the Public Service Commission. On October 3, 1951, the Government passed an order under sub section (2) of section 162 of the Code, suspending the appellant pending enquiry into charges framed against the appellant. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the order of suspension was bad because it was made without the approval of the Government. The order was not in accordance with the provisions of section 162(3). The order was therefore illegal. The order could not be sustained because it was not approved by the Government. It was not necessary for the Government to obtain the approval of Government before it passed the order. The order did not amount to approval of Government within the meaning of section 162 (3). The Government had no power to suspend the order.
508: The petitioners were displaced persons who owned land in the non suburban village of Chak. They were also co sharers in a joint khata owned by some evacuees in the village Sultanwind. On their displacement, they were allotted in the year 1949 a total area of 38 standard acres and 13 units of agricultural land. In 1950, a total area was allotted to them in the year 1950. This allotment had to be disturbed under the following circumstances. The Director General of Relief and Rehabilitation (Additional Custodian) directed that out of the 1,263 standard acres and 1 3/4 units of suburban land of Amritsar, a total extent of 38 standard acre and 13 units were to be allotted to allottees of Provincial Gardens. Thereafter, the petitioners moved the Custodian General for revision of the order of cancellation which was rejected by him. The word "law" is defined in article 13(2) to include an ordinance, rule or regulation. The word 'law' in article 31 A(1) means a law made by Parliament. The word law' in article 13 (2) includes an ordinance, rules or orders. 2406: The appellants brought a suit against the respondent for possession of a plot Kharsa No. 1227 on the ground that they had been unlawfully dispossessed from this land. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it and held that the appellants were not entitled to any relief. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The right in respect of a plot is a personal right which can be enforced only by a person claiming through or under him. The right in regard to a plot is not merely a right to hold the property as a tenant or a subtenant. It is a right to enjoy the property as such till his death. [280 B] (2) The right to hold property is a personal one and not an interest in immovable property. The right to continue in possession is a personal interest of the owner. The right of the owner is a mere right to remain in possession without having any right to create a tenancy. [281 C D] (3) The right of a mortgagee to possess the property as his own is a right in rem. The right is a right of ownership. The right must be a right in personam. [282 E] (4) The right is not merely personal to the mortgagor but is a right arising out of the mortgage. It is not merely an interest in the property. It is merely a right in favour of the mortgagee. It is only a right to retain possession of the property as the mortgagor has. [285 F] (5) The right under section 53(a) of the Transfer of Property Act is a personal or individual right. It is an interest in property. It does not come within the purview of section 53(b). [286 A] (6) The right conferred by section 53(c) is a personal and not an estate. It is therefore not a personal right. [287 G]
6141: The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, is engaged in the manufacture of Ossein and Gelatine in Rajasthan. It has been granted an application for permission to establish an undertaking for the manufacture of Oceanic Oil. The appellant made representations before the C.G. objecting to the grant of the application by the Modis. The C.G., after considering the objections raised by the appellant, rejected the application on the ground that the grant was against public interest. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Central Government which was also dismissed. In the meanwhile, the Modi Gas Company Ltd. had applied for permission to set up a gas plant in Rajasthan. The CG, however, did not pass any order on the application. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated 20th September, 1988. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the order dated 23rd September, 1988 was vitiated as it was passed without giving an opportunity of hearing to the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order dated 20.9.88 is vitiated because it ignores the fact that the appellant had no opportunity of meeting the new case. [819B] 1.2 The order dated 23.9.1988 does not show that the C.C. had considered the objections raised in the application. It merely states that the application was rejected. The order does not indicate that the CCC had considered the objection raised in the earlier application. [820E F] 1.3 The order dated 30.11.1988 does contain a finding that the CG had considered the application and had rejected it. The order dated 31.12.1988 does nothing more than stating that the application had been rejected. [821F] 1.4 The order dated 29.10.1988 does no mention that the CGC had considered the representation of the appellant. The order merely states that it had considered the said representation. The order simply states that the CQC had considered the same. [822A B] 1.5 The order dated 21.9.89 does not state that the CAG had considered the matter
1090: The appellant, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was granted leave to its employees for a period of three months. The company claimed that it had not been able to avail of the said privilege leave on account of sickness and that it should be granted to the staff members covered by the reference as follows: "1. Leave to the staff member covered by the references as at present completed years of service in a year with full pay and dearness allowance on completion of 11 months service in a particular year." The Tribunal held that the demand was unreasonable and unjustified because the company did not take into account any such provision in regard to privilege leave which was not available to the staff of the company at the time of their application for leave. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions made by the award in regard to the privilege leave were not arbitrary or unreasonable but were based upon the principles of fair play and justice. [300 F] (ii) The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to make an award having regard to the provisions of section 79 of the , and the effect of section 79 is to introduce standardisation in the matter of leave. [301 G] (iii) The Tribunal could not have made an award in regard thereto unless it was satisfied that the workmen concerned had been given an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to them. [302 A B] (iv) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to pass an award in respect of privilege leave. [304 C]
199: The respondent, a non resident person in the State of Mysore, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. He filed an application before the Income Tax Officer for assessment and collection of income tax and super tax on the ground that he had been assessed to income-tax in respect of the period from April 1, 1950 to March 31, 1951. The Income tax Officer rejected the application holding that the proviso to section 13 of the Indian Finance Act, 1950, which provided that income tax shall be payable by an assessee in respect of any chargeable accounting period ending on or before the 31st day of March, 1949, was not applicable to the case because the proviso was not applicable as it was not applicable when the assessment was made. The respondent 's appeal against the order of the Income tax Officer was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the proviso was ultra vires and void as it was enacted after the Constitution of India. On further appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the Explanation was intra vires and void. The High Court allowed the petition of the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The proviso is not unconstitutional as it is not inconsistent with article 277 of the Constitution. [539 D] (ii) The proviso does not affect the operation of the proviso. It merely provides that the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, shall apply only to cases where income has accrued or arisen in India during the previous year relevant to the assessment year ending on or after the 1st day of April, 1949. [540 E] (iii) The proviso applies only if the income has accrued in India during a particular year and not in the previous year. [541 F] (iv) The proviso cannot be read as an independent provision. It is not intended to operate retrospectively. It is only intended to provide that the provisions relating to income tax shall apply only in relation to those years. [542 B C] (v) The proviso must be construed as a whole and not in isolation. [543 A] (vi) The proviso would have no bearing on the interpretation of the proviso if it were held that the income of the respondent had accrued in India within the meaning of the proviso to the proviso

1984: The appellant company was a public limited 'company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. 2172: The appellants were vendees to the sale of their land which was the subject matter of the sale deed. The vendees had no share in the village from before and the land which they had purchased under the sale deed was the subjectmatter of the sale. The suit was filed on the basis of their being collaterals and co sharers and wanted that they should be given out of the land allotted to them in consolidation proceedings such land as they would be entitled to after pre emption of the sale in question. The trial court held that the suit was maintainable with respect to the land which had been obtained by the vendees during consolidation proceedings in lieu of the land which was subject matter of sale deed. On appeal, the High Court held that the land which has been sold was not a part of the land purchased by the vendee but was a part of his land which he had purchased under a sale deed. It therefore held that the plaintiffs respondents could not get any pre emption decree for pre emption. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit for pre emotion was not maintainable because the suit was not maintainable with respect thereto. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit is not maintainable in view of section 24 of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913. [819C] 2. The right of preemption is a right to acquire property and the right of pre emption arises only when the property is acquired by means of a contract between the parties. The right to acquire the property is not an absolute right. The right can be exercised at any time after the passing of the title. [820D E] 3. The right conferred by section 24 of Punjab Preferential and Resumption of Property Act, 1930 is a right of preemention. The right is not an empty formality. It is a substantive right. It is open to the preemptive right of pre-emption to take away the preemptician rights of preemption in favour of the vendee. [821F G] 4. The right under section 24 of Act is a right in rem and not a right in personam. The right in rem is a right which is not an indefeasible right.
5497: The petitioner, a member of the Indian National Congress (I) Party, was elected to the Presidentship of India in July, 1987. He filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election of the 528 President of India at the election held in July,1987 for electing the President of India and praying for a declaration that he is the successful candidate at that election. The petitioner contended that the election of Shri R. Krishna Iyer respondent No. 2 was void as he had not been duly nominated as a candidate at the election and that the nomination paper of the petitioner was improperly rejected by the Returning officer. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had failed to prove that he was duly nominated as the candidate at the poll and that the rejection of his nomination paper was improper. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner having failed to establish that he was validly nominated as a contesting candidate, the election of respondent No. 1 was void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner has failed to establish either that he was disqualified under section 14A or that he was not duly nominated as such. [530G] 2. The petitioner did not produce any evidence to show that he was qualified to be chosen to fill the seat. The petitioner merely produced some documents which were not proved before the Tribunal. The Tribunal found that the petitioner was duly nominated and that the election was properly conducted. [531C D] 3. The petitioner had not produced any evidence to establish that the nomination papers of the respondent No.1 were improperly rejected by him. The petitioner could have easily produced the relevant documents before the Tribunal to show that the nomination of the respondent was improperly accepted. [532E] 4. The petitioner was entitled to succeed on the ground that he was a duly nominated candidate. [533F] 5. The petitioner failed to establish any of the grounds mentioned in section 14 A of the Act. The petitioner 's failure to plead and prove that he had been duly nominated cannot be taken into account. [534B]
2946: The appellant was appointed on April 10, 1949, as Head Mistress of St. Aloysius Higher Secondary School, Urva, then in State of Madras. On June 1, 1955, the Manager of the school reduced her to the post of Assistant Teacher and directed the Management to reinstate her to the said post. But no effect was given to that order by the Management. On June 26, 1957, the appellant filed a suit for mandatory injunction directing the Management to revere the appellant 's service as Head Mistry. The trial Court held that the appellant was not bound by the Madras Elementary Education Act or the rules framed thereunder; that the Manager alone was responsible for the "efficiency, strength and progress" of the school and for internal discipline which were all matters left to his discretion and the management could not be compelled to reinstate the appellant as Head Master when she did not command their confidence. The District Court decreed the appellant ' s suit and issued a mandatory injunction directing its reinstatement as Head Master. In appeal the District Court reserved the Judgment passed by the Trial Court and decreed the appellant' s suit. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not entitled to claim reinstatement as Head Masters when she did neither command their confidence nor obeyed the orders passed by the manager. [880 E] (ii) The appellant had been working as an Assistant Teacher since the date of her appointment till the date of the suit. She was not entitled, therefore, to claim reinstatement. [881 C D] (iii) The appellant is not entitled to any relief against the Management. [882 F]
38: The appellant was a licensee of two petrol filling stations. He was convicted in each case on the 18th July, 1946, and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 30 on the first count. In the second case he was found guilty of the charges brought against him and sentenced to one week 's imprisonment in default. The appellant contended that the conviction was illegal as the appellant had not been charged with the offence under section 3(1)(a) of the ,and section 3(2) of the Act. Held, that the conviction could be set aside if it was based on the evidence which was admissible in law. The evidence which was led before the Magistrate was inadmissible because the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence of the witnesses examined by the prosecution did not establish that the appellant was carrying on business in petrol at various places. The evidence was insufficient to sustain his conviction. The evidence showed that the appellant had been carrying on business for several years and that he had issued instructions to the customers to stop the use of petrol. The evidence also established that the appellant used to carry on business in excess of the limit prescribed by the rules. The evidence did not establish the charge of criminal breach of trust or misappropriation.
6452: The appellant, a minority institution, applied for the post of lady Principal in the degree section of the college. She was selected and appointed as a teacher in the degree Section of the college on the recommendation of the Selection Committee. The appellant challenged the decision of the University by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the selection committee had no power to relax the qualifications prescribed by the University. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the College being a minority institution is not entitled to relaxation of qualification prescribed by the State Government. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have been invested with powers of judicial review under article 226 of the Constitu tion. [780C] 2.1. The High courts are empowered to exercise jurisdiction under article 226 only when there is an error apparent on the face of the record. [773D E] 2.2. The High court has got wide discretion in the matter of granting or refusing approval of the appointment of a teacher. It cannot be said that the High Court has exercised its jurisdiction in excess of its jurisdiction. [774E] 3.1. In the present case, the High Court rightly held that the Selection Committee was not justified in relaxing the qualification without reserving that fight to itself in the advertisement. [775F] 4.1. There is no merit in the contention that the College is a minority institution. The High Cour t erred in interfering with the decision of t he Selection Committee. [776A B]

4281: The appellant was the adopted son of one Mansaram. He executed a deed of adoption in favour of his mother, who was a minor at that time. The respondent filed a suit for declaration and injunction against the appellant on the ground that he was not in a fit state of mind when he executed the deed of adoption. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal the District Judge held that the adoption was valid and that the deed of the adoption was duly registered. The High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court 's judgment was erroneous because the adoption was not in accordance with law and the deed of adopting was not properly stamped. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the deed was not properly registered. [597 F] (2) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the courts below. [598 D] (3) The High court was wrong in its view that the deed did not contain any reference to the adoption of the appellant. The deed merely stated that the appellant was a minor. It is not clear from the record whether the appellant was actually a major or a minor at the time of execution of the deed. The deed does not mention about the adoption of any of the parties. The deed only states that the appellant 's father was a minor and that he would be able to give him a proper adoption. The deed also does not say that the appellant had been given a proper adoption by the guardian. [599 E G]
3193: The appellant and the respondents were candidates for the Safidon Assembly Constituency No. 30, two candidates having already withdrawn from the contest, the first respondent was declared elected on March 13, 1972. The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the first respondent on several grounds of corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123 of the Act. 3771: The respondents, Indian Goods Supplying Co., were imported by the Port Trust for home consumption in India. The first 2 consignments arrived on February 16, 1957. Suffice it to say that the Port Trust claimed demurrage for the period from March 25, 1957. The respondents disputed the right of the Port Trust to charge demurrage on the ground that the Port was not entitled to collect the demurrage levied on the respondents and that as they failed to pay the demurrement the Port Trust was entitled to sell the goods by public auction. The appellants contended that the Port trust had no authority to demand demurrage in respect of the period during which the goods were detained for analytical test certified by the Customs authorities. Held: (i) The Port Trust is not entitled to claim demurrage under section 3(1)(a) of the Bombay Port Trust Act, 1879. Section 3(1) (a) of that Act provides that if the owner or occupier of any land or building refuses to pay the amount payable by him under sub section (1), the Port Trust may recover such amount with interest thereon at 6 per cent per annum from the person who has illegally occupied the land or building. [639 E] (ii)The Port Trust is a statutory body constituted under the Bombay Port Trusts Act, 1879 and it is empowered to levy and collect demurrage charges. The Port Trust cannot be compelled to pay the same. The Port trust is not entitled either to collect the amount of demurrage or to recover it from the owners or occupiers of the land or buildings. The Port Trusts are not entitled to recover demurrage. The Ports are not entitled, therefore, to recover demu rrage. [640 F H; 641 A B]

[841G H]

4879: The appellants in the appeals were teachers in the service of the State of Punjab. 2301: The appellants, who were the owners of a suit land, leased it to a school for a period of three years. On September 9, 1924, a suit was filed by the appellants against the State of West Bengal and obtained an ex parte decree against them. On June 27, the State Government issued the notification under sec. 6 of the Land Acquisition Act in respect of the suit land. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification on the ground that the notification was mala fide and null and void as the State Government had not taken possession of the land before the notification was issued. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The notification under sec 4 is not a mere declaration but it is a final order passed after the notification under section 6 has been issued. [683C] (2) The notification does not make any mention of the land being transferred to the school or the school itself. It merely states that the land is transferred to the School or the school. It only refers to the transfer of the land to a school or the School. [685E] (4) The notification must be read as a whole and not in isolation. [686F]
940: The appellant company was incorporated in 1945 in the United State of Rajasthan. After the formation of the State of Rajasthan, there was no law in force in Kotah State. Till the formation of State of Rajasthan there was no such law in force. For the assessment year 1950 51, income tax was sought to be imposed in the State of Rajasth an area. The Indian Finance Act of 1950 made the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 applicable to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, and thereafter amended the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 by adding section 14(2)(c) as it stood before the amendment. The appellant contended that the exemption granted under section 14(1) (c) of the Indian Income 'tax Act, 1922, was not affected by the amendment of the said provision in 1953 even though the amendment was retrospective from April 1, 1950, unless the Finance Act, 1950, which applied the Income tax Act to this area was also amended. Held: (i) The exemption granted under the proviso to section 14(l)(c) of that Act is not affected by any amendment of the Act in 1953. The proviso to section14(1) of the Income tax, Act, 1922 is a substantive provision and does not affect the retrospective operation of the proviso. The proviso cannot be read as a substantive provision for granting exemption or exemption. The proviso must be read with the main provision and if so construed, it would be clear that the proviso applies only to cases where the income tax has been levied prior to April 1, 1951, but not prior to that date. (ii)The proviso to section 13(1)(c) is not intended to operate retrospectively. It merely provides that the income tax shall be deemed to have been validly levied on the income of the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1949 50.

26: The respondents were the tenants of a building in which the appellants were tenants. On the question whether the respondents had committed non payment of rent within the meaning of section 11(1) (a) of the Bihar Act, the High Court held that the respondents had not committed any default and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the Controller had no jurisdiction to decide whether or not there was non payment of arrears of rent. HELD : The High Court was right in its view that the Controller assumed jurisdiction under section 11(2)(b) of the Act when he assumed jurisdiction on being satisfied that there has been non payment of the rent for the month of March, 1947, and that the respondents could not be said to have committed non payment. [12 C D] The respondents were tenants of a house in which they were tenants. They paid rent for three months and thereafter defaulted in payment of rent for the whole month. The respondents did not pay the rent for three days as required by section 11(3) of the Rent Control Act. The respondents were therefore liable to eviction under section 12(5) of the U.P. Act. [13 E F] The respondents had not paid the rent for two months from April 1, 1947, but had paid only one month 's rent for the entire month.
