1696: The Bhopal Reclamation and Development of Lands (Eradication of Kans) Act, 1954 was enacted to provide for the improvement of the agricultural production in the State of Bhopal. Section 2(1)(c) defines "land" as meaning land which is used for agricultural purposes or is cultivated or owned by a person who owns or occupies it personally. Section 3 provides that the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare any area of the State as a "Kans infested area". Section 4 empowers the State Government to notify areas of the State to be "kans infest areas" and on such notification officers of the State were enabled to enter on the lands within the notified areas and conduct deep ploughing tractorisation operation with a view to eradicate the kans. The Act provided for the cost incurred in these eradication operations being recovered from the farmers on whose lands the tractorisation was effected. The Act also provided for the payment of charges claimed as due. Five of the farmers on whom the demands were made, filed petitions under article 226 before the Judicial Commissioner, Bhopal challenging the constitutionality of the Act as well as the legality of the levy, even assuming the law to be valid, and these petitions were allowed and the learned Judicial Commissioner held the Act to be unconstitutional and the levy illegal, granted the declaration and mandamus prayed for. The appellants then applied for and obtained certificates of fitness under article 133(1)(b) and (d) and have preferred the appeals which are now before us. The respondents contended that the Bhopal Reclamation & Development Act, 1954, was not applicable to the Bhopal area and that the Bhopal Act was not saved by article 31A of the Constitution. Held: (i) The Bhopal Act was a piece of colourable legislation and was not protected by article 31 A. (ii)The Bhopal Act was enacted to secure the protection of the rights conferred by articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution and was not intended to deprive the citizens of the rights guaranteed by article 31(2). (iii)The Bhopal State Act was not a law relating to agrarian reform but was a law relating only to agrlopents. The Bhopal Act did not fall within article 31A. (iv)
6210: The appellant, a Hindu widow of a Hindu male who died intestate on June 6, 1942, filed the present suit for possession of certain properties de fendants. HELD: (i) The right of the widow to adopt a daughter to her husband is revived by her remarriage. The widow cannot take advantage of the provisions of section 4(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. [880 A] (ii)The right of a widow to adopt is revive when there is nobody to continue the line. The widow can adopt only after her death. The adoption of the second defendant was not illegal or void. [881 B] (iii)The right to adopt is not revived merely because the widow has remarried. The widow may adopt a son or a daughter to the estate of her deceased father. But the widow cannot adopt a son except to the extent of her own life. [882 C] (iv)The right under section 4(2) (b) of the Act is revived when there is nothing to discontinue the devolution of the property of the widow. [883 D]

Examination from that college in Broad specialities and their ancillary discipline. (ii) Candidates who had graduation from other Municipal Institutions in the city of Bombay. In so far as it applied to the Government Medical College, the Maharashtra Government, by its resolution dated June 18 1960, decided that the Government Medical Colleges should be divided into two categories, namely, (1) those established by the Government Medical colleges in the city and (2) those established and maintained by the Government institutions in the city, and directed that the Government medical colleges should be divided on the basis of the number of seats available for the Government Medical college. The High court held that the Government of Maharashtra was not competent to make a reservation of seats for the Government medical college in the city because the Government Medical Medical College was established and maintained in the city itself and the Government Medical Degree College was established in the city alone. It also held that the reservation of seats made by the Government of Bombay Medical College could not be said to be discriminatory or unreasonable. The appellants challenged the validity of the rule in these appeals. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The Government Medical College is established and maintained and administered by the Government and the Government medical College is established in the City. The Government medical college is established and run and maintained by Government institutions in Greater Bombay. The Government of Bombay is the authority to grant permission to establish and maintain medical college in Greater Bombay and the Government of Maharashtrashtra is the authority empowered
2079: The appellants were convicted under section 353 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 4 months ' rigorous imprisonment. The High Court set aside their convictions and acquitted them. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Court erred in holding that the appellants had committed an offence under section 352 of the Indian penal code; (ii) the High court erred in holding the appellants guilty of the offences under sections 353 and 354 of the Indian IPC; and (iii) the High Courts judgment was not justified in convicting the appellants under section 355 of the Indian Code. HELD: (1) The High Court has rightly held that the appellants could be convicted under section 354 of the Code only if they had committed an act which was likely to cause hurt or grievous hurt to the person who gave the blow. [447 E] (a) There is no doubt that the appellants were convicted for the offence under section 354. [448 A B] (b) The High court was right in holding that there was no intention on the part of the appellants to commit the offence. [449 C] (c) The High Courts judgment does not suffer from any infirmity. [450 F] (d) The High courts judgment did not suffer from error of law. [451 D] (e) The High 'Court was wrong in holding that since the appellants had been convicted under section 357 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the sentence imposed upon them would be a term of imprisonment for life. [452 G]

In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the order was invalid as it did not comply with the provisions of r. 125 of the Defence of India Rules and (ii) the order had been passed in violation of the principles of natural justice. HELD : (i) The order was bad because it contravened the provisions of section 3(1)(a) of the . It was not necessary for the respondent to have been served with the notice of the order. 39: The appellant was a public servant and was charged with offences under sections 161, 165 of the Indian Penal Code and section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. He was arrested on the 27th of October 1947 and was granted bail by the Magistrate. On the 1st December, 1947, sanction was granted by the Provincial Government to prosecute him for an offence under section 161 of the Indian penal code. The appellant was produced before the Special Magis trate on the 28th of November, 1947, but was released on bail on the 26th of November. 1948. On the 31st January, 1949, the appellant was again taken into custody and was remanded to judicial custody till the 30th of November 1948. On his release on bail he was served with a notice to show cause why he should not be tried for an offence punishable under section 161 or 165 of the Penal Code. The appellant contended that the prosecution of the appellant was illegal because the warrant issued by the Magistrate on the 22nd of October, 1947, was invalid as it had been issued without the sanction of the Government. Held, that the proceedings against the appellant were illegal because the appellant was in police custody when he was arrested and was in police remand. The order of detention passed against him was illegal because he was in police lock up at the time when the warrant was issued. The fact that the appellant was arrested and released on bail did not make any difference because the arrest and detention of the appellant were made after the warrant was actually issued. The appellant could not be prosecuted for an offence which was committed within the jurisdiction of the Magistrate.
2511: The appellant was charged with offences under section 120B of the Indian Penal Code read with section 135 of the New Act and sections 23(IA) and 23 B of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. He pleaded that he had been falsely implicated in the case by the Customs authorities. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court on appeal reversed the order of acquittal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the statements recorded by the customs officers were inadmissible in evidence because they were not admissible in evidence; (ii) the statements were made by the accused persons to the customs officials who had recorded them; (iii) the statement was a voluntary one and was not hit by any of the provisions of section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code; (iv) the statements made by the appellant were inadmissible in view of the bar under section 25 of the Evidence Act; (v) the statements could not be used against the appellant as they were not relevant to the investigation conducted by the customs authorities; (vi) the statements given by the appellant to the customs authorities were inadmissible in law; (vii) the statements of the appellant were not admissible under section 25 Of the Evidence Act. HELD : (1) The statement of the appellant must be excluded from consideration in view of section 25 of Evidence Act. [701 E] (2) The statement is admissible in evidence only if it contains some material facts which are inconsistent with the statement made by the person making it. It cannot be used against another person unless he is proved to have made such statement before the police officer or other officers empowered under section 151 of the Criminal procedure Code. [702 A C] (3) Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act does not apply to the facts of the present case. The statement of an accused person recorded by the Customs Officers under section 107(8) of the , is admissible in the trial of an offence under section 120 B of the Indian IPC. [703 D]
5302: The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the sale deed executed by her mother was invalid and was not binding upon him and for recovery of possession. In appeal, the appellate court confirmed the decree and the High Court dismissed the appeal. In second appeal, the High Court reversed the Judgment of the District Judge and restored the order of the Subordinate Judge. In second appeals, the High Courts held that the question of improvements could be decided only after the decree had been passed in the first appeal and that the decree could not be executed without delivery of the property. In this appeal, by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the question whether the respondent had made any improvement or not was a mixed question of law and fact and therefore, the High court should have refused to grant certificate under section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the defendant has made any improvements or not is a mixed question which can be decided only by the executing court. [780C] 2.1. The question as to whether the defendant had made any improvements cannot be decided by the executing Court. [781D E] 2.2. The question of the defendant having made any improvements is a mixed issue of law and facts and the same cannot be decided in execution proceedings. [782F] 3.1. Section 20 of the code of Civil Procedure does not bar the jurisdiction of the executing court to decide the question of title. [783A B] 4. The question regarding the right of the plaintiff to seek delivery of the properties involved in the case is a mixed one. It is open to the plaintiff to raise such an objection before the executing court at the stage of execution. [784B C] 5.1. If the executing court finds that the decree is vitiated by fraud or collusion, then the executing court may pass appropriate orders according to law. [785E F] 6. The question about the validity of the sale deed is a mixed matter of law and factual dispute between the parties. [786G] 7.1. In the instant case, the trial court had decreed the suit for a declaratory decree declaring that the sale transaction was void and not binding upon
6345: The appellants who were duly elected Directors of the respondent No. 3, a Cooperative Society registered under the Maharashtra Co operative Societies Act 1960, filed a requisition dated 5.9.89 to call a special meeting of the Committee of the Karkhana for con sideration of the proposed motion of no confidence against the Chairman of the Committee, Dattatraya Waman Patil, respond ent No. 1 and the said requisition was signed by more than 1/3rd of the total members of the Committee in accordance with the provision of Clause (2) of Section 73 ID of the Maharashtra Cooperative Socie ties Act 1960. On 6.9.1989 the respondent No 3 issued a notice convening a special meeting on 25.9. 1989 to discuss the proposed motion for no confidence against him as Chairman of the Managing Committee of the respondent Society. Over and above a copy of the notice was sent to the office of the Joint Director of Sugar and Joint Registrar, Cooperative Societies, Maharashtra State, Pune as by way of this notice, the Managing Director had been directed to produce the minute book of the Committee meeting and hand over possession thereof to the Presiding Officer at the commencement of the special meet ing. On 18.9.1990 the respondent No 2 issued a notice calling upon the appellants to convene a special meeting for discussing the proposed motion. The appellants challenged the notice dated 18.9,1989 before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the requisition notice dated 5. 9.1989 was not valid and it was invalid. Hence this appeal by Special Leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Section 73 ICCA are mandatory and non compliance thereof would vitiate the entire proceedings. [490E] 1.2 The requirement of the proviso to sub section (2) is that the notice must be given in writing to the person concerned or to his authorised representative. In the instant case, the notice was given to the respondent No 1 and not to the appellants. Therefore, the requirements of the proviso have not been complied with. [491F G] 1.3 The requirement of giving a notice in writing to any person is mandatory and noncompliance thereof would render the notice invalid. [492G]
6683: The appellant was a Customs Officer in the Customs Department. He was charged with offences punishable under the provisions of the Gold Control Act, 1968 and the Gold Control Rules, 1968. After examination of the prosecution witnesses and recording of the statements of the accused under section 342 of the old Code of Criminal Procedure (corresponding to Section 540 of the old code) he filed two applications both the cases under Section 540 and 311 of the new Code for recalling Mr. Mirchandani for further examination and issuing summons to two more witnesses. The learned Judicial Magistrate rejected both the applications on the ground that the application made by the appellant was not maintainable as it was barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the revision petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that the appellant had been convicted for offences punishable under Sections 120B, 420, 468 and 471 IPC and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay fine of Rs.100/-, the order of conviction and sentence passed against him is set aside. [639E] 2.2 It is true that the appellant has been acquitted of all the charges levelled against him but the acquittal of the other accused cannot be said to have been reversed merely because another person has been acquitted. The acquittal of the appellant can only be set aside if there are two views possible on the evidence available on record. [637F G] 3.1 In the instant case, the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. The trial court and the High Court were justified in rejecting the applications of the appellant. [638A B] 3.2 The appellant was entitled to an opportunity to cross examine the prosecution witnesses or to produce any other witness in his defence. The prosecution was also entitled to rely upon the documents which were produced by the prosecution during the course of the trial. [634C D] 3.3 The appellant was not entitled to any such opportunity. [635D] 4.1 The appellant was rightly held guilty of the offence under Section 120B, 467 and 471 I.P.C. and was rightly convicted and sentenced. [636G]

5318: The appellant company was incorporated in the United Kingdom under the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947. It had a business connection with the Indian Company and its non resident companies in Group B. The Indian Company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957-58 on the basis that it was an agent of the non resident company in India in respect of goods sold by it to customers in India. The Income Tax Officer held that the non resident companies were not agents of the nonresident companies in India and that the Indian Company was entitled to the benefit of section 90(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Indian company was not liable to pay income tax on the sale proceeds received by it from the non resident persons in India. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner. In reference, the High Court held that the assessee was not liable for payment of income tax on sales made by the non resident parties in India. In the appeals before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the Tribunal was right in holding that the nonresidents were not agents within the meaning of section 163 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and that the Tribunal erred in holding that any profit could be deemed to accrue or arise in India to the non resident applicants in India. 653: The appellant was a company incorporated in 1934 and was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. In 1947, the appellant obtained an order for compulsory winding up of the Company under section 3 (1) (b) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The liquidator obtained sanction of the Court to lease out the Mills with all the lands, factory and residential buildings and machineries etc. The terms and conditions of the lease were that the appellant would be put into possession of the leased properties in a proper working order and would work and run the factory without any interference or obstruction by or on behalf of the lessor and would appropriate the entire income and profit thereof and the lessor would have no concern with profit or loss made by the lessee in running the factory without interference or obstruction. The appellant was not to be in any way liable or responsible for any of the liabi lities of the Company or of the liquidator or of the out going lessees or any of the persons who had been working from before except the employees who were mentioned in Cl. 11 of the lease and the appellant also agreed not to retrench any staff already employed at that date in the Factory. The appellant, however, was not bound to employ any or all of the employees of the Company as mentioned in cl. 11 of its lease. The appellant contended that the terms and conditions contained in the lease deed were not binding upon it and that the appellant was not entitled to any compensation for the breach of the covenant. Held: (i) The appellant was entitled to recover damages for breach of the covenants of the lease deed executed between the parties. (ii)The appellant was not liable to pay any compensation to the workmen for breach of any covenant of the lease. (iii)The appellant could not claim any compensation for breach of contract. (iv)The appellant had not committed any breach of the terms of the lease agreement. (v)The appellant did not commit breach of the condition of the lease as provided in the lease agreement and therefore the appellant was liable to pay damages for breach.

The impugned provision is not discriminatory nor is it intended to offset the inequality between the cooked meal and the cooked eating houses. [523A] 1.5. The impugned Section is not discriminatory because it imposes a tax burden but is merely a measure imposing an evil element. [526F] 1.8. The impugned notification is not discriminatory. [527G] 1.9. The impugned clause is not discriminatory since it imposes a burden on the consumers of Cooked food. The impugned proviso is not discriminatory and is not intended to off set the cookery industry at the cost of the cookeries. [528H; 529A] 1:1. 1385: The appellants filed a complaint in the court of the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta against four persons, alleging that they had been guilty of offences under section 120B read with section 420 I.P.C., and that they were not guilty of any offence under section 409 I.P,.C. The complaint was dismissed by the Chief Presidency magistrate on July 8, 1954. On April 3, 1959, the appellants applied to the High Court for a certificate under article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution but such a certificate was refused by a Bench of the Calcutta High Court on July 8. The present appeal is directed against the order refusing to grant the certificate. The question for decision is whether the second complaint can be entertained by a Magistrate who or whose predecessor had, on the same facts, dismissed a previous complaint under section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the second complaint cannot be entertained by the Magistrate who or whom or whose predecessor has, on the earlier occasion, dismissed a complaint under section 204 of the Code. The first complaint was made on March 17, 1955, and was dismissed on July 8 and the second complaint was made after the dismissal of the first complaint. The second complaint was not maintainable as it was barred by limitation. It was not necessary for the complainant to file a fresh complaint because the cause of action arose on the date when the first complaint was filed.
4865: The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court set aside the acquittal of the appellant but confirmed the conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The evidence of the eye witnesses is not reliable. The High 'Court has rightly relied on the evidence of the two eye witnesses. [862B] (2) The High Court has given good reasons for accepting the evidence of these two eye witnesses in preference to that of the other two eye witnesses who were examined by the prosecution. [863C] (3) The High ' Court has also given good reasons why the evidence of two eye witnesses should be discarded. [864A] (4) The High court has rightly held that the evidence of a single witness cannot be accepted as trustworthy. [865D] (5) The High. Court has rightly relied upon the evidence of P.W. 2, the brother of the deceased. He is an independent witness. His evidence does not suffer from any infirmity. [866E]
4832: The appellants were students of the State Government and were selected by the Selection Committee. The selection was made on the basis of a test conducted by the State Government. The appellants challenged the selection on the ground that the selection was arbitrary, discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the selection could not be said to have been made in violation of the principles of natural justice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the selection was vitiated because: (a) the State Government had failed to provide for the constitution of a committee; (b) the selection of books for general reading was arbitrary and discriminatory; and (c) the selection is vitiated due to mala fides. HELD : (1) The selection of books is based on the principle of "lifting" and "initiation", as explained in the case of State of Punjab vs Gurdial Singh , and the selection of the books for general teaching purposes cannot be said to be arbitrary or discriminatory. [330 G] (2) The selection must be made on the recommendation of a committee consisting of experts in the field. The selection can be made only after such an enquiry as may be considered necessary. The selection should not be unfair or biased. It is open to the State Government to make a rule prescribing the qualifications or eligibility criteria subject to which candidates are called for interviews. If there is any discrimination in the selection by the selection committee, the mere fact that some other person has been selected does not entitle the candidate who is selected to be included in the selection list. [334 E F] (3) The selection is solely based upon the interview. There is no question of malice or arbitrariness in the selection. [335 A B] (4) The selection has to be made on objectively assessing of the circumstances in which the candidate was found to have secured the highest marks at the examination. The selection board has to satisfy itself that the candidate was entitled to be selected. [336 C D] (5) The selection committee has to apply its mind independently to the relevant materials before it and determine whether the selection is to be made. The selection committee must also consider the relative merits of the candidates

1487: The assessee Company purchased sugarcane from the sugarcane growers and crashes them in its factory to prepare sugar. The Sugar Mills entered into an agreement with the sugarcane growers, who are known locally as "Oppigddars" and advances them sugarcane seedlings, fertilisers and also cash. The agreements take place at the harvest season each year, in preparation for the next crop. In 1948 49 due to drought, the assessee Company could not work its sugar mills and the Oppig ors enter into a written agreement called the "Opposite Agreement", by which they agreed to sell sugarcane exclusively to the assessee Company at current market rates and to have the advances adjusted towards price of sugarcane, agreeing to pay interest in the meantime. For this purpose, an account of each Opposingdar was opened. By the agreement, the assessee company agreed to pay interest on the amount advanced to it under the agreement. The Sugar Mill was taken over by the Government and the assessee Company paid the amount advanced under the agreement to the Sugarcane growers. The Sugar Factories were closed down and the Sugar Mills were re-instated. The Sugar Factory was closed down and there was no dispute between the parties. The Sugar Industries were closed down. The Sugar Industry was closed down. In the assessment order dated March 31, 1956, the Income tax Officer held that the sum of Rs. 2,87,422/was a loss of capital. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to deduction under section 10(3) (xi) and 10(2). 4851: The respondent was employed as a driver by the appellant. He was paid Rs.1,000 per month and Rs.2,000 per annum in lieu of the salary payable to him. The respondent claimed that he had been paid Rs.5,000 per year as salary and Rs.10,000 per day as additional remuneration for his services. The appellant denied the claim on the ground that the respondent had not been paid Rs,5,000 as salary. The respondent contended that the term 'wages ' is wide enough to include any payment to an employee in respect of any period of authorised leave, lock out, strike which is not illegal or lay off and other additional remuneration, if any, paid at intervals not exceeding two months. The appellant contended that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the definition of 'wages' in section 2(22) of the , and that the respondent could not be said to have been paid Rs.,5,000 in respect of the period of his employment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of 'Wages ' in section 2 (22) of 'the Act includes remuneration paid or payable to an employee under the terms of the contract of employment express or implied. [780G] 2. The definition is comprehensive enough to cover all payments made to an employee during the course of his employment, but it does not include any contribution paid by the employer to any pension fund or provident fund or under the Act, any travelling allowance or the value of any ticket or permit to be used for any purpose other than those specified in the definition. The respondent was paid Rs, 5,000 per quarter as salary and the amount of Rs. 10,000 per week as extra remuneration for his service. The respondent cannot be said to be paid Rs. 5,000 in view of the definition. The respondent would be entitled to the additional remuneration, even though he may not have been paid the same. [782C D] 4. The definition does not include anything paid to an employee who is required to work in the night shift. It is only such employees who are required to work during the night shift

5358: The petitioners, who were members of the Administrative Tribunal, were appointed as Chairman and Vice Chair man and administrative members of the Tribunal. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the petitioners that they had a valid legal right to continue as Chairman and members of the Tribunals until the disposal of their cases by the Tribunal and also held that the Tribunal was not bound to grant extension of time for the Tribunal to dispose of the cases pending before it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal has power to extend the period of extension of time granted by it to make selections to the posts of Chairman and Vice chairs of the Tribunal during the pendency of the proceedings before it. [766A] 2. The Tribunal is not bound to accept the recommendations made by the Selection Committee or the Selection Board unless it is satisfied that there are sufficient reasons for doing so. It is open to the Government to consider the recommendation of the Selection Committee and the Selection Board and take appropriate decision after considering all relevant aspects. [767B] 3. The Tribunal cannot sit in judgment over the opinion expressed by the Selection Com mittee and substitute its own opinion for that of the Selection Committ ee. [768C] 4. The Tribunal can only examine whether the Selection Commi ttee has taken into account any extraneous factors or whether it has ignored the relevant considerations and if it finds that the selection has been vitiated by some illegality, it would certainly set aside the selection. [769D] 5. The Tribunal could not have substituted its opinion merely because another view was possible. [770E] 6. The Tribunal was not justified in interfering with the observations made by the High Court. [771F] 7. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the findings of fact recorded by the Selection Board. [772G]

The petitioner filed a suit against the Bank for recovery of certain dues from it on the ground that the Bank had contravened the provisions of article 19 (1) (f) and (g), and that the sale was void as being in contravention of article 19(1)(f). The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The petitioner 's right to freeUGUST trade guaranteed by article 19 (I) (f), is not absolute and the restrictions imposed by article 19(2) are reasonable. The restriction must be reasonable if it is calculated to prevent the person affected from exercising his right or carrying it out. [539 B C] The object of the article is to protect the citizens against arbitrary action by the State. It is not intended to protect any citizen against the State action which may be taken by the State in its discretion. The protection given by article 19 is not limited by the terms of article 19. But the restrictions imposed on the exercise of the right conferred by article 19 are reasonable in the interest of the general public. [540 D E] The right to carry on business cannot be considered to be an essential part of the freedom guaranteed by article19 (1) and (2). The restrictions imposed by the article are reasonable only if they are reasonable in their nature and extent. [541 F] The right of freeUGUST is not absolute. The restrictions imposed are reasonable in its nature and extent; they are reasonable only when they are calculated to prevent acts which would be injurious to the community. [542 A B]

The company contended that the policy was not liable to be deducted under the provisions of the Act, because, (i) the policy was a contract between the company and its employees; (ii) the policy did not cover the risk of fire insurance; (iii) the policy being a contract between an insurer and his employee was not covered by the Act; and (iv) the policy having expired before the policy could be taken into operation, the company was entitled to deduct the amount of premium from the profits of the year. 6018: The respondent was promoted to the post of Deputy Engineer in the Gujarat State Electricity Board. 5892: The All India Entrance Examination was conducted by the Central Board of Secondary Education in respect of 15 per cent of the total number of MBBS/BDS seats in medical colleges of different States. 3044: The appellants in the appeals were candidates for admission to the Integrated M.B.B.S. Course in Government Medical College, Guntur, Andhra Pradesh. They applied for admission to that course and appeared at the entrance test held by the State Public Service Commission. The results of the examination were declared on June 23, 1970. The appellants were not selected because they did not pass the qualifying examination. On June 23,1970, the Government issued G.O. No. 1.648/Health dated July 23, 1970 as also under G.O., No. 1793/Health, dated September 23, 1970 regarding reservation of seats for Socially and Educationally Backward Classes of students, having regard to the recommendations made by the Andhra Pradesh Backward Classes Commission. The appellants challenged the validity of the said G.Os. before the High Court contending that the Government had no power to issue such a notification since it was not a rule or order made by the Government before the finalisation and communication of the selection of candidates. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the Government could not issue a notification under section 3(1) of the Act after the finalisation of the selection process. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Government has no power to make any rules or orders which are contrary to the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. [847 E] (ii) The Government cannot issue a notification in exercise of its powers under section 3 of the Act. It is only when the Government makes an order under section 3 that it can be published in the Gazette. But there is nothing in the Act or the Rules framed there under which the Government can issue a notification to the effect that the Government can do so without making any provision in that behalf. [846 F H] (iii) The Government can issue the notification under section 4 of the Act only if it is satisfied with respect to any particular class of persons who are eligible for admission to a course or training in a professional college. The Government can also issue a notification specifying the classes or categories of persons who may be admitted to a course of study or training in the professional colleges. [849 A B]
6924: The respondent was a licensee under the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949. He was manufacturing and selling country liquor in the State of Gujarat. The High Court held that the State had no privilege in regard to the manufacture or sale of potable alcohol and that the State could not impose any tax on the manufacture or sales of potable alcoholic liquor by the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The State has no privilege in respect of potable liquor. [875C] (2) The State can regulate and ensure that non potable alcohol is not diverted and misappropriated. The State can also regulate and ensure the maintenance of such revenue as it likes. [876D] (3) The State cannot levy excise duty on potable alcohol which is unfit for human consumption as no levy can be made by a State either under Entry 8 of List II of the VIIth Schedule read with entry 66 of List I of VIIth Schedule. [877E] (4) The State Government may grant licences to distilleries for the manufacture of potable liquors. But the State Government cannot charge excise duty on such liquor. [887B] (5) The State is entitled to regulate and maintain the price at which potable liquor is sold. [886G]

1969: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. It had a branch office in Calcutta and its head office at Calcutta. In the year 1948, it entered into an agreement with the respondent for the sale of certain businesses of the appellant company. The agreement provided that the sale price would be Rupees thirty four lakhs ninty nine thousand and three hundred and ninety eight rupees. The respondent agreed to sell all the business of the appellant on the basis of the said agreement. The relevant portion of the agreement is as follows: "The Vendors agree to sell and the Company has agreed to purchase all the business including the benefit and advantage of all contracts. The purchaser agrees to purchase all such business together with all goodwill attached to the business or in any way used in the same including the benefit of all contracts." The respondent purchased the business from the appellant company for Rs. 2,50,000. The respondent claimed that the sale consideration was not taxable under the Indian Incometax Act. The Income tax Officer held that the sale was not taxable because the sale was made by the appellant company to the respondent and that the respondent was entitled to the exemption under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the transaction was not taxable. He also held that the profit was not assessable. On reference, the High Court held that the respondent could not claim the benefit of section 10(1) (xv). In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the respondent had no business connection with the business of sale of the goods sold by it to the appellant company and that the sale proceeds were liable to be taxed under section 10 (1) (xi) of the Income tax Act. [613 D E] The respondent was a firm carrying on the business of selling the goods manufactured by the appellant. The respondent had no concern with the business carried on by the firm. The respondent was not a mere agent of the firm. It was merely acting as a commission agent. The respondent did not have any concern with the firm. [614 F G]

The Sessions court has not taken this aspect into account. [748 A B] 3.1 The Sessions Judge has committed an error in convicting and sentencing the appellant under Section 304 Part II I. P. C. P., but the High Court did not consider the evidence on the record in its proper perspective. [750 F] 4.1 The High Court was wrong in reversing the conviction of the appellant under s.302 I. P, C. 1940: The authorised capital of the Company was Rupees fifty lakhs divided into 50,000 ordinary shares of Rs. 100/ each. By the end of April, 1946, the company was able to find subscribers for 4,860 shares only. In view of section 277(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, the company decided that they or their nominees would subscribe for a large number of shares. In order to comply with the requirements of section 276(1), the directors of the Company decided that they and their nominees would raise loans from the Bank of Poona Ltd., to the extent of Rs. 60,000. The directors also sanctioned a loan of Rs. 30,000 to Ramnath. On May 28, 1946, Ramnath obtained from the Company the loan of Rs, 60,000 in favour of Ramnath. The loan of Rs,. 60,000 was not paid by Ramnath to the Bank of the Bank of Pune. On May 29, 1946, a cheque for Rs. 15,000 drawn on the Bank of Bombay, was issued by the Bank of India in favour of the Bank. The cheque was dishonoured on May 29, 1947. On May 30, 1947, the bank of Poona, filed a suit against the Bank of Maharashtra for recovery of its dues. The Bank of Poonam Ltd. contended that the suit was barred by limitation as it had been instituted after the expiry of three years from the date of the loan. Held: (i) The suit was within time. (ii)The suit was barred under section 277 of the Indian Contract Act. (iii)The suit is barred by limitation. (iv)The suit has been filed beyond three years from May 28, 1947, when the loan was taken by the Bank. (v)The suit having been filed beyond the period of limitation, the suit was bad for want of notice under section 276 of the Indian Act. (vi)The suit being barred by limitation, the Court could not entertain it. (vii)The suit must be held to have been filed within three years from 5th May, 1947, and the suit was within limitation.
2436: The plaintiff Bank advanced a sum of Rs. 11,723.56 nP on the guarantee of defendant No. 2 to the plaintiff for Rs. 11.723.57 nP on account of principal and interest thereon two days after demand. The surety agreed to pay and satisfy the liabilities of the principal debtor upo Rs. 12,000/ and interest thereon three days after demand but not later than six months from the date of the suit. The surety was discharged by the creditor in spite of demands. The surety became a guarantor and the principal debtor had no right to restrain execution against him until the creditor exhausted his remedies against the principal debtor. The surety failed to discharge the liability of the principal and the creditor obtained a decree against the principal. The surety died on September 30, 1951. On October 1, 1952, the creditor filed a suit against the principal for recovery of the amount due under the bond. The defence of the principal was that the debt was payable by the principal debtor to the creditor and the creditor could not enforce its dues against the principal borrower. The creditor resisted the suit contending that the debt had become payable by the creditor because the principal debtor was solvent and the creditor had no right or claim against the principal and that the creditor had waived the right of the creditor to enforce its dues. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal the High Court held that the debt did not become payable by reason of the fact that the creditor was solvent or that the creditor might have relief against the principal, and that the debt could be enforced only against the principal if he had discharged his liability. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that (i) the creditor had the right to enforce its debts against the principal; (ii) the creditor could enforce its dues only against the creditor; (iii) the creditor was entitled to enforce its liability against the principal as well as against the principal in some other proceedings; and (iv) the creditor 's remedy was barred by limitation. HELD : (i) The creditor was entitled only to enforce its rights against the principal but not against the principal who was not a party to the suit. 5332: The respondent was an Inspector General of Police, Haryana. He was the Inspector General of Policeconduct and was duly authorised by the State Government to write confidential reports assessing the performances, character and conduct and qualities of the respondent as Inspector General of police, Haryana. After such acceptance, the adverse remarks were communicated to him about two years after the close of the relevant period of March 31, 1980. The respondent did not make any representation against the adverse remarks nor made a representation against the said adverse remarks. Instead, he chose to file a writ petition before the Punjab & Haryana High Court challenging the authority of the Home Secretary to write a confidential report assessing the performance of the respondent for the aforesaid period during which he was the Inspector general of Police, Punjab. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding inter alia that the Home Secretary had no authority to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the respondent for his failure to discharge duties in time and that the State Government was justified in making rules under section 3 of the Act. In appeal, the Division Bench set aside the judgment of the Single Judge and allowed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Home Secretary is specifically empowered by the State to write confidential report assessing his performance, character and personality of the respondent. [1035E] 1.2 The Home Secretary has no authority to give any report against the performance of an officer during the period when he was the inspector General of Police. [1036F] 1.3 The Home Secretary being the competent authority under the Rules, he could have written confidential reports only if he was authorized by the State government to do so. But the Home Secretary having no authority to delegate the same to any other person, the Home Secretary cannot be held to have acted contrary to the Rules. [1037A B] 1.4 The Home Secretary having been empowered by the Central Government to write the confidential report assessing performance of an employee, it must be presumed that he had the power to write the same. [1038C D] 1.5 The Home Secretary cannot delegate the same powers to another person. [1039D] 1.6 The Home Secretary can exercise all the powers conferred on him by the Rules

The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the State Government 's Order No. 643 HTE dated July 25 1969. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the constitutional point which arises for consideration in this case relates to interpretation of section 133(2) (b) of the Constitution and that the Public Service Commission for the State of Jammu and Kashmir, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, has been consulted in accordance with its requirement. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The constitutional question whether the Public Service commission for the State is bound to consult the Public Service Commissiion before making any selection or appointment to a civil service or post under the State or the Union, depends upon the language of the provision contained in article 16(4) of the constitution. [739E] 2.1. The expression "the Commission shall be consulted" in clause (a) of sub section (2) of section 133 of the Constitution means the Commission or the Governor acting on his own discretion; and the word "shall" used in the said clause does not mean the Commission or a Governor acting on their own discretion. It only means the Commission. The Commission must have the power to make recommendations to the Governor for appointment of the persons to the civil services and posts. The Commission can also recommend the names of candidates from the list prepared by the Commission for consultation with the Governor. [741A] 3.1. Article 320(3)(c) of the Constitu tion provides that the Governor shall act in his discretion. The Governor shall act on the advice of the Commission. He cannot act in his own discretion. [742C] 4.1. Under article 309 of the Constitution the Governor is required to consult the Commission. This consultation is necessary when there are
725: The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that she was the owner of the lands in dispute and that she had passed to Sahib Singh 's mother, Kishen Kaur 's sister, as the heir of her father. The Tehsildar entered the respondent 's name as the owner of these lands. On appeal by the appellant, the Collector of Amritsar directed the name of the respondent to be removed and the appellant 's name to be entered in its place. On June 11, 1945, the respondent filed a civil suit against the appellants seeking a declaration that he was the owner in possession of the lands. In paragraph 3 of the plaint it was stated that the respondent ' s wife was entitled to the properties under the general custom of the family of her father and that she was entitled to inherit the property left by her father. In paragraph 5 it was stated " According to the general custom, the right of inheritance of the daughter and her descendants and in their absence that of the collaterals beyond the fifth degree; no matter whether the land is ancestral qua reversionary heirs or it is self acquired. " The defence taken in the written statement was that the respondent as the agnatic relation or collateral of Sahib Singh was entitled to his properties under the custom of the Punjab in preference to the respondent. The trial court held that the respondent was the heir of the deceased father and that the appellant was the nearest heir of the father. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The respondent was not entitled to the property under the general customs of the Punjab. The respondent was entitled to succeed to the properties left by her husband. [880 E] (2) The respondent being the nearest heir to the estate of the deceased, the appellant was entitled to claim the properties under his special custom. [881 G] (3) The respondent could not be said to have been excluded from the property under section 8(2)(b) of the Punjab Regulation 1 of 1827. [882 A B] (4) The respondent had not been able to prove that the appellant had any title to the properties. [883 C D] (5) The respondent did not claim any right to the properties on the basis of
4121: The respondent was the landlord of a suit premises. He had paid the arrears of rent and an agreement to pay the same within one month from the date of receipt of the notice. On the failure of the tenant to comply with the terms of the agreement, the respondent served a notice on the appellant demanding him to pay the arrears of the rent. The appellant tendered the amount demanded by the respondent but the respondent did not accept it and instead instituted the suit for damages and eviction. The trial court held that the arrears of arrears were in arrears and therefore, no ground for eviction had been made out under section 3(a) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act No. III of 1947. The appellate court confirmed this finding. In second appeal, the High Court held that the respondent 's defence was bona fide and that the arrears claimed were not in arrears. The High Court also held that the appellant was entitled to recover the arrears of Rs. 75 only as arrears of rent. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the respondent was entitled to the protection of section 3(1)(b) of the Act. [880C] The respondent was entitled only to the benefit of section 3 (1) (b). The respondent was not entitled to the benefit under section 3 (2) of the said Act. [881D] The respondent 's case was that the arrears were in arrear. The respondent ' could not be allowed to take advantage of his own wrong. [883E] The respondent had not pleaded that he was entitled to any relief under section 3 of the Act because the arrears were not in arrear. [884A] The respondent could not claim any relief under the Act because he was not entitled under section 3 to the benefit thereof. [885B]
6979: The appellants filed an application under section 145 of the Code before the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Sadabad in which they claimed ownership of the suit property. On 31st May 1976, the learned Magistrate passed a preliminary order under Section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code directing that the attachment would continue till the competent civil court determined the rights of the parties with regard to the said property. Against this order, the appellants filed a revision before the Sessions Judge who by his order dated 18th August 1977 stayed the order of attachment and directed the police to restore the possession of the appellants from whom allegedly the possession was taken. The appellants thereafter filed a suit for permanent injunction against the 1st respondent and her husband and in that claim an interim injunction against them. The trial court dismissed the application for interim injunction but on appeal, the District Court allowed the appeal and issued an interim injunction restraining the appellants from alienating or disposing of the suit land. In the Revision Petition filed by the appellants before the Sessions judge, the High Court held that the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and that the order of the Magistrate revived. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the civil courts is barred in respect of any matter relating to immovable property. [575C] 1.2 The jurisdiction of a civil court is barred in case of any dispute between the parties relating to title to the property. [567E] 1.3 The jurisdiction of civil courts is not barred in case the dispute between the appellant and the respondent is purely civil in nature. [568A] 1.4 If the dispute between two private persons is purely civil one, the civil court has no jurisdiction to decide the same. [569B] 1.5 The jurisdiction of criminal courts is barred when there is a specific provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which makes it clear that the jurisdiction of civil Courts is barred in cases where the dispute involves complicated question of law and fact. [570D] 1.6 The jurisdiction of Civil Courts is barred when the dispute involves questions of fact and law. 87: The plaintiff, who was the daughter of a Hindu undivided family, filed a suit for partition against the defendants. The defendants contended that the family of the defendants consisted of a joint Hindu family and that the family had no separate property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the family was not a joint Hindu Family and that the properties were not ancestral properties and that the suit was not maintainable as a suit for joint possession. HELD : (i) The family of the parties consists of a single member of a family and the other members of the family are entitled to share in the properties which belonged to them jointly. The family is a joint family and the members of the joint family are entitled only to the benefit of the family 's self acquired property. [880 D] (ii) The family has no separate property and the family cannot be said to have been separate from its members. [881 C] (iii) The family was not joint with the other members and the family was merely a camouflage for the family. The family was joint with the others. The family had no independent right or interest in the properties of the family. [882 E] (iv) The family had a common ancestor and the other coparceners were also entitled to share. The family could not claim any share in the property of the family because the family was joint. [883 F] (v) The family did not own any property in the hands of the other coparcener. The family continued to be joint even after the death of the father of the plaintiff. The family never possessed any property in its own hands. [884 G] (vi) The family being joint, the family was entitled to share only in the properties owned by it. [885 A] (vii) The family continued as a joint family even after the demise of the father. The family did continue to be joint till the death of one of the coparceners. [886 B] (viii) The family, therefore, was not joint till the time of the death of its father. [887 C]
931: The respondent firm carrying on tannery business at Chromepet near the city of Madras, was assessed to sales tax under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the assessment order on the ground that the order was illegal and not supported by the authority of law. This contention was accepted by the High Court and the petition was allowed with costs. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the respondent firm was liable to pay sales tax in respect of hides and skins which were sold by it to its customers in the State of Madras and that the imposition of the sales tax after the repeal of the rule was illegal and invalid as it had been made without the authority of the law. HELD : (i) The liability to pay sales-tax in respect of the transactions of sale of hides or skins is not an independent liability of the dealer but of the State. It is only when the State Government makes a declaration under section 5(1)(vi) of the Act that the liability to pay the tax arises. [447 E] (ii) The liability of the respondent firm to pay sales Tax in respect of its dealings in hides and kins cannot be said to have been imposed by the State Government under section 5 (1)(vi). The State Government has no power to impose such a tax. [448 F]
1225: The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of a aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and stores at Ranchi. After the works were completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and ultimately by an agreement dated February 6, 1948, they were referred to arbitration of one Col. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents filed objections under sections 17 and 20 of the . The appellant contended that there was no valid agreement of reference to arbitration in terms of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and that the award was not binding on the Government. Held: (i) The provisions of section 175 of the Government Of India Act, 1915, are mandatory and not merely directory. Section 175(1) of the , which is in the matter of referring to arbitration does not require that there should be an arbitration agreement between the parties. It only requires that the agreement must be in writing signed by the parties or otherwise held to be duly stamped. The words "in writing" in section 175(2) do not mean that the agreement should be in writing but must be accompanied by a certificate from the Registrar of Coooperative Societies certifying that the agreement has been registered. The certificate must be in the prescribed form and must contain the name of the person signing it. The certificate may be either general or special. In the present case, the certificate did not specify the date on which the agreement was registered. The agreement was therefore not in writing. (ii)The provisions of section 176(3) are mandatory and cannot be waived. The agreement must be registered. The provisions of sections 175(3), 176(4) and 176(5) are mandatory. The agreement being in writing, it is not necessary that the document must be in such form as the rules prescribe. The agreement need not be in writing. 447: The appellant, a registered body under the Indian Trade Unions Act, gave a notice to the respondent of its intention to establish a new market. The respondent replied that the appellant had no right to the land and that the market was not a part of the land. The respondent thereupon filed a suit for declaration that the appellant was entitled to the land on the terms of the agreement dated March 31, 1937, and for a decree for possession of the land in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 3(a) of the Control Act because the appellant did not have any right to the property in question. [880 D] (ii) The appellant could not be said to have acquired any title to the land in question. The appellant was merely a licensee and not a lessee. The appellant had no title to the property. [881 E] (iii) The appellant had not been able to prove that the land was a part of a larger area of land than what was originally allotted to it. [882 F] (iv) The appellant has not been able even to show that the land in suit was a part or parcel of the larger area of the land allotted to it as a result of the agreement exhibit D 5. [883 A B]
6063: The appellants are manufacturers of 'Supercem Water proof Cement Paint ' and other allied products in their factory at Madras. They manufacture and market the product throughout India. It is stated that the appellants were a small manufacturing firm with no branches and/or sales offices in any other State, city or town. In these circumstances an agreement for sale described as an 'agreement of sale' was entered into with Gillanders. The appellants by their letters dated 23rd April, 1979 and 15th May, 1980 to the Excise authorities claimed a refund of Rs.2,39,153.63 on account of excess excise duty paid on the assessable value on the basis of price at which the Gillandars had sold the goods to its customers during the period July, 1977 to March, 1979. Both the Assistant Collector and the Tribunal rejected the contention of the appellants and held that the assessable value was the price at which Gillands had sold the products to its customers, during the period 7th July, 1977, to March, 1978. The Tribunal also referred to clause (a) of Section 2(1) of the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 which defines "article" to mean any article used or capable of being used for human consumption. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the appellants had not produced any evidence to show that the goods manufactured by them were sold by them to the customers. The Tribunal held that the appellants could not be said to have sold the goods without the aid of the agreement. The Tribunal further observed that the appellants did not produce any evidence to prove that they had sold the product to the customers and therefore, the Tribunal held that it was not an agreement for sole selling agency. The Tribunal accordingly dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly come to the conclusion, that the true character of the agreement was that it was an agreement for the sole selling agency and not an agreement to sell. [790C] 2. The definition of "articles" given by the Central Excis e Board in the Central Excise & Salt Act is not exhaustive but only illustrative. The word "article", in the context of the definition
2435: The petitioner was detained under section 3(3) of the Bombay Police Act, 1951. He challenged his detention on the ground that he had been deprived of his right to make a representation against his detention. The District Magistrate held that there was no delay in sending the report and therefore the order of detention was illegal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the delay in sending a copy of the report was not fatal to the case of the detaining authority because the delay was due to causes not of his making but of causing some damage to his reputation. HELD: (1) The delay in sending an order of detention is not fatal to any proceedings before a court of law unless the delay is explained by showing sufficient cause which is due to causes beyond the control of the person concerned. [1036 E] (2) The object of section 8 of the Act is to prevent vagrancy and destitution. It provides that where the period of detention exceeds one year, the State Government may direct the detaining authority to send the communication to the detenu within that period. The words "forthwith" are used in the first proviso to sub section (3) of section 8. The word "forth with" means "instead of" or "outside", and the word "detention" means "to be done after the expiry of the period of one year". [1037 C D] (3) The expression "forthwidth" has been used in the second proviso to sub sections (3) and (4) of section 7 of the Act. The word 'forthwith' is used in the third proviso to sub sec. (3) to sub section 1 of section 7. The wording of the proviso clearly shows that the time limit prescribed therein is not mandatory but directory. [1038 H; 1039 A B] (4) The fact that the District Magistrate sent the communication to him does not mean that the District magistrate did not take into consideration the period of time spent in communicating the grounds of detention. 3489: The respondent, a displaced person, filed an application under section 7 of the , for fixation of standard rent. The Estate Officer passed an order on September 28, 1960, fixing the standard rent in respect of the respondent 's premises. The respondent challenged the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition and the respondent could not be permitted to recover the amount in arrears from the appellant. HELD : (i) Section 7 does not bar the remedy of recovery of rent or damages in respect of public premises as arrears of land revenue. It is only where the arrears are disputed by the respondent that the question of limitation would arise. [892B] (ii) The High Court was wrong in holding that the amount in question could not be recovered under section 7 because the time for instituting a suit to recover the sum had expired. [893C] (iii) The High court was right in its conclusion that the amount was due within three years from the date of the order of eviction. [894D]
1145: The appellant was a cotton textile mill situated in Bombay. It had made losses from 1950 to 1955 and the appellant applied for an award under section 114(2) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, before the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Bombay, in respect of bonus for the years 1952 and 1953. The Tribunal passed an award on March 13, 1956, directing that the award be enforced against the appellant. Thereafter the Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh wrote to the Government of Bombay requesting that the award should be enforced against it. Thereafter the appellant applied to the Government for enforcement of its award. The Government refused to enforce the award as it was not enforceable as an award by the Industrial Court. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the award. The High Court held that the award was not enforceable and directed the Government to enforce the same. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award is not enforceable as a decree passed by the Industrial court. [411 D] (ii) The award does not create any right or liability in favour of the appellant. The award merely declares that the appellant will pay bonus for the year 1952 and also for the years 1954 to 1957. The award only directs payment of bonus for those years. The award does nothing more than directing payment of bonus. [412 E F] (iii) The award cannot be challenged on the ground that it has been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation. The award is therefore void. [413 G H] (iv) The award can be enforced only against the appellant and not against the appellant as the award itself provides for payment of bonus to the employees. [414 A B]

The cotton was ginned and pressed by the respondent, the ginning process was used in the manufacture of cotton textiles while the cotton seeds were sold by it. During the assessment period from April 1, 1956 to March 31, 1956, it purchased unginted cotton worth Rs 5,93.266/from unregistered dealers and pay tax on the unginned goods purchased by it. The respondent applied for refund of the purchase tax paid on the un-ginned cotton under the Bombay Sales tax (Exemption, Set off and Composition) Rules, 1954. The respondent filed a revision before the Gujarat Sales Tax Tribunal. The Tribunal rejected the revision on the ground: "the purpose underlying the applicant 's purchases was primarily the production of ginned cotton for manufacture."
