The respondent could not be said to have produced any material to justify its claim that the cotton seed purchased by it was intended for use in the manufacture or production of cotton seeds. [702 D E] The respondent was entitled to the refund of the amount paid by it as purchase tax under the Bombay sales Tax Act, 1954. [703 F G] The respondent cannot be said to
3786: The appellant was appointed as a Subordinate Judge in 1935. He joined the erstwhile State of Manipur as a junior clerk in 1935. After the Government of India took over the administration of Manipur, he was appointed as the Judge of that subordinate court from that date. On the enactment of the Manipur Court Act 1955, the Court of Subordinate Judge was abolished and the appellant was appointed to the post of the Judge of the District Court. The appellant was served with notice dated 30 June 1966 that he was required to retire from Government service with effect from 1 October 1966 in pursuance of the direc tions of the President in Paragraph 6 of the Government of Indi a Decision No. 23 below Fundamental Rule 56. The appellant filed the writ petition challenging the order of compulsory retirement on the ground that the impugned order of compulsory ret irement was null and void because the Fundamental Rule 56 at the material time contained no provision for the retention of an officer who had completed years ' qualifying service. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The impugned order of compulsorily reti rment is not invalid because it does not contain any provision for retention of an employee after attaining the age of 55 years. [439 E] (2) The rule does not say that the appointing authority can retain an officer who has completed years' qualifying service even if he has been promoted or appointed to a higher post before attaining the age. It merely says that the appointing authorit y may permit him to continue in service beyond the age of 50 years. This rule cannot be read as enabling the appointing authority to withhold the pension of an officer whose services have been terminated on account of his being found unsuitable for the purpose of employment in the public interest. [440 F H] (3) The rule is intended to prevent the arbitrary exercise of power conferred upon the appointing authority by Article 311 of the Constitution. It is not meant to punish a person who is merely trying to get away by invoking the rule. [441 G] (4) The rule contemplates that the appointing autho rity should take into consideration the conduct of the officer during the period of his service and determine whether the said conduct of the government servant has become good or not. If the said conduct is good
3266: The appellant company was carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In the year 1959, the assessee entered into a contract with M/s. Lachhminarain Kenoria & Co., to sell the aforesaid quantities of TDS and corn sacks. The contracts were entered into between the parties. On June 18, 1958, the assessee had contracted to purchase bales of B Twill and 2500 bales of corn sack. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534/ to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions involving mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods were of a speculative character as contemplated in explanation to section 24(1) and the loss could be set off only against speculation profits, and as there were no speculation profits in that year he held that the loss would be carried forward and set off against speculation profit in the future. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal by the assessee held that the transaction involving mere transfer was not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court. The Tribunal relied on two decisions in D. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income Tax, West Bengal (1), and D. Wadi Ram vs Commissioner of Incometax, West Bengal(2). The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transactions were not speculative because they involved mere transfer of the goods and not actual sale thereof; that the transaction was not speculation but was an ordinary commercial transaction and therefore the loss could not be set off against the speculation profits under section 24(2)(a); that the transaction did not involve any speculation but only a transfer of the property in the goods and therefore the losses could not be allowed to be set off under section 24 (1) and (2); that the transactions amounted to speculation and were therefore not covered by Explanation 2 to section 24 (2) and therefore the provisions of section 24(3) were not attracted; and
5384: The appellant was appointed as Chairman of the Board of School Education, Haryana, on 10 12 1985. At that time he resigned his post as Professor Director, Punjabi University Regional Centre, Bhakra, Chandigarh. His resignation letter dated 11th December 1985 was accepted by the Government and he joined the Board on 11th December, 1985. He resigned from the post of Professor Director, P.S.E.B., Chandigarh on 11th January 1986. His writ petition challenging the order of appointment of the appellant to the post of Chairman of the board was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the appellant had a better service record than the respondent and his services were not terminated at any point of time; (2) the respondent had been given an opportunity to improve his performance and if he failed to do so, he would have been discharged from service; (3) the respondent was entitled to continue in service till the age of 60 years and the appellant could not be denied the benefit of extension of service; (4) the respondent having been appointed as Chairman, he ceased to hold office after his tenure expired. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant has no right to continue in the post of the Chairman of the Haryana Board of School Educa tion, which is a statutory body constituted under the Haryana Board 's Act, 1969. [5G] 2. The appellant cannot claim to be continued in the post for the period of two years from the date he took over charge of the post. [6H] 3. The appellant had been appointed as the Chairman of a Board of School Ed uation, Haryana, in place of the Chairman. He resurveyed his position and assumed the charge of the Chairman on 11th February 1986. He resiled from the same and did not join the Board. He was not entitled to continue beyond the said period. [7A B]
5431: The appellant, a tenant of a building in a town, filed an application under section 18(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for payment of interest on the amount awarded by the Land Acquisition Collector. The Land Acquisition Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant had not been able to prove his case and accordingly he was directed to pay interest at the rate of 12% per annum from the date when possession was taken till the date of payment. The appellant 's appeal before the District Judge was dismissed. In second appeal, the High Court held that the application was barred by limitation and as it was not made within three years from the date of the award, the application was time barred. On appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 23(1) are mandatory and not directory. [1048C] 2. Section 23(1), which is a part of the Act, makes it clear that the Act does not make any provision for payment of compensation or interest on the land acquired. It only provides that the provisions of the Act shall be applicable to all acquisitions of immovable property. [1049E] 3. The question whether the application of section 23 (1) of Land Acquisition Act is intended to exclude the application of this general rule in the matter of payment of interest arises only if the statute expressly so provides. [1050F] 4. The expression "the Act" used in section 23(2) of the Act means the Act itself. The word "shall" in section 23 (2) of Land Acquisi tion Act, 1894 has been used in the sense of giving a right to file objections to the award. The word 'may' in section 23 of the Land Acqui sition Act, 1894 means "shall". [1051G H] 5. The word `may' in the context of section 23 of Land Acquisition act, 1894 means `shall'. [1052A] 6. The wording of section 23 shows that the Act applies to all acquisition proceedings. The Act does not contain any provision for interest on the compensation awarded. The Act is silent about the mode of computation of the interest. The Act also does not contain a provision for payment or adjustment of the
4401: The appellant was a District Judge. He had been trying to get the respondent dismissed from his court. The appellant filed a petition under section 19(1) of the , for the issue of a warrant against him. The High Court issued notice to the appellant and the Judge, who was directed to take the appellant in custody but the appellant did not turn up. The appellant 's version is like this: On the previous date of hearing, the Judge asked the appellant to pay fresh process fee and supply the address of the respondent to the Rent Court. The appellant told the Judge that he would be taking action under Order 9 Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code. The Judge also made a reference to the High Court of Himachal Pradesh under section 15(2) of the . The High Court passed an order directing the appellant to deposit the process fee and to supply the address to the respondent. The appellant then moved the High Court under section 15 (2) of . The High court issued notice to him intimating the Judge that the appellant was unable to comply with the order because the respondent had been admitted to a hospital and had since left the hospital. The appellant did not dispute the High Court that he had not paid the process fee. The appellant pleaded that the Judge had no jurisdiction to pass any order under section 19 of the . On the question whether the High Court could have entertained a petition under article 226 of the Constitution, HELD : The High Court should have considered the matter on merits. [739 E] The High Court has rightly held that the High Court was wrong in issuing notice to the respondent under section 19 (1) of . It is true that the High court may entertain a petition under Article 226 of the constitution if it finds that there is a patent lack of jurisdiction or other defect which goes to the root of the matter. But the High Court cannot exercise its power under article 226 when it comes to consider the legality of the order passed by the subordinate court. [740 F H] In the present case, the High Court ought to have taken into consideration the fact that the appellant had not paid process fee and supplied the address of respondent to the respondent and therefore the High Court should not have entertained the petition under article 227. [741 A B]
1251: The appellants were the members of a body of proprietors of a village. The property in suit was in the estate known as 'Bargad, Tehsil and District Rohtak. The appellants filed their objections to the notice issued under section 7 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance No. XXVII of 1949, stating that the appellants were in unauthorised possession of the house in dispute up to July 1947. The Deputy Custodian passed an order declaring the house to be evacuee property. The appellants challenged this order by filing a revision before the Custodian General. The Additional Custodian rejected the objection raised by the appellants and declared the house to vest in the appellants. The Custodian General held that the provisions of the Administration Act had been complied with throughout and that the house in question vested in the appellants as tenants. The appellants then moved the High Court for quashing the orders of the Custodian General on the ground that the Deputy Custodian had no jurisdiction to pass the order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the provisions contained in the Administration of the Evacuee Property Act, 1950 (Act XXXI of 1950), had not been complied with. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The order of the Custodian was correct. The appellants did not raise any contention that the Deputy Collector or the Custodian had no power to make the order. [205 D] The Deputy Custodian had jurisdiction to decide whether the property in suit belonged to the appellants or not. He could only decide whether the house in suit was evacuee property. [206 G] The Deputy Collector had jurisdiction to determine whether the house was evacuee property within the meaning of the Administration Of Evacuee Property Act. The Deputy Collector could not go behind the order of the Deputy Custodian. [207 H] The Deputy Commissioner had jurisdiction to enquire into the question whether the house belonged to the appellant or not. The Deputy Commissioner could not go into the question as to whether the house belongs to the appellant. [208 A B] The Deputy Director of Evacuee Property had jurisdiction to inquire whether the house is evacuee property. It was open to him to decide whether it was evacuee property or not. [209 C] The Deputy Commis sioner had jurisdiction to investigate the question whether it was an evacuee property. He could also enquire whether the house had been allotted to the appellant
6183: The plaintiffs filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 15.40 lacs claimed as their dues from the owners of the vessel, which was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs on 6.4.1989. On 10.8.1988, objection was raised by the plaintiffs to reception in evidence of the depositions of the defendants witnesses examined on commission on the ground of absence of witness ' signature on the deposition; the objec tion was upheld by the learned single Judge as also by a Division Bench in a Letters Patent Appeal. The suit was decreed on 6.6.1989 on the unrebutted evidence of the plaintiffs. In the meantime, one of the plaintiffs died while another was alleged to be critically ill and the vessel continued to be detained at the Calcutta Port even after the owners had furnished security demanded from them by interim orders in the suit. Even at the risk of this description being labelled as oversimplification, this was the scenario of the forensic battle in which the point raised has to be decided. The plaintiffs filed an application before the High Court under Order VI Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint. The High Court allowed the application holding that the amendment sought was not necessary since the question of jurisdiction was involved and the issue was not relevant. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The amendment is not intended to change the nature or character of the suit. [193C] 1.2 The amendment does not amount to changing the nature or substance of the case nor does it amount to any addition or subtraction to the original pleadings. [191E] 1.3 The amendment is only clarificatory in nature. It does not amount merely to adding or subtract ing new facts or events. [192F] 1.4 The amendment does neither alter the nature or the character of the case so as to bring it within the scope of the trial. [190G] 1.5 The amendment does nothing more than add or subtrash anything else. [194H] 1.6 The amendment does no more than add, transpose or add to the original pleading. [1904A] 1.7
2148: The Assam Primary Education Act, 1947 was repealed by the Assam Elementary Education Act, 1954. Section 3 of the Act provided for a State Advisory Board for Basic Education which was to be constituted in each district and the State Government was empowered to constitute a State Advisory Committee for the purpose of making grants to schools under section 10. The State Government appointed a Committee to advise the State Government on matters relating to the control and management of elementary education. The Committee submitted its report to the State Government and the State Govt. made rules for the constitution of a State Advisory Council. The State Advisory Board was constituted under section 10 of the Act. The State Govt. also made rules for selection of teachers of elementary schools. The State Legislature passed an Act known as the Assam Elementary School (Regulation) Act, 1953. Under section 3 of the said Act the State Government may, by notification in the official gazette, make rules for regulating the conditions of service of teachers of primary schools. The Rules framed by the State Government were published in the Gazette. The Rules were published in a Gazette. The appellants contended that the rules were ultra vires the powers of the State Government under article 309 of the Constitution and were therefore invalid. Held: (i) The rules framed by the Governor under section 3 of Act No. 1 of 1951 are valid. (ii)The rules framed by a State Government are not ultra vires the power of the State Legislature under article 309. (iii)The rules are not ultra virus the power of Parliament under article 246(4). (iv)The rules have been validly made by the State Legislature. (v)The rules cannot be challenged on the ground that they are ultra vires the provisions of the Constitution. (vi)The rules can be challenged only on the grounds mentioned in section 3 of The Act. (vii)The rules do not contravene the provisions of section 3 of Bihar Act No. XXXI of 1962. (viii)The rules could not be challenged on any other ground. (ix)The rules were not ultra vires. (x)The rules had no force of law. (xi)The rules did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution because they were made after the coming into force of the Constitution Act. (xii)The rules having been made after the Constitution Act

3522: The appellants were convicted under section 7(1) read with section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250 each. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence to one year R.I. The appellants filed special leave petitions in this Court against their convictions. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 342 Cr. P.C., are mandatory and not directory. [741D] 2. The provisions contained in section 342 Cr, P.C. do not require that there should be an oral statement by the accused before the court that he has committed any offence punishable under the Act or that he is guilty of any other offence. It is only when such oral statement is made by the accused that the court can proceed to convict him on the basis of such oral evidence. [742E F] 3. In the instant case, the prosecution had led sufficient evidence to prove that the appellants had committed offences punishable under sections 7(1), 8(2) and 16(1A) of the Act read with sections 7(i) and 16 (1)(a). The trial Magistrate was right in convicting the appellants under section 7 (1) and 16 of the Act. [743B C] 4. Section 16(1) provides that if the court is satisfied that it is necessary for the ends of justice to hold a trial, it may take cognizance of any offence without the accused being committed to it for trial. The court is empowered to take cognizance of an offence after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed therefor. [744F G] 5. The provisions relating to the procedure of the court have been incorporated in section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The procedure laid down therein is substantially similar to the procedure laid down in section 342. [745G] 6. 231: The appellant, who was the adopted son of a Hindu, instituted a suit for partition claiming half share in the family properties. He claimed that he had become a preferential heir to the property of his father and that the properties were set out in Schedules A and B to the plaint. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the adoption of Devji was not valid and that the plaintiff 's claim was barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court held that the adoption was not valid because the adoption was made after the death of Devji and that the suit was within time. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the adoption having been made before the death of the adoptive father, the adoption was invalid as it was made after his death and that the adoption must be deemed to have been made before his death. HELD : (i) The adoption is voidable under section 16 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Section 16(1)(c) provides that if a male Hindu dies after the commencement of this Act, any property inherited by him from his adoptive father after the commencement Of the Act shall devolve on his widow, son or daughter (whether married or unadopted), if such widow has left no child or children, and on her death the property shall devolve firstly upon the heirs, then upon the heirs; then upon the surviving relatives specified in clauses (a) to (g). [901 G] (ii) The adoption of the appellant was not valid since the adoption was after the death and the appellant had not taken steps to bring his case within the mischief of section 16(1) (c) of the Act. [902 D] (iii) The adoption was not invalid merely because the adoption took place after the death. [903 C] (iv) The adoption being voidable under s.16(1)(d) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the adoption would be valid even though the adoption was subsequently found to be valid. [904 E]

245: The petitioners were the Rulers of certain Indian States. They entered into a covenant on 18th March 1948, which brought them to the notice of the Government of India and the Government of the Dominion of India. On 13th March 1948 the Ruler of the erstwhile State of Vindhya Pradesh granted the villages Rigwara to the petitioners and on 28th January 1948 the Ruler executed a covenant on the terms that the grants made by the Ruler before the integration would be respected. In pursuance of this agreement the Government of Indian issued a notification dated 7th December 1948, under section 3(1) of the . By this notification the grants in question were declared to have been made by the Government of Vindhy Pradesh for the purposes of the Vindhya State. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was ultra vires the powers of the Government as well as the Central Government. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. The rights conferred by the covenant could not be enforced against the Government of a foreign country. The rights of the petitioners were governed by the covenants of the V.P. and the agreements of the Villaqs entered into by the parties. The Vadaqs were not new States but were merged in the Indian Union. The Vasias were not new units. The Varsha was not new States. The Vasaas were not older States. The petitioners had no right to claim the rights of the Vasias. The Vapals were not new territories. The Vodka-Sidhri (Vidyadhar) was not a part of the Indian Union and therefore the Vasia was not a new State.
2027: The workmen of the company were employed in the factory of the appellant company. They claimed that they should be given a fixed age of retirement at 60 years and that their age should also be increased to 55 years. The company contended that the age of retirement should be fixed at 60 years for all workmen. The company further contended that the workmen should be given the benefit of the same age of retirement as the existing workmen. The tribunal held that the age was 55 years but it did not fix any age of retirement for clerical and subordinate staff, and that the company had no power to alter the age of superannuation at 55 years. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The age of retirement is fixed at 55 years for clerical and sub staff and it cannot be altered except with the consent of the company. [526 E] (2) It is not correct to say that the age fixed for clerical and Subordinate staff should be 58 years. The age of superannuation of the head office and factory workmen is fixed at 60. But the company has no power to change the age of the clerical and subordinate employees from 55 to 55. [527 F] (3) The company has no right to alter the terms of employment of its employees. [528 A]
3351: The respondent was a broker of foreign machinery parts. He had agreed to purchase certain goods from the appellant and had also given him a receipt for the same. The appellant, who was a broker, had entrusted the said documents to the respondent. The respondent did not supply the goods to the appellant as he was not in a position to arrange for the same at the time when the goods were purchased. The respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 420 read with section 511 Indian Penal Code alleging that the appellant had committed an offence punishable under section 420 I.P.C. The trial court convicted the appellant under sections 420 and 471 Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal the High Court acquitted the appellant but on revision it set aside the conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the charge under section 420 was not framed against the appellant because the appellant had not been charged under section 420, I.P., Code; (ii) the charge was vague and the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. HELD : (1) The charge under section 417 is not vague. It is a question of fact which has to be decided on the facts of each case. [279 B] (2) The charge was vague. The evidence showed that the appellant was a broker and he had entrusted the documents to the accused. There was no reason why the appellant should have been charged under sections 420, and 471 I.P, Code. [280 C D] (3) The charge could not be held to be vague if it was based upon the evidence of the witnesses examined by the prosecution. [290 E] (4) The charge must be read as a whole and the statement of the accused recorded under section 313 Cr. P.C. cannot be treated as substantive evidence. [291 F] (5) The charge can be struck down only on the ground that the accused has not been prejudiced. [292 G H]
317: The appellant was a practising advocate. He had been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for five years by the Additional Sessions Judge, Madras, on the file of the Additional First Class Magistrate 's Court at Masaulipatam. On appeal, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of all the accused including the appellant. The appellant contended that the High Court could not have passed an order staying the realisation of the fine under section 12(1) of the Act. Held, that the High court could not pass any order staying the realization of the fine in view of the provisions of section 12(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The words "in the opinion of the High Court" mean that the Court has to consider whether it is necessary or expedient to do so. The word "may" means "shall". The word "shall" means "may be directed to be done." The word "discretion" means "the discretion of the Court to act according to law". The word 'discretiveness ' means "liberty to follow". The word does not include the liberty of the person to move the Court either directly or indirectly. The word 'fraudulently ' means that there must be some element of abuse of power or fraud or gross negligence of justice in performance of duty or actuate or indifference to the performance of duty. The word is used in the sense of compulsion. It means doing something wrong or adopting an act contrary to law or equity which another person would not do. In the present case, the High court was right in holding that the appellant was guilty of criminal contempt.
3956: The appellant was a Research scholar and he had been arrested on the night of 31st March 1967. The High Court set aside the order of the Sessions Judge and directed the trial court to frame charges against the accused under section 120 B read with sections 406 and 420 Indian Penal Code. 6920: The respondent purchased one acre land in T.S. No. 981, Block No. 34 of Waitair Ward, Vishakapatnam for a housing scheme. The Collector awarded at Rs. 1.58 per sq. yard and on reference the Civil Court enhanced the compensation to Rs. 10 per sq. Yard. On appeal and cross appeals the High Court confirmed the award and dis missed the appeal as well as cross objections for enhancement. Two contentions were raised by Shri Narsimhachari, learned counsel for the appellant. Under exhibit B. 6 dated August 3, 1961; under exhibit B 7 dated Sept. 5, 1961; the respondent purchased one2000 sq. yards in each document in the same T.S., He sold one2000 sq yo. under exhibit B 8 dated January 24, 1961. Therefore, the aforesaid sale deeds, exhibit B 6, B 7, B 8 and B 10 will reflect the correct market value of the land in question. The Trial Court and the High Court committed grave error in placing reliance on a decision of the High Court in A.S.No. 1008, Block No, 39, Waitair Beach Road which was acquired under a notifica tion dated March 19, for the purpose of Caltex Oil Refinery. The price fixed therein does not reflect the correct Market Value while the bona fide sale deed of pur chase and sale by the respondents relating to the acquired land are available on records and form the correct market price. The courts below committed grave error of law in completely ignoring the fact that the respondent purchased the land in T S. No. 39, Waitingair Ward, vishakapattam for a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/- and paid the entire amount of compensation. The High Court committed serious error in fixing the market value of land in question at Rs. 10,000/ per sq. yd. In view of the above discussion, the appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree of the High court are set aside. No costs.

5745: The Rajasthan Public Service Commission (Promotion by Competitive Examination) Rules, 1962 were amended in the year 1973 and the amended rules provided that the candidates for selection to Administrative Service, the Police Service and the Forest Service of the State should secure a minimum of 33% marks in the viva voce test. In the year 1976, the Rajasthan Public Service Commissiion was constituted under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution and the Rajasthan Public Services Commission was constituted under Rule 3 of the said Rules. The Rajasthan Public Services Commis sion framed its own rules known as the Rajasthan Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964. Rule 2(a) defines "Board" to mean the Board of Revenue, Rajasthan. Rule 4 provides that the Board shall prepare a list of candidates selected for appointment to the posts of Assistant Engineers and Executive Engineers in the service. Rule 5 provides that the list shall be prepared on the basis of merit and suitability with due regard to seniority. Rule 6 provides that the names of the candidates included in the list shall not be forwarded to the Board unless they are considered unfit for such appointment or unless their services have been terminated. Rule 7 provides that the select list shall contain the names of candidates who have qualified for appointment to all the three services. Rule 8 provides that the number of candidates to be recruited by direct recruitment shall be equal to the number of vacancies advertised. Rule 9 provides that the candidates selected for direct recruitment shall also be required to undergo a training for a period of two years. Rule 10 provides that the candidate selected for appointment shall be required to pass the examination within the prescribed chances subject to the provisions of the rules. Rule 11 provides that the successful candidates will be appointed to the post of Assistant Engineer and Executive Engineer in the service on the result of which they would be confirmed. Rule 12 provides that the probationers will be confirmed on completion of the period of probation. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to exemption only if the appellant was manufacturing Vanaspares and not a new industrial unit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The appellant was not manufacturing Vanasspares but was manufacturing the same. The appellant was manufacturing the Vanaspathi and was selling the same. 4551: The appellant was a Judge of the High Court of Bombay. He was appointed Chief Justice of that High Court and his term expired on May 4, 1956. On October 27, 1956, the Central Government issued an order appointing Bombay to be the principal seat of the High court for the new State of Bombay with effect from November 1, 1956. By another order dated May 4, 1957, the Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court directed that the Judges and Division Courts of the Bombay State shall also sit at Aurangabad with effect from August 27, 1956. The appellant challenged the validity of this order by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court struck down the order as invalid because it did not comply with the provisions of section 51(1) of the States Reorganization Act, 1956, which provided that the Judges or Division Courts of a High Court shall also sit with effect from the appointed day. The appellant contended that the Chief Justice had no power to issue the notification under sub section (3) of section 51 of the Act and that the Chief justice had no authority to issue such a notification. Held: (i) The Chief Justice could not issue the notification in question because he was not competent to issue it. (ii)The Chief Justice had jurisdiction to issue the notifications under section 51(2) of the Act. (iii)The Chief justice had the power to issue a notification under section 51 of Act. (iv)The Chief Judge had no power either to issue a general notification or to issue any other notification. (v)The Chief judge had no power merely to issue a special notification but he had only the power to direct that the Judges of the High Courts should sit at Aurangabad and that the Judges should sit at Bombay. (vi)The Chief Justices were competent to issue the orders of the Chief Justice under section 51 (1) of Act. [660 E F]
1208: The appellant filed a suit for injunction against the Municipal Committee, Khandwa, and obtained an ex parte decree. The Municipal Committee appealed to the High Court which set aside the decree on the ground that the tax was not validly imposed by the Municipal Committee. The Judicial Committee held that the tax could be validly levied only from the date of its imposition and not from the date when it came into force. The appellant then applied for a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. The High Court granted the certificate but refused to grant it on the ground: (i) that the tax had been lawfully imposed by the Municipality; (ii) that the validity of the tax could not be challenged in any court except by way of appeal or revision; and (iii) that the appellant had failed to establish that the tax imposed by the municipality was illegal or ultra vires. Held, that the High Court erred in holding that the tax did not become invalid because the tax was no longer valid as it was not validly levied by the Municipal committee. The tax was not legally imposed by the municipal committee but was imposed by the State Government. The tax being a tax on trade, it was not necessary to prove that it was not passed by the municipality. The tax must be deemed to have been lawfully imposed from the date on which it comes into force.

The petitioners contended that the provisions of clause (3) of Article 372 of the Constitution were not applicable to the present case because the said clause did not apply to the present cases. The petitioners also contended that the impugned clause (5), which provided for the absorption of the petitioners in service after the formation of the State of A.P., was ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioners' contention that the provisions contained in clause (3), namely, clause (5); and clause (5A) are ultra vires the constitution is without substance. [888F G] 7. 5814: The petitioners, who belong to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) on the basis of a competitive examination held by the DDA. The petitioners were not given any opportunity to be heard before their services were regularised. The petitioners challenged the regularisation of the service of the petitioners on the ground that they had been discriminated against inasmuch as they were denied an opportunity to appear at the examination held by DDA. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the petitioners were entitled to be considered for regularisation. Hence this appeal by special leave. The petitioners have no right to claim regularisation of their services. [326E] 1.3. The petitioners cannot be said to be similarly situated as the petitioners in the Writ Petition. [327F] 1.4. The petitioners do not fall within the category of persons who are entitled to regularisation. [328G] 1.5. The petitioners will be entitled to be treated as regular employees from the date of their initial appointment. [329A] 1.6. The petitioners would be entitled to all benefits available to regular employees from 1st January, 1986. [330B] 1.7. The petitioners shall be entitled to the benefit of the regularisation of their service from the date they became eligible for regularisation. [331C] 1st.7. 4741: The petitioners in these writ petitions are agents for the sale of lottery tickets of other States in Maharashtra. They challenge the ban on the sale of lotteries organised by the Government of India or the Government of a State in Maharashtra. The Press release is as follows: "The Government of Maharashtra has made a condition that the lottery tickets of all States shall be sold within the State of Maharashtra without the express consent of the State Government. No such permission has been given in Maharashtra for the sale outside the State ofMaharashtra without the express approval of the State of Bombay. The Government of Maharashtra, in giving permission for the sale in Maharashtra of lottery tickets in respect of the lotteries organized by the Government, has imposed a ban on the selling of lottery tickets outside the State. The ban is not applicable to the lottery tickets sold outside the State and the State Government has no authority to impose any such ban. The ban does not apply to lottery tickets sold in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The ban also does not apply in respect of lottery tickets sold inside the State. It is further contended that the ban is illegal because the ban is not limited to the sale of the lottery tickets but it applies only to the sale in the State. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The ban imposed by the Government is not confined to the sale outside Maharashtra State alone but extends to the sale at the State level. [447C] 2. The ban cannot be extended to the sale inside the State of Karnataka. The ban can be extended to other States also. [448E] 3. The ban under Article 303(2) is not applicable in the State where the ban is imposed. [441D E] 4. The ban may be imposed by the State Government in exercise of its power under Section 3 of the Act. But the ban should not extend to the sale within the State. [443F] 5. The ban will operate only if there is no prohibition in law. [442G]
4976: The petitioner was a member of the Rajasthan Judicial Service. He retired as a Judge of the High Court on July 21, 1984 and his pension was fixed at Rs. 15,320 per annum. His pension was revised to Rs. 11,500 per annum with effect from July 1, 1975. The petitioner 's pension was also revised to Rs, 12,000 per annum with retrospective effect from July 31, 1977. The petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 13243 of 1983 in this Court challenging the revision of his pension by the State Government. The petition was allowed by a Division Bench of the High court on March 4, 1986. In the writ petition, the petitioner contended that the revision of pension should be made effective from July 1 , 1974, when he had been appointed a Judge of a High Court, and not from August 1, 1973 when he retired. The High Court held that the revision should be made applicable from July 1. 1975, and that the petitioner would have retired on July 31, 1979. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The revision of pension is not permissible under Article 235 of the Constitution of India. [612E] 2. The revision cannot be made retrospectively from July 1., 1975. [613F] 3. The petitioner has already retired from service on July 31 , 1978. The petitioner will therefore be entitled to the benefit of the revision of the pension payable to him from July 1,. 1975. [661G]
3344: The appellant, a State Transport Undertaking, applied for a stage carriage permit on the route from Tuticorin to Chennai. The application was rejected by the Regional Transport Authority, Madras, on the ground that the appellant 's application was not accompanied by a certificate of registration and that the appellant had not produced any evidence in support of his claim that he had a valid permit. The Appellate Tribunal upheld the order of the Regional Transport authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the appellant ' s application was not supported by a certificate issued by the Regional transport authority; (ii) the appellant had been awarded marks which were higher than the marks obtained by the second respondent; (iii) the appellant was entitled to be granted a permit under Rule 155 A of the Rules; and (iv) the refusal of the Regional Tranport Authority to grant the permit was arbitrary. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant 's right to get a permit is not absolute but subject to the condition that the applicant has to produce a certificate of the Transport Authority certifying that the applicant is a holder of a permit. [560C] 2. The appellant had no right to insist upon a certificate of a Transport Authority certifying the fact that the applicant had a valid stage carriage permit. The appellant was not entitled to insist upon the certificate of a Regional Transport Authority certifying a fact that the second respondent had a valid route permit. [561E] 3. The appellant could not have been denied the permit on the ground of non production of a certificate of fitness. [562A] 4. The appellant having failed to produce a valid certificate of a permit, the Regional Transport Officer was justified in refusing to grant the permits. [563B] 5. The appellant cannot be said to have been deprived of the benefit of the concession made available to him under the rules. [564D]

5524: The Uttar Pradesh Nyayik Seva (Adhyapak) Adhiniyam, 1972 was enacted by the Uttar Pradesh State Legislature in 1973. Section 2(a) of the Act defines 'Selection Board ' to mean a Board constituted under section 3 of the Act and includes a Committee appointed by the Governor under sub section (1) of section 4. Section 5 provides that the members of the Board shall be nominated by the Governor on the recommendation of the Board. Section 6 provides that the Board shall prepare a list of candidates selected for appointment as Munsifs in order of merit in accordance with the rules made under the Act. The appellants who were candidates for recruitment to the service applied for selection to the post of Munsifs. They were duly qualified and they were called for viva voce test. On receipt of the list of candidates the Public Service Commission forwarded another list of 33 candidates on April 25, 1974 for appointment to the service under Rule 19 of the Rules. Meanwhile, the Public Service commission sent another list of 35 candidates on April 26, 1974 for appointments to the service which shall hereinafter be referred to as the 1972 Examination. The appellants challenged the validity of the said list contending that the list prepared by the Public Service Commissiion was not valid because it did not contain the names of the successful candidates in the list prepared under Rule 19. The High Court held that the list was invalid because it contained the names of only those who had secured more than 40 per cent marks in the aggregate and that the list did not contain any name of the successful candidate. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The list prepared by Public Service Commission is not invalid because it contains the names of all the successful candidates. [550C] 2. The list does not contain the name of any candidate. It merely contains the names and addresses of the successful persons. The list is therefore invalid because it does not contain any names of the candidates. [552D] 3. The list must be deemed to have been approved by the Governor. [553E] 4. The list cannot be treated as valid unless it contains the name of the candidate. [554F] 5. The list has to be treated as validly prepared. [555G]

2428: The appellant was the lessee of a plot which consisted of agricultural lands and a homestead. The homestead was later separately leased to defendants 2 and 3 (appellants). The trial court decreed the plaintiff 's suit but the first Appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed it. The High Court held that if the main lease is a lease for agricultural purposes all sub leases of portions of the properties included in the main lease are agricultural leases although they may be that of a homesthere and therefore the main lease would cease to be a purely agricultural lease as it must be held to relate to both agricultural and non agricultural lands. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. Section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply to a lease of a homousty. [646C] 2. The definition of "agriculture" in section 2(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 is not confined to agriculture only but includes horticulture. [647D] 3. The definition is not exhaustive. It covers all kinds of agricultural or non agricultural land. It is not intended to cover any other kind of land. [648E] 4. The definition does not include agricultural land. [604F] 5. The definition cannot be extended to include agricultural land also. [605G] 6. The definition has no application to the facts of this case. The lease in favour of the appellants was for agricultural purposes and not for agricultural purposes. [603A]
