[880C] (2) The expression 'business' has been defined by section 2(7) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 to mean "any business or profession carried on by or on behalf of any person." The definition is comprehensive enough to cover all kinds of business activities. It does not exclude the activity of buying and selling of goods from the purview of the definition. [881D E] (3) The expression business means any business, profession and calling. [882E]
4798: The plaintiffs brought a suit for recovery of Rs. 26,000 against the Dominion of India through the Defence Secretary, New Delhi. It was pleaded that their late father Seth Lachman Dass Gupta entered into a contract with the Governor General in Council for supply of charcoal to the Military Supply Depot at Agra during the period from April 1, 1946 to March 31, 1944. In pursuance thereof he made necessary supplies and received payments for the same at the contractual rates from time to time. It was alleged that from 232 the date of the contract, the rate of charcoil went up continuously to 44.8% in July, August and September 1943, 93.1% in January, February and March 1944. Accordingly, Seth Lavan Dass served a notice exhibit A 8 on the Dominion of Indian under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The defendants contested the claim inter alia on the ground that the notice exhibit A8 did not give any notice to the plaintiff under section 80(a) of the Code. The trial court held that no further notice could be given under section 80, Code of Civil Procee dure 1908. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court holding that no further steps were required to be taken under section 80. The defendants appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The notice exhibit A 7 was not a valid notice under section 80 Code of Civil P.C., 1908. [411 D] (ii)The notice exhibit A 10 was not a notice under section 76 of the Code but was a notice under Section 80 of the Civil Procedure Code. The notice exhibitA 8 was a notice issued under section 80 and it was not a proper notice under section 77 of the Code as it was not an "intimation" under section 80 (a). [412 E F] (iii)Section 80 does not require that the notice must be given to the person concerned. The notice is only a intimation to the person who has been named therein. The notice can be given to him personally or to his agent. The notice may be addressed to the person to whom it is directed or to his principal or agent. [413 C D] (iv
532: The respondent was a constable in the Uttar Pradesh Police Force. He was sent up for selection to the post of Head Constable and was selected by the Selection Board. On December 8, 1948, he was sent up to training at the Police Training College, Moradabad. He failed in the Hindi test and was not selected and was not recommended for appointment. On March 15, 1950, the respondent was dismissed from service under section 240 of the Government of India Act, 1935. The respondent challenged his dismissal before the High Court which held that the order of dismissal was void as it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. Held, that the respondent was entitled to be reinstated in service with full back wages. The order of dismissal passed against him did not contravene article 311(1). The respondent was not governed by the provisions of section 240 of Government of India, Act, 1935, but was governed by the Regulations made under the Act. The respondent was entitled only to reinstatement if there were no charges against him. The order dismissing him was illegal because the respondent had been acquitted by the criminal court.
6517: The respondent No. 1 was the owner of a Petrol Pump which was set up on a site in Dehradun, of which respondent No. 2 was the lessee. Respondent No. 1 is the lessee. The 'No Objection Certificate' granted for conducting the said Petrol Pumps was cancelled by respondent No. 5, the District Authority and the State Government. The respondent No, 1 filed an appeal before the District Collector against the order cancelling the 'No objection certificate ' passed by respondent No, 2. The District Collector dismissed the appeal. Respondent No, 1 appealed to the State Government against the order of the District Collector. The State Government allowed the appeal and set aside the order of cancellation of 'No Objection Certificates ' passed by the District Collector and directed that the respondent No. 3 should issue a fresh 'no objection certificate ' in respect of the said Petiesel Pump. The respondent Nos. 1 and 4 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of respondent No. 4. The High Court held that the District Authority under Rule 151 could cancel the 'No Objection Certifi cate ' granted under Rule 144 and set aside its own order. The High court also held that the respondent Nos. 2 and 5 were not entitled to any relief as they had no right to use the site for storing petrol. However, the High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of District Collector. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the District Collector had no power to cancel the 'NOC ' granted to respondent No. I and that the District Magistrate had no jurisdiction to cancel the same. HELD: (1) The District Magistrate had the power to cancel a 'NOC' granted to respondent NO. I. The District Magistrate has no power to revoke a 'NO Caveat ' granted to a licensee. [880 A] (2) The District Collector had the power under Rule 151 to cancel a licence granted to a person who was not entitled to use the land for storing petrol or to use it for any other purpose. The District magistrate had no power under Rule 152 to cancel a "NOC" granted to a licencee. [881 B] (3) The District Officer had no power
1859: The assessee was permitted under section 26 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 to omit the word "Limited" from its name by order of the Government of Madras. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed on the ground that the assessee had not produced any evidence in support of its claim that it was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to the deduction claimed and that the income of the assessee was derived from the sale proceeds of the building and the rent received from the building. On reference, the High Court held that the Income Tax Officer was right in disallowing the claim for deduction on the ground of non production of evidence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The assessee was entitled only to the benefit of section 9(2)(a) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. [568 D] (2) The assessee did not produce any evidence in respect of the expenditure incurred by it. The assessee could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 9 of the Income tax Act. [569 E] (3) The assessee had failed to prove that it was carrying on business or profession within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Income Tax Act. The assessee was therefore entitled to the deductions claimed. [570 F] (4) The assessee has failed to establish that it was engaged in any activity which would bring into existence an asset or a part thereof. It is not possible to accept the contention that the assessee must have been carrying on business as a body corporate. [571 G] (5) The assessee cannot be said to carry on business as such. The assessee is not carrying on any business. The assessee cannot claim the benefit of the provision of section 9 (2)(a). [572 B C] (6) The assessee is entitled to the benefit under section 9(1)(b) of the Act. [572 D]
2083: The Mysore Public Service Commission (Functions) Rules, 1957, were made under article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 3 of these rules provided for recruitment by examination and r. 4 with which we are primarily concerned provides for recruitment by selection. Rule 4(1) provided that the Commission shall prepare a list of candidates selected in order of preference and forward to the Governor the names of the candidates included in the list. The appellants who were candidates who had not applied in response to the advertisement of the Government, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the Rules on the ground that they contravened articles 320(3) and 309 of the constitution. The High Court held that r. 3 was ultra vires the powers of the Governor as it did not provide for consultation with the Commission before making appointments to civil services and posts. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court erred in holding that r. 4(1), which is an executive instruction, is not a rule framed under article 309. [696 G] The power conferred by article 320(3)(c) is not an executive function but quasi judicial. It is only the exercise of the executive power which is delegated to the Commission. The power to make appointment to civil services or posts is not an administrative power. [697 B] The power to appoint persons to civil services is conferred by article 309 on the Governor. The Governor has the discretion to select persons from amongst the members of the service. [698 D] The Governor can also prescribe qualifications for members of the civil services. [699 C] The Governor may prescribe qualifications for the members of civil services. But he cannot prescribe any qualification for members of civil service without consulting the Commission. [695 E] The Governor is the sole authority to frame rules regarding conditions of service of members of civil Services. [694 F] The Governor has no power to issue orders appointing members of civil posts. [690 A] The Governor does not have the power to appoint members of civil employment. [692 B] The Governor must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. [693 C]
2736: The appellants were the sons of one Kothandaram, who died in 1943. After his death, the respondents, who were the plaintiffs, filed a suit for partition claiming a share in the joint family properties. The trial court held that the adoption was valid and that the various transfers made by the respondents were not binding on the appellants. On appeal, the High Court held that the adopted son had no right to adopt a son after he had attained majority and that the properties which were transferred by him were not liable to be partitioned. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The adoption of a son is not a matter of succession to the property of the deceased. It is only when the adoption is found to be invalid that the question of the validity of the adoption can arise. [839 E] (2) The adoption is not a mere change of status or change of residence. It is an act of adoption. It is not merely a change of residence within the meaning of section 16(1)(c). [840 F] (3) The adoption must be proved like any other fact. [841 G] (4) There is nothing in the Act to show that the adoption of a daughter was a change of her birth. The adoption of daughter was not a change of birth. [842 D] (5) The adoption was not a mere transfer of property but it was a transfer of property. [843 C] (6) The adoption did not involve any change of residence and was therefore not a change in the character of the family. [844 B] (7) The adoption took place before the death of the father of the respondents. The adoption was therefore not void. [845 A] (8) The adoption having been found to be valid, the question of its validity does not arise. [881 C] (9) The adoption by the respondents was not a transfer of the property of their father. [846 D] (10) The adoption deed did not create any interest in the property of a Hindu female. The adoption deed was not a deed of adoption. [847 E] (11) The adoption made by the respondent was not a result of any agreement between the parties. [
1631: The appellant, a Hindu, executed an otti in favour of his wife, and the respondent, a minor son, on 9.3.1102 M.E., for 3500 fanams. The appellant, who was the guardian of Sivaraman, filed a suit for redemption of the otti and possession of the fields from the respondents, claiming to be the heirs of Sivaravan, and also for improvements, if any, as determined by the court. The suit was valued at 3500 fans, and the claim was for redemption of otti, offering to pay fanams in equivalent money and for improvements, as determined in the auction sale held on 3.4.1114 M.E. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant had not taken any interest in the jenmom rights, but he had only a right to get the same under the contract of sale. The appellant could not have claimed that he had no right to redeem the ottis or that he had obtained the sale deed. [639 G] (2) The appellant did not take any interest in any other property which was subject to a mortgage. He merely gave a right to the mortgagee to sell the mortgaged property. The mortgage was created by the appellant in favour of the first respondent, and the mortgage was created in favour of a third party. The appellant had no right in the property. [640 D E] (3) The appellant was entitled to redeem the mortgage. [641 F] (4) The appellant could have easily brought the present suit for redemption on the basis of the mortgage. The mortgage is not vitiated by fraud. [642 C]
4749: The petitioner retired as Chief Justice of Madhya Pradesh High Court with effect from February 28, 1978. At the time of his retirement he was drawing salary of Rs. 4000 per month as provided under Constitution. This Court in the case of Union of India vs Gurnam Singh (1) decided that under the ( 'Act ' for short), Judges were entitled to payment of cash equivalent of leave salary in respect of the period of earned leave at their credit on the date of retirement as provided in Rule 20B of the All India Services (Leave) Rules, 1955 ( 'Rules ' for short). The Accountant General of Madhya Pradesh authorised the petitioner to draw a further sum of Rs. 750 by his communication dated July 17, 1982. The petitioner informed the Accountant General that he was drawing the amount as indicated in the communication without prejudice to his right to claim Rs. 24,000 to which sum under the law he was entitled. On July 19, 1982, the petitioner was authorised to draw a second sum of Rs, 750 by his letter dated July 19,1982. The petitioner intimated the Accountant General of the State about the excess payment made to him and requested the Government to refund the excess amount paid to him. The Accountant General, however, did not accede to the request of the petitioner. The petitioner moved this Court for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to pay him cash equivalent of the unutilised earned leave due on the date when he retired. The petition was resisted by the respondents contending that the petitioner had been paid cash equivalent of unutilized earned leave on the basis of the decision of this Court in Union of India & Ors. vs Gurnami Ram (supra) and that the petitioner was not entitled to any relief. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner is entitled to be paid cash equivalent to unutilised leave due on 855 full allowances as defined in section 3 and 9(1) of the Act. [856C] 2. The petitioner has been paid cash equivalents of Rs. 15,240 by his letter of August 7, 1982. He has also been paid cash allowance of Rs. 500 by his letter. The petitioner cannot be said to have been paid cash equal to the unutilized leave
3110: The appellants purchased the land in dispute from the respondent for a sum of Rs. 1,000/ per acre. The Land Acquisition Officer fixed the market value of the land at Rs. 1.08.5 acres and the High Court took judicial notice that the land was situated on the main road but it was situated on a narrow strip of land. The High Court accepted the price as a basis for determining the market value. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in adopting the price in the sale deed Ex C 1 executed on 6 5 1953 by the Ranchi Club Ltd., in favour of the President of India in respect of 1.085 acres bighas kathas chhataks in Plot No. 1221 for Rs. 45,000/. [212A] (2) The land in question was situated on one side of the main road and the sale deed executed on 6 4 1953 showed that the land had been sold for Rs. 1 lakh. It was not only the land under acquisition but also the land under the leasehold rights which were subject matter of the sale deed. The land in dispute was situated on an interior part of the land under a lease granted by the Government. The land was situated in a small strip of the land. There was no evidence to show that the land in question had been put up for sale or that the land under sale was put up for any other purpose. [213B C] (3) The High court was wrong in adopting the market value as a basis because it was not only a small piece of land but also a large area of land. [214D] (4) The High 'Court was right in accepting the price as the basis for determining compensation. [215E] (5) The High Courts were wrong in adopting a price of Rs. 10,000/per acre. [216F]
1550: The appellant purchased an Austin 10 Horse Power Car with the registration No. DLA 4796 from Dewan Ram Swarup in the name of her minor daughter Nalini aged about six months at that time. She signed the proposal form as Nalini and also the receipts acknowledging the payments of compensation money as Nalya. On a complaint made by the company alleging fraud on the part of Dr. Vimla, the police made investigation and prosecuted Dr. Vimlesh Kumar for offences under sections 120 B, 419, 468 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The Sessions judge acquitted both of them but convicted both of them under section 467 and 468 of the Code and sentenced them to imprisonment till the rising of the court and to pay a fine of Rs. 100/ or in default to under go simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of both the accused under sections 467 and 468. The State preferred an appeal to this Court against their acquittal. The question for consideration was whether the High Court could interfere with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the courts below. Held: (i) The High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. The High 'Court should not have interfered with the acquittal of the accused unless it was shown that there was some perversity in the appreciation of evidence or that the view taken by the trial Court was one which no reasonable person could have taken. The High Courts are not competent to reappraise the evidence and come to different conclusion. It is only when the High Court has given a finding that the view of the trial court is perverse or based on no material that it can be said to be perverse that the High Court would be justified in interfering with such a finding. The High court cannot substitute its own opinion for that of the trial Court. The High, Court cannot substitute its opinion for the opinion of the trial Judge who has given his decision. [501 E] (ii) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the trial court had no jurisdiction or authority to take a contrary view. The High courts were wrong in assuming that the trial courts had no jurisdiction. The High Cour t had no jurisdiction in the matter. The High.
387: The appellants were charged with having committed offences under sections 435 and 436 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted them but the High Court on appeal reversed the acquittal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants had been rightly convicted by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 435 of the Indian penal code. The conviction was not based solely on the evidence of the eye witnesses but on the circumstantial evidence. [801 B C] (ii) The prosecution case was that the appellants had set fire to the Palani and had caused injuries to the deceased. The first information report was lodged at Gopalganj Police Station in which the appellants were named as the assailants. The second information report was made at the police station at about 3 p.m. and the third information was given at the police post at about 5 p.m., and the fourth information was given to the police at about 6 p.m.. The first information was recorded at the police Post at about 7 p.m.; the second information was given after a considerable time and it was not possible to say whether the first information report had been ante litem moto or not. The first informant was not examined by the prosecution. He did not state that he had seen the appellants setting fire to the palani and the appellants setting the house on fire. The first Information Report was lodged at about 3 P.M. and the second information report is lodged at about 5.30 p.m, and the third intimation was given at about 6.p.m. The first two informants were not examined by any of the prosecution witnesses. The first informant was not examined. The first witness was not examined and the second witness was not produced. The first accused was not examined either by the prosecution or by the defence. [802 D E; 803 A B] (iii) The first information Report was lodged within a short time after the occurrence. It was not true to say that the first information was lodged at the police Station at about 5-30 p. m. The first FIR was lodged at 6 p. m., and the second FIR was lodged after a considerable delay. There was no reason why the first information should have been lodged at 6.p
2470: The respondent firm was awarded a contract of purchase of certain quantity of timber by the appellant. The appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent firm for purchase of the said quantity of timber at a loss and the appellant agreed to pay the price of the timber at the rate of Rs. 9/12/Vet c.ft. on or before 26th January, 1958. The respondent firm made a claim of Rs. 3,50,085/9/ against the appellant for excess quantity of timber alleged to have been delivered and certain other matters. The appellant contended that the respondent firm had not supplied the timber at its own premises at Halisahaar and Lillooah and therefore the contract in question was not covered by the arbitration clause contained in the form W.S.B. 133 and therefore the reference of the dispute to the arbitrator was incompetent. Held, that the appellant could not be allowed to raise the question of jurisdiction of the arbitrator to decide the dispute between the parties. The arbitration clause in the form of W.S.,B. 133 did not provide for any adjudication of the dispute between parties. The award of the arbitrator was binding upon both the parties and it was open to them to agitate the same in proceedings under section 30 of the Arbitration Act. The award was not vitiated merely because the arbitrator had failed to act according to law but the award was liable to be set aside if the arbitrator had acted contrary to law. The award being void would not be enforceable. The award is not liable to be challenged on the ground that the arbitrator has misconducted himself or the proceedings; nor can it be challenged on any other grounds. The award cannot be set aside unless it is shown that the arbitrator had misconducted himself in proceeding with the matter. The award does not become invalid merely because it is based on an erroneous view of the law or on the evidence. The award may also be set aside even if it is based upon a wrong statement of the law. But the award is not unilateral but is subject to judicial review. It is open to the court to examine whether the arbitrator has exceeded his jurisdiction or has acted in excess of his jurisdiction. In the present case the arbitrator had no jurisdiction to make the award. The award therefore was not valid.
2366: The appellant was convicted under section 5(3) (a) of the , and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and also to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000 in default to undergo rigorous imprison ment for six months. The High Court did not find the two other accused persons guilty, and State appeals against them were dismissed. In appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that (i) the three minor boys, Kashi Bhokta, Guhi Bhoktta Gobardhan and Mohan Bour died during the pendency of the trial; (ii) the conviction of the appellant under section 5 (3) (b) of the Act was illegal because he had been charged with an offence punishable under section 304A, IPC, and was sentenced to undergo imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine which may extend up to five thousand rupees, or with both; and (iii) the sentence of imprisonment imposed on the appellant was too severe. HELD : (1) The conviction of the three minor girls, Kashi, Guhi and Subhas, under section 5 of the Explosive Rules, 1940, is not vitiated by any error of law. [646 D] (2) The conviction under section 5 is not vitiated merely because the three minor children were employed in any event. [647 E] (3) The conviction was not vitiated merely on account of the fact that the three minor women were employed in a factory. [648 F] (4) The conviction could be sustained only if the three minor persons were employed in the factory. [651 C] (5) The conviction cannot be sustained merely because the two other persons were employed as labourers in a factory and were not employed in the manufacture of fireworks. [652 A] (6) The conviction is not vitiated simply because the three minors were employed in some other factory. [669 D]
3303: The appellant, a tenant of a land in the State of Haryana, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act was not applicable to the State of Punjab and that the Act did not apply to the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Act had no application to the State and that the High Court erred in holding that the Punjab Security Act applied only to the State Government and not to the State as such. HELD: (1) The Act does not apply to any land which is held by a person who is a small holder. [631C] (2) The Act applies to all persons who are tenants of land in the same state. [632A] (3) The Act has been enacted to provide for the rehabilitating landless tenants and for their rehabilitation. The Act provides for the reabulbility of the surplus area of a tenant. Section 2(4) defines 'small land owner ' to mean a person owning or holding land in excess of the ceiling area. [633B C] (4) The Act is a special legislation intended to protect the weaker sections of the society. It is a complete code in itself. The Act is not intended to be used to defeat the objects of the Act. [634D E] (5) The Act makes a provision for the reformation of the tenants and landless persons. The Act does nothing more than make them eligible for rehabilitate them. [635E] (630F) The Act cannot be said to have been made with a view to give protection to the weaker sections. [636G]
3630: The appellants purchased raw hides and skins from the State of Tamil Nadu. They purchased raw hide and skins in the course of interState trade and commerce. The tax under section 4 of the State Act was payable by them on the sale or purchase inside the State of declared goods. The appellants challenged the validity of items 7(a) and 7(b) of the Second Schedule to the State Act on the ground that they were not declared goods within the meaning of section 14(iii) of the Central Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellants are dealers in hides and kins as well as dressed hides and sms. The question whether raw hides or skins are of special importance in inter State trade or commerce is a matter for decision by the State Legislature. [1068 E] (2) The State legislature has no power to levy tax on raw hides manufactured in the State except by way of taxation under Entry 56 of List II. [1069 A B] (3) The State Legislature has no power under Entry 56 to impose tax on raw materials which are not raw materials but are cut into pieces. [1070 C D] (4) The State Government can levy tax only on raw materials and not on the raw material. [1071 F] (5) The State Act does not impose any tax on raw material. It imposes a tax on the manufacture of raw hides. The State Legislature cannot impose a tax on raw or dressed hide and the dressed hose. [1072 G] (6) The State has no power either to levy tax or to collect tax on raw and dressed hue. [1073 H]
6931: The appellant State Government in exercise of power under section 68 D of the approved a draft scheme for the route Anantapur to Dharmavaram via Mamillappalli. The scheme was challenged by the respondents on the ground that the non exemption of the routes from the approved scheme had been granted without any basis and that the exclusion of the routes was discriminatory. The High Court upheld the contention and held that the exclusion was discriminatory. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme is not discriminatory. It is open to the State Transport Undertaking to prepare a scheme giving particulars of the nature of the service proposed to be rendered, the area or route covered and such other particulars respecting thereto as may be prescribed. [780G H] 2. The scheme does not provide for any reason whatsoever which would justify the exclusion of certain services from the scheme. The scheme merely provides for the manner in which the scheme has to be prepared. The scheme cannot be said to be arbitrary or unreasonable. [771C] 3. The scheme must be reasonable and should have some rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. [772D E] 4. The scheme has to satisfy two tests; (i) it must be within the four corners of the statute and (ii) it must also be in conformity with the provisions of the Act. [773E F] 5. The scheme having been framed in accordance with the provisions contained in section 68 C of the approved scheme, the scheme cannot be struck down on the ground of arbitrariness. [774F G]
3971: The appellants obtained licences for the import of nylon yarn. They cleared the goods on May 10, 1966 and paid duty under protest and applied for refund of the excess payment on the ground that the amended provisions of the Act were not applicable as the consignments had been received, stored and assessed to duty before the promulgation of the Ordinance. The Customs Authorities rejected their applications for refund on the ground, inter alia, that the amended provision was not applicable as they were not in possession of any document evidencing the receipt or storage of the goods. The Appellate Collector dismissed the appeals. In revision, the Central Government held that the amended section 14 of the Act was applicable to the consignments in question. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the orders of the Appellate Collector and the Customs Authorities. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the amended sections 14 and 15 of the Act are applicable to the cases in which the goods have been delivered to the customs authorities after the date of the commencement of the Ordinance and that the appellants could claim refund only if the goods had been actually removed from the customs premises before the date of their clearance. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The amended section 14 applies to cases where the goods have already been delivered to a carrier or other bailee for transmission to the proper officer of customs. [103C] 2. The amended provision is not applicable to cases where goods have been actually removed by the carrier or other person from the customs house to the place of destination. [104E] 3. The amended provisions apply to cases where there has been no actual removal of the goods from the customs houses to the place where the goods are actually removed. [105B C] 4. The amended Section 14 applies to all cases where the property in the goods has passed to a carrier, or other baailee. [106D] 5. The amended clause (b) of sub section (1) of section 14 applies where the goods had already been delivered for transmission to a carrier. [107F] 6. The amended clauses (b), (c) and (d) of sub sections (2) and (3) of section 15 are applicable to cases of non delivery of goods
3896: The assessee, a registered firm, was engaged in the execution of works on behalf of the Government. For the execution of the works undertaken by the assessee certain material such as cement, coal, items of steel etc. were supplied at fixed rates specified in Schedule to the contract by the Government for being used in the works. Such material though in custody of the contractor always remained the property of the Government and if any surpluses are left at the completion of the contract, the contractor (the assessee) has to account for it at the same rates at which the supply was made to him (wear and tear excepted) and return the same to the Government. The Income tax officer estimated the cost of such material at 50% of the cash payments, namely, at Rs. 2,22,311 and by adding this figure to the net cash receipts of Rs. 4,44,622 he arrived at total receipt (including the cost of materials) at 50% and worked out net income or profits at Rs. 66,693. The assessee firm did not furnish any figures about the stores received by it from the M.E.S. The Income Tax Officer estimated the cost at 50% which was the difference between the actual cost of materials and the actual cost incurred by the assessee. The assessee failed to do so on the ground that the Departments were not cooperating with it. The Income 'tax officer adopted a flat rate of 10% and worked it up to Rs. 66.690 and on that basis the tax assessed the assessee to be liable to pay the tax. The assessee contended before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the Department had no business connection with the assessee and that the Department was entitled to deduct the amount of the tax from the gross profit of the assessee. On the question whether the Department was liable to pay tax on the value of the goods supplied by the assessee to the Government, HELD: 1. The Department was entitled under section 5(2)(a) of the Act to deduct the tax payable on the value thereof. [780C] 2. The Department is entitled to deduct tax on the amount of tax paid by it on the value to be sold. [790D] 3. The Department cannot escape its liability to
3794: The respondent was a Government servant and was allotted to the new State of Mysore. He was posted as an Accountant in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hyd erabad. 6116: The appellant, who was the successor in interest of the mort gage-holder, filed a suit for redemption on 28.12.1973 contending that the sale deed dated 1.11.19 13 constituted a fresh starting point for computing the period of limitation and that the suit for redemption could have been filed on or before the 1st of November, 1973. [303 B] (iv) The respondent has no right to recover the sum of Rs. 31,250/ which he had deposited with the Divisional Forest officer. [304 C]
3366: The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge, Chatarpur for offences under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and section 27 of the Arms Act. The two eye witnesses were permitted to be cross examined by the Public Prosecutor as they supported the case of the prosecution only partly. The two principal witnesses turned hostile and did not support the case of prosecution. The two main witnesses turned hostile. The trial court convicted the appellants under section 302/34 of the Penal Court and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the appellants on the ground that the two eye witnesses had resiled from their police statements and it was evident that they have no regard for truth. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court has erred in relying upon the dying declarations of the two eye witness. The first dying declaration was recorded by the Magistrate and the second one was recorded by a Sub Inspector. The third one was recorded at the instance of the deceased. The first one was recorded after the Doctor had certified that the patient was fit to make statement. The second one was made before the Police Officer who certified that the deceased was fit to give statement. The third was recorded after a period of more than three months. The fourth was recorded after about three months. There is nothing in the evidence of the doctor or the Sub Inspector to show that the deceased had been in a fit condition to make the statement. [768 C D] (2) The High 'Court was right in holding that the dying declaration was reliable and trustworthy. [769 E] (3) The High Courts were wrong in convicting the appellants under s. 302 read with s. 34 of the Indian Penal Code. [770 F]
3199: The appellant, a nationalised institution, was entrusted with the responsibility of collecting and forwarding goods to the Port Trust. The respondent, a foreign company, had entered into an agreement with the appellant for the sale of certain goods. The appellant claimed that the goods were not delivered within the time prescribed by the agreement but were returned on account of some technical defects in the goods. The respondent contended that the appellant had no right to claim the value of the goods as it was not liable to pay any amount under the contract. The trial court held that the appellant was entitled to the value of goods as it had been received from the respondent and that the appellant could not be said to have committed breach of the contract. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the finding of the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The appellant was not entitled to claim the price of the goods at the time when they were delivered. The appellant was entitled only to the price of goods which were actually received. [390B] (2) The appellant had no legal right to claim any amount under a contract. The appellant had a right to retain the goods if he had done so. The appellant could not claim the value without having paid the price. [391C] (3) The appellant could have claimed the value of all the goods sold or delivered by the respondent. [394A] (4) The appellant did not make out a case of breach of contract. It is not necessary that there should be a breach of contract by the seller. The appellant has not made out a case for breach of contract and therefore, the appellant cannot be allowed to raise the question of limitation. [395D]

Thereafter, for every year, the liquidator used to prepare only an income and expenditure statement for submission to the Reserve Bank of India. The assessment year with which we are concerned is 1963 64 i.e., the year ended March 31, 1963. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that in the hands of the liquidator there was only one integral fund which could be distinctly classified as constituting a part of the funds in the hands. The assessee had not submitted any return under the Act, a notice under section 9 (a) of the Income tax Act, 1961, or under section 9(b) of the Companies Act, 1956. The assessee did not submit any return under section 9 of the Act. The assessee could not therefore claim any benefit of the provision contained in section 2(6) of the Finance Act, 1960. [66A C] 2.2. 470: The widow of a deceased person died in September, 1927. The properties were allotted to her daughter and the other two sons. The widow was given a share in the income of the property. The widow had no right to claim any share in the property. She was entitled to a share in her husband 's property. The suit for partition was filed by the four sons of the deceased. The suit was decreed on July 22, 1933. The decree provided for payment of Rs. 10,000 as expenses for the marriage of the minor daughter Kamala Devi, in addition to a maintenance allowance of Rs. 50 per month to her until she was married. The decree further provided that the amount should be paid out of the income of her husband. The widow appealed against this decree. The High Court held that the widow was not entitled to a portion of the income from the properties allotted to her. The High court also held that the share of the widow in the income from her husband ' s property was her own and that the widow could not claim any share out of the property allotted to her under the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The widow was entitled to the share of her husband in the income which accrued to her during her life time. [447 E] (2) The widow had only one share in the estate of her husband and the remaining six shares were allotted to the heirs of her husband who were entitled to a half share in the properties allotted. The widow did not have any right to claim a share in any property allotted to the widow. [448 A B] (3) The widow could not be said to have any interest in the property allotted or transferred to her. [449 C] (4) The widow would be entitled to a proportionate share in the profits of the property if she had been alive at the date of the decree. [450 D] (5) The widow is entitled to a sum of Rs. 5,000 as maintenance allowance. [451 F] (6) The widow has no right to make a claim for maintenance. [452 G] (7) The widow cannot claim a share out of her income from the property allotted. [453 H] (8) The widow
6761: The appellant was a manufacturer of wagons. The railway Board supplied the wagon charged by the appellant from the Railway Board to the Railway Board. The invoice value of the wagon chargeable under the contract was Rs. 1,00,000. The appellant challenged the demand raised by the central excise authorities on the ground that the excise duty could only be charged on the invoice value of goods supplied by the Railway Board without charging any price. The Central Excise authorities issued various show cause notices in respect of different transactions calling upon the appellant to show cause as to why the excise duty should not be computed and charged on the value of the completed wagon including that of the "Free supply items". The appellant challenged these notices by way of writ petition before the High Court which was heard by a learned Single Judge who allowed the writ petition and quashed the demand raised. The Union of India filed appeal against the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court. The Division Bench held that the excise duties could only be levied on the invoice price charged by the petitioner and not on the value. The Union filed appeal against this judgment of the High court to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The excise duty is payable on the 'fty supply ' articles. It cannot be charged on any other article. [963E] 2. The Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 does not contain any provision for payment of excise duty on the 'turnover '. The expression 'value ' has been defined in section 3(d) of the Act to mean the value of any goods for the purposes of the Act. The definition of 'value ' in section 4(1)(a) of the Central Excises & Salt Act,1944 includes all materials, articles and commodities used in the manufacture or processing of goods for sale. [964A B] 3. The Central Government can levy excise duty on any commodity manufactured or produced within the State. [965C] 4. The Central Exercise Board has been constituted under the Central Excise and Salt Act. The Board is an expert body. The Board has been entrusted with the task of collecting information about the manufacturing process of the commodity. The Board consists of experts. The Board may also have some
1915: The first respondent was a Brahmin woman. During the life time of her husband she became the concubine of Lingayya. After the death of Lingaya, the second respondent was separate in estate from his brothers and brothers. The parties were residents of Choragudi, Bapatla, now in Andhra Pradesh and governed by Mitakshara school of Hindu law. In the plaint, as originally filed, the respondents claimed that they were exclusively entitled to the estate left by Lingayyya. The Subordinate Judge decreed the respondents ' claim for maintenance and consequential reliefs and awarded them maintenance during their lifetime out of the estate of Lingayat. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that the relevant provisions of the Act applied only to the estates of Hindus dying after the commencement of the Act and that the right of the respondents to maintenance during their life time under the Hindu law in force at the time of the death of the deceased Lingayaya was not an A category of A category of persons. The appellants contended that the provisions of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (Act No. 2 of 1956) were retrospective and that the rights of the respondents under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act had been acquired before the commencement of that Act. Held:(i) The provisions of the said Act are applicable only to the estate of the deceased and not to the estates which have already vested in the respondents. (ii)The provisions of the section are not retrospective in operation. (iii)The provisions relating to maintenance are not retrospective. (iv)The provisions regarding maintenance are not intended to apply to the estate or to any portion thereof. (v)The provisions contained in section 3(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 are not applicable to the estate. (vi)Section 4(2) of the Act is not applicable to a case where the property has already vested in a person who has died after the commencement o f the Act.
826: The respondent, a textile mill, was an employer. The respondent claimed that the reserves were used as working capital and that the said reserves should be deducted from the amount required for rehabilitation. The appellant contended that the reserves could not be deducted from its amount because they had been utilised as working capital, but it did not give any credit to the rehabilitation amount. The Industrial Court rejected this contention. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The respondent was entitled to deduct the amount of Rs. 2.20 lakhs from the amount of rehabilitation which would be available to the respondent for rehabilitation on a proper application made by it. [839 E] (ii) The respondent is entitled to deduct from the amount payable to the employees the amount that should have been spent for rehabilitation. [840 F] (iii) The respondent cannot claim that the reserves must be utilised only in the manner prescribed by section 42(2). [841 A B] (iv) The respondent has no right to claim that the amounts so required should be deducted under section 43A of the Act. [842 C]
6061: The petitioners are the Assam Rifles Multi purpose Co operative Society Limited and Major General Guraya, AVSM (Retd.), Vice Chairman of the said Society. They have been working as Inspectors General Assam Rifles in various capacities in the State of Arunachal Pradesh. They were allotted land at the rate of Rs. 10,000 per annum for a period of five years from the date of allotment. The petitioners claimed that they had been allotted land at a rate higher than the rate fixed by the Government of India. The petitioners contended that the scheme was not implemented by the Government and that the scheme should be extended to them. The respondents contested the claim on the ground that the scheme had been approved by the Central Government and that it was not implemented because the scheme was being implemented by the State Government. The High Court held that the scheme could not be implemented because the State Government had not taken any action against the petitioners. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme is intended to benefit all those who are members of the armed forces. It is meant to help the armed forces in maintaining their security. [855C] 2. The scheme has been framed with a view to provide for the rehabilitation of the personnel belonging to the armed forces and to ensure their safety. It is intended to give effect to the object of the Act. [856D] 3. The scheme does not cover persons who are members or employees of the armed force. The scheme provides for the payment of compensation to such persons who are entitled to compensation under the Act. The scheme also provides for the grant of additional compensation to those who are not covered by the scheme. [857E F] 4. The scheme cannot be implemented because it is intended to help the members of the Armed Forces. [858F] 5. The scheme will be implemented only if the State Government takes appropriate action against the persons who are not members of the Force. [859G] 6. The scheme would be implemented only when the State Government makes an order sanctioning the scheme. The scheme shall be implemented only after the State Government gives its sanction. [860A]
418: The respondent was tried and convicted by a Magistrate of the First Class for an offence under section 7 of the East Punjab Essential Services (Maintenance) Act, 1947. He was acquitted on appeal by the Sessions Judge. On revision, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of acquittal was illegal as the respondent had not been given any opportunity to explain his conduct and that the order was bad because the respondent was not afforded an adequate opportunity to defend himself. HELD : (i) The order of acquittal is not vitiated merely because the respondent has been acquitted by the Magistrate. It is only where the acquittal is based on a ground of "no evidence" or on some evidence which is wholly inconsistent with the charge that he was found guilty of the offence that the court can interfere with such an order of acquittal. [839 B] (ii) The order in question must be held to have been passed on the basis of the evidence before the court. There is no reason why the High Court should not have interfered with the order of the acquittal. [884 D E]
795: The appellant was the descendant of a devotee of " Shri Venkatesh Balaji". He died in 1701. His eldest son, Timmayya, at the time of his death was 12 years old and he had been managing the properties as devotees. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties which were described in the schedules attached to the plaint. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the suit was barred by limitation; (ii) the suit having been instituted after the death of the appellant, the suit was within time; and (iii) the suit should have been dismissed under section 5(3) of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920. HELD : (i) The suit was clearly within time. It was not barred by limitation. [787 E] (ii) The suit is barred by limitation because the appellant did not bring the suit within the period prescribed by section 5(1)(a) of the Act. [788 D] (iii) The suit must be held to be within time. [789 F] (iv) The suit being one for possession of immovable property, the limitation would start from the date when the plaintiff has come to know about the trust and the suit must be deemed to have been instituted within the period of limitation. [792 B C] (v) The suit cannot be said to be barred by limitation merely because the appellant had made an application to the District Court under section 3 of the Charitable & Religious Trusts Act. [794 A B] (vi) The suit having been brought within the period provided by section 5 of the Act, the suit must fail. [785 G]
888: The petitioner, a Ruler of the State of Vadia, executed two documents in favour of the petitioner granting him in perpetuity and in heredity a village called ' Mota Pithadia ' in the State for enjoyment as ' Kapal Giras '. The word ' Bhayat ' means a cadet or the descendant of a younger branch of a Talukdar 's family where the State follows the State followers. In terms of this covenant the assets of each State excepting the private properties of the Ruler were vested in the United State. On September 13, 1948, the United State of Kathiawad executed a fresh instrument of accession to the Dominion of India recognising the rights of all Rulers including the petitioner. On November 13, 1949, the United States of Kathiawar merged with the Union of India. On January 23, 1950, the United Stale of Kathiavaru executed a new deed of accession in respect of the State with which we are concerned in this petition. On December 1, 1951, the United state of Kathiawa passed an Act called the Constitution (Twenty Eighteenth Amendment) Act, 1950, whereby the provisions of article 31A(1)(a), article 31B(2) and article 31C(3) were repealed. By section 3 of the Act, the provisions of the Act were deemed to have been incorporated in the Constitution of India with effect from the date of its commencement. The petitioner was not a member of the Indian Nationality. He filed a writ petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that it contravened his fundamental right guaranteed by article 14 of the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 31A(l)(a) of the Constitution is not attracted because the Act has been passed after the Constitution came into force. It is only when the Constitution came in to force that the provisions of Article 31A would be applicable. (ii)The Act does not make any provision for giving effect to the provisions of Articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Constitution and therefore the provisions of articles 31A(4) and 31C(5) cannot be said to be inconsistent with the provisions of Part III of the Constitution, and so
2685: The appellant was the sole proprietor of a partnership firm. He carried on business in partnership at three places in Madhya Pradesh. By an agreement dated December 18, 1947, he transferred his business to the respondent. On December 18, 1948, the arbitrator entered upon the reference and gave him time for making the award. The arbitrator entered upon it but before that date, the respondent filed an application under section 28 of the Arbitration Act for extension of time for making an award. The Subordinate Judge held that the application was maintainable and directed the appointment of receiver. The High Court allowed the appeal. In the meantime, the respondent applied under section 34 of the for stay of the suit. The application was rejected by the Subordinate Judge. The respondent appealed to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. The appellant contended that the application under section 34 was not maintainable as the period of limitation prescribed by the Limitation Act had expired. Held: (i) A suit is instituted when there is a right to apply within the prescribed period; the suit must be instituted within a reasonable time from the accrual of cause of action. If the right to apply accrued only after the filing of the suit, the suit would be barred by limitation. It is not necessary that the right should have been accrued at the date of the suit or at the time when the suit was instituted. [781 C D] (ii)The right to apply arose when the court passed the decree and the suit was filed within the prescribed time. The right to apply arises when the court passes a decree and the right to make an award is exercised. But if the right to move the court is claimed within the prescribed limitation, the suit will be barred by time.
53: The appellant, a Hindu, brought the suit out of which this appeal arises for possession of certain properties. The respondent claimed that the properties were joint family property and were im pendently held by him as his separate heirs. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it on the ground that the properties being the exclusive and separate properties of the ghatwal, the respondent was entitled to succeed to them in preference to the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The respondent had no right to claim partition of the properties. [156 D] (2) The respondent could not be said to have any right to the properties in dispute. The respondent had only a limited interest in the properties. He could not therefore claim to be the sole proprietor of the properties in question. [157 A B] (3) The respondent was not entitled to succeed in preference to her husband. [158 C] (4) The respondent did not acquire any title to the properties. It was not necessary for him to establish that he was the sole proprietor or owner of the properties and that he alone was entitled to the same. [159 E] (5) The respondent cannot claim to be a sole proprietor of all the properties in suit. [160 F] (6) The respondent is not entitled to claim any share in the properties in issue. [161 G]
176: The appellants were accused of the offence of criminal conspiracy and for the commission of the offence under section 120 B, Indian Penal Code, read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the two appellants in the course of their official capacity obtained illegal gratification from one Nagindas Mehta, a representative of the Panna Diamond Mining Syndicate, and that later on they entered into a conspiracy to obtain illegal gratification by a public servant for doing an official act and for the payment of illegal gratification to the said Nagindas. The trial court acquitted both the appellants but the High Court convicted them under sections 161, 165, 466, 471, 477, 478, 479, 470, 474, 475, 476, 477A, 478B and 479 of the Indian Penal Code. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that (1) the charge against them was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; (2) the evidence showed that the two officers had conspired together and the demand of illegal gratification was made by the two appellants to the President of India; (3) the evidence did not show that the two Officers had any connection or interest in the conspiracy; (4) the evidence indicated that the two servants had been acting as a result of the conspiracy and that the two were merely members of the conspiracy; and (5) the evidence established that the two persons had conspired with each other and the two officers were guilty of the offence charged. Held, that the conviction of the appellants must be set aside. The evidence clearly established that the appellants had conspired and the two servants were acting as a part of the conspiracy. The evidence did not establish that the two agents had any connection with the conspiracy. It was not necessary that the two should have known the nature of the transaction which resulted in the conspiracy. In the present case the evidence did indicate that the two officials had gone to the place where the two agents were sitting and the two agents brought the money and took out the money and the money was paid to the two agents who were present at the time of the alleged agreement. The evidence also established that the money was received by the two agents and the money had been paid
4581: The appellant, a dealer in respect of sales and purchases of goods other than newspapers, was assessed to tax under the Orissa Additional Sales Tax Act, 1975 (Orissa Act 24 of 1975) as amended by the Orissa Additional. Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1979 (Act 24 of 1975). The appellant challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that it was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the levy was not discriminatory but was discriminatory. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The State Legislature has power to make laws with retrospective effect from a date not earlier than the date of the commencement of the Act. [369C] 2. The State legislature is competent to enact a law with retrospective operation if it so desires or considers it necessary or expedient for implementing its objects. But the power conferred on the State Government by section 3B of the Principal Act is not an independent power. It is a legislative power. [310D E] 3. The State Government can make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Principal. [311A] 4. The State cannot impose additional tax on dealers who are not liable to pay tax under the Principal Act. [312E] 5. The State has no power to impose any tax retrospectively. [313F]
5785: The petitioners in the batch of writ petitions were directly recruited Assistant Engineers in the Engineering Service of the Roads and Buildings Division of Andhra Pradesh Government. They were promoted as Deputy Executive Engineers by order dated August 8, 1973. The Chief Engineer of the Public Works Department issued a letter on September 9, 1974 to all the Deputy Executive Engineers who had been appointed as Assistant Engineers on ad hoc basis with effect from April 1, 1965. The petitioners challenged the said order by filing a Writ Petition No. 12401 of 1985 in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to be considered for promotion as Executive Engineers and directed the State Government to consider the claim of direct recruits for promotion as such. In the batch of Writ Petitions, the petitioners contended that the retrospective regularisation made by the Chief Engineer of their promotees to the posts of Assistant Engineers was without authority and was in gross violation of the prescription of the Rules. The petitioners also contended that the rules were discriminatory inasmuch as the quota rule was not applied to the direct recruits and the promotees. Dismissing the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The quota rule is applicable only to the direct recruitees and not to the promotees. [382C] 1.2. The quota Rule is not applicable to the direct recruitment but to the promotees as well. The quota is fixed according to the length of service rendered by the direct recruits. The promotees are given the benefit of the weightage of service rendered in the higher post. The promotees have no right to claim seniority over the direct recruits or to get the benefit of continuous officiation in the higher posts. [383E F] 1.3. The quota of 50% is prescribed for direct recruits and 50% for promotees. The quota has to be calculated on the basis of the number of vacancies available in each category. The quota system is based on the number of posts available in each cadre. The quota principle is based on a rational principle and it cannot be said that the quota rule is arbitrary or unreasonable. [384A B] 1.4. The quota provision does not contemplate any artificial breaks. It is intended to provide a reasonable percentage of vacancies for direct recruits. If the quota rule provided for a certain percentage of vacancies
183: The appellant was a member of the Uttar Pradesh Civil Service. He was appointed in 1948 to serve what was then known as the Tonk State in various capacities, and during such service he is alleged to have helped the Nawab in obtaining the sanction of the Government of India to the payment of Rs. 14 lakhs to the Nawab out of the State Treasury for the discharge of his debts, and to have induced the Nawab by threats and deception to pay him in return for such help, sums totalling Rs. 3 lakhs on various dates. On these allegations the appellant was charged with having committed offences under section 383 (Extortion) and 575 Section 420 (Cheating) of the Indian Penal Code which were extraditable offences under the (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). The warrant was issued mala fide on account of enmity. Various technical objections were also raised to the validity of the warrant and to the jurisdiction of the Magistrate at Nainital to take cogni sance of the matter and arrest the appellant. Alladi Krishnaswami Aiyar contended that section 7 of the Act under which the warrant purports to have been issued had no application to the case and that the entire proceedings before the Magistrate were illegal and without jurisdic tion and should be quashed. The High Court rejected all the objections and dismissed the application for release of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 8 of the Act provided that nothing in Chapter III of the Act shall apply to any treaty or agreement between two countries, or to any treatya tion entered into between them prior to the coming into force of the Constitution. HELD : The provisions of section 8 of Act 1 of 1869 are not applicable to the present case. The provisions of the Act are not applicable in the present case because the treaty entered into between the British Government and the Tonkar State on 28th January, 1869, though declared by section 7 of Act 1 1 of 1850, to have lapsed as from the date of its coming into force. [880 E F]
3873: The appellant assessee was a manufacturer of cotton, woollen or silk. In the year 1956, he manufactured cotton yarn and woollens. The assessee claimed exemption from sales tax on the ground that the cotton yarn was not covered by Item 30 of Schedule 'B ' of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948 and therefore, not exempt from sales tax. The assessing authorities held that the cotton fabric was not covered under Item 30 of the Schedule 'B' and hence not exempt from Sales Tax. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner held that the goods were not covered by item 30 of Schedule B 's gross turnover and hence not liable to sales tax. He also held that the assessee had failed to prove that the cotton was not covered in Item 30 of schedule 'B ' and hence not exempted from sales tax and on this view he rejected the claim for exemption. The Tribunal held that the appellant was entitled to exemption from sales Tax on the sale of cotton yarn and that the assessee was not entitled to exemption. The High Court dismissed the reference holding that the appellant did not fall within the description of "all varieties of cotton, whether it is cotton or silk". In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "all varieties" used in the definition of "textiles" in section 2(g) of the Act means all varieties of cotton including woollers, woven fabrics and silk fabrics. [548C] (2) The expression 'all varieties of yarn ' in section 2 (g) of Act means all variety of cotton, cotton cloth and silk. [549D] (3) The expression used in the Explanation to section 2(h) of the Punjab Act means all kinds of cotton, all varieties of yarn other than wooller, woof, silk, woopen, etc., which are not included in the expression "all types of cotton, millet or woolled, as the case may be." [554E] (4) The expression in section 2 of the Act includes all varieties of woolls, wooppers, silk, silk, etc., as the case maybe. [556A] (5) The expression has been defined
1769: The petitioners, who are dealers in coal and other minerals, were assessed to sales tax under the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947. They challenged the validity of the demand for sales tax on the ground that the appropriate authorities purporting to act under the various Sales Tax Acts including the Central Sales Tax Act and the State Transport Undertakings (Transportation) Act, 1948, had no jurisdiction to levy the tax on the sale or purchase of goods effected by them outside the State. Held, that the petitioners could not be said to have a fundamental right under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. Article 32(2) does not confer any new fundamental right but merely provides for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution and it is only when the infringement complained of is of a fundamental right that the question whether the action taken by the appropriate authority was justified or not would arise. The petitioners cannot complain if they have a right to move this Court under article 32. The petitioners do not have a fundamental or statutory right which can be enforced under article 226 of the Constitution; they have a remedy under article 32 and the petitions must therefore fail.
3944: The assessee was a private limited company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of duplicating machines and accessories. 6677: The appellant Corporation was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. It had obtained a loan of Rupees thirty lakhs from the respondent No. 1 for setting up a factory and for securing the loan. In order to secure the loan Respondent No. 1 executed a deed of guarantee dated 29th June 1979 by executing a deed of mortgage of certain properties on 29th June, 1979 and Respondents Nos. 2 to 4 stood surety for repayment of the said loan. The amount of loan was to be advanced in phases and after the Corporation had advanced a part of the total sanctioned loan, the Company did not want to avail of the balance of the amount as it seems to have lost interest in setting up the factory for reasons with which we are not concerned. The Corporation consequently called upon the Company to repay the amount already advanced together with interest and on its failure to do so took steps to recover the same from the sureties whose liability was coextensive and for this purpose it filed a petition in the High Court under Sections 31 and 32 of the Act arraying the Company as Respondent No. I and the sureties as Resigned Directors. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the liability of the respondents with regard to the amount payable to the Corporation was coextricted with the liability of Respondent No.1 and the sureties to the extent of the amount payable by the Corporation to the Corporation. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The liability of the Corporation is coextensive with the liability to pay the Corporation on the date of making of the petition. The liability is coextricably linked with the liability arising out of the loan. [839E] 2. The liability arises when the loan is borrowed for the purpose of carrying out an obligation or undertaking which may be necessary for the benefit of the borrower. The liability can arise only when the loan has been repaid in full or part. The liability cannot be enforced against the guarantor unless he makes payment of the amount due to the Corporation on account of the loan and the liability is co-extricted to the extent provided in the agreement between the parties. [840F G] 3. The liability to pay interest is a statutory liability and the Corporation is entitled to recover
2299: The respondents filed an application under section 11 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953 for permission to fell the trees and the transit pass. The Compensation Officer held that as the applicant was a cultivating tenant over the land he was entitled to acquire right, title and interest of the land owner on payment of Rs. 62.56 as compensation which should be deposited. On appeal by the respondents, the Divisional Forest Officer held that the respondents were not entitled to any proprietary rights in the trees and that the application was barred by limitation. The respondents then applied for a writ of mandamus directing the Divisional Forest officer to issue or get issued the necessary permission for felling the trees and to take back the timber from their land. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the respondents had no right to the trees and directed the Divisional Forest Officers to grant the necessary permission. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The respondents were not in possession of the trees standing on their land as tenants but they were in actual possession of the land. They were not entitled, therefore, to the trees. [114 E] (2) The respondents had no interest in the trees standing in their land as they were not 'land ' as defined in section 2(5) of the Act. The respondents were, therefore, not entitled to the trees in question. [115 F] (3) The respondents could not claim any proprietary rights on the trees standing upon their land as the trees were not 'lands ' within the meaning of section 2(6) of the Himachal Act. [116 G] (4) The respondents did not have any interest in the land as they had no title to it. [117 C] (5) The respondents are not entitled to a proprietary right in the trees. The respondents had only a right to cut the trees and remove them. [118 D]

The word 'import' is used to mean the movement of the goods from one state to another. [1102 B C] (b) The sales are not exigible inter alia to tax. The sales are made in the course. of export. They are not ex
5869: The petitioners who were candidates seeking admission to post graduate courses in the colleges affiliated to the Rajasthan University, challenged the validity of Ordinance 278 E (d) (ii) of the Ordinance of University of Rajasthan which provided for uniform addition of 5% marks in the percentage of aggregate marks by way of institutional preference if the concerned candidates had passed the final MBBS examination. The Ordinance has been enacted to provide for uniformity in the matter of admission to postgraduate courses in medical institutions. The Ordinance makes provision for uniformity of standards of education in medical institutions and lays down that all medical institutions shall have to follow the standards laid down by the Medical Council of India. The Ordinance also prescribes the minimum standard of medical education required for granting recognition or affiliation to medical institutions. [496G H; 497A] 4. The Ordinance, as it stands now, is not a law providing for uniformity for admission to post-graduate courses in any medical institution. It is merely a piece of legislative enactment. It is not a mere piece of subordinate Legislation. It is a piece of substantive legislation. It must conform to the provisions of the parent Act under which it is framed. [497B C] 5. 2405: The respondent brought a suit for pre emption of the land in dispute, which was sold under a sale deed dated February 6, 1942. The case of the respondent was that there was such a custom of pre emption prevailing in the city of Benaras and therefore he was entitled to pre emption as a shafi i jar. The trial court held that there was a custom of prede grace in the city, and therefore, the respondent was entitled to the pre emption. On appeal, the High Court held that the respondent had no right to pre empt the property sold, but only the talabs were performed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not entitled to pre encumber the property sold by him, because the talabs did not exist at all; that the talabs had been performed in Calcutta and therefore the respondent could not be said to have any right to preemption. HELD: (1) The respondent was not a mere owner of the property sold. He was not entitled, therefore, to pre emature the respondent from his right to preempt. [839 E] (2) The respondent had no title to the property sold and therefore the bar of limitation would not apply. [840 F] (3) The respondent could not claim to pre emotion. The bar of limitation is applicable only if the conditions mentioned in section 4 are satisfied. [841 A] (4) The respondent has no right to the preemption. [842 B] (5) The respondent cannot claim to preemption merely because he had a right to preemect the property sold or to put up a new construction thereon. [843 C]
1567: The appellant was the landlord of a premises in Delhi. The respondents were the landlords of the premises. The appellant filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the premises had been let out to the appellant for his residential purposes and that the case should proceed again with the eviction petition. The respondents contended that the premises were bonafide required by the appellant for their own residence, as the first respondent was about to leave the employment of a certain hospital which provided him with residential accommodation. The trial court dismissed the suit but the appellate court confirmed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The contention of the appellant that the premises have been let out for residential purposes is not well founded. It is true that the premises are not bona fide because the premises are reasonably required by the landlord for his own residence. But if the premises are bona fide required by the tenant for his own use, the requirement of the landlord cannot be said to be bona fide. [263 B C] (2) The appellant has failed to prove that he was in occupation of the premises since 1950. He has also failed to establish that he was not a tenant. [264 D] (3) The appellant did not produce any evidence to show that he was a tenant. The appellant merely produced some documents showing that he was residing in the premises since the year 1950. There is no reason why the appellant would not have produced those documents before the Rent Controller when he was in possession of the premises in question. [265 E] (4) The appellant could not be said to have proved that he was entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act. [266 F] (5) The appellant had not led any evidence to prove that the premises in dispute were required by him for his own occupation. The appellant had only produced some documents to show that the premises was required by him. The appellant did neither produce any evidence nor lead any evidence to rebut the presumption under section 114(e) of the Evidence Act. [270 G H]
1585: The respondent, a contractor, entered into two contracts with the Deputy Commissioner of Bhandara for construction of certain buildings for the Bai Memorial Hospital and the Dispensary Funds Committee in the other two suits. The contract was to be completed within six months from the date of its execution. The Deputy Commissioner of the Bhandara District, as the administration head of the hospitals entered into the contract on April 1, 1948, and the Deputy Commissioner, Bhandara, as the Administration head of the hospital entered into the contracts on May 5, 1949. The contract contained an arbitration clause which provided that all claims arising out of or relating to the contract shall be referred to the arbitration of the Deputy Commissioner. The respondent, who was the Deputy Commissioner at the relevant time, filed a suit against the Deputy Commissioner and the Deputy Commissioners of Bhandara, the Deputy Commissioner respectively, for recovery of money due under the contract. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court reversed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Deputy Commissioner, the Deputy Commissioners and the Deputy Com missioners were not parties to the contract. [983 C D] (ii) The Deputy Commissioners had no authority to enter upon the contract. They could only enter upon the contracts if they were entered into after the contract was entered into. [984 E] (iii) The Deputy Commis sioner, Bhandara was not a party to the contract and he could not have entered upon the contract without his consent. [985 F] (iv) The Deputy Commi ssioner, Bhandarara, as a Deputy Commissioner, was not a necessary party to the suit. [986 A B] (v) The Deputy commissioner, Bhandara had no authority either to enter upon or to enter upon any contract. He was merely a servant of the Deputy Commiss ioner. [987 G] (vi) The Deputy Commissioner, Bhandaria, was not the proper party to the proceedings. [988 D] (vii) The Deputy commissioners were not the proper parties to the suit and the suit should have been dismissed. [989 D]
