894: The respondent, a candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the Punjab Legislative Council was declared elected. He filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the appellant on the ground that he had not complied with the provisions of section 117 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and that the receipt enclosed with the petition did not constitute a valid tender of money by him as security for the costs of the petition. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order of the Tribunal dismissing the petition was wrong because the terms of section 117 were complied with. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order under section 98 was made under section 99 and not under section 117. HELD: (i) Section 117 does not provide for any appeal against an order dismissing an election petition but only provides for an appeal against an appellate order. [519B] (ii) The order of the Election Tribunal dismissing the election petition is not appealable under section 116A of the Act. It is open to the appellant to file an appeal against the order of dismissal of his petition under section 98 or section 99. If he files an appeal against such an order, he can do so only if he has filed an appeal against that order. [504C D]
3404: The assessee appellant M/s Kalyanji Mavji & Company was a registered partnership firm dealing in various commercial activities. The said firm filed its return for the year 1956 57 corresponding to the accounting Gujarati Diwali Year 2001 showing a total income of Rs. 7,44,551/ after claiming a deduction of a sum of Rs. 43,116/ being the amount of interest paid by the assessee on the debts incurred for the partnership business. The Income tax officer accepted the return but disallowed the deduction claimed by the appellant. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had not been able to prove that the amount of the deduction claimed was utilised for giving interest free loans to the partners for clearing up their income tax dues and that the amount spent by the assessee for clearing up the income tax dues was not a loan incurred for the purpose of clearing up the arrears of tax due from the partners. The Appellate Tribunal confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court erred in holding that the assessee was entitled to claim deduction of interest paid on the debt incurred for clearing up of his income tax dues. HELD: (1) The expression "information" used in section 34(1)(b) of the Income tax Act, 1922 is very wide and includes information which may be necessary or proper for the purposes of assessment. It does not include information which would have been necessary if the assessee had shown that he had made a true estimate of his income. [969 E F] (2) The word "information " has a wider connotation than the word "or". The word "duty" is not defined in the Income tax law. It is an expression which is generally used in interpretation clauses in order to enlarge the meaning of words or phrases occurring in the body of the statute. It is also used in the sense of information as distinguished from material. The word "document" in the context of the Income-tax Act means documents required to be furnished or furnished under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. [970 A C] (3) The word 'information ' in section 34 of the Income ' tax Act, 1961, must receive a liberal construction
3367: The appellant purchased the managing agency of the Elphinston Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd. for Rupees six lakhs and thereafter entered into a separate managing agency agreement with the managed company for a period of seventeen years. In implementation of this agreement the appellant wrote to the managed company, Elphinstone Spinning and weaving Mills Ltd., tendering resignation of its office as managing agents. The assessee received from Mulshanlal Magan Lal a sum of Rs. 10,00,000 as Compensation for premature termination. The amount received was credited to Capital Reserve Account. The assessee sent a letter to the managed Company, Elphinson Spinning & Weaving Mills Limited, tendering resignation of the office as managing agent. The assessee did not accept the offer and filed a return of income tax for the assessment year 1955 56 for which the assessee received a sum of Rupees ten lakhs as compensation. On further appeal the Tribunal held that the compensation received by the assessee was not taxable under section 10 (5A). The High Court answered the question against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The compensation received by a managing agent is not taxable under the provisions of section 10(1)(b) of the Act. [780 E] The payment of compensation is not a mere reimbursement of expenses incurred by the assessee but it is a payment made to him by way of remuneration for services rendered by him. It is only when he receives remuneration in consideration of his employment or service that he gets the benefit of the provision. [783 F H] The payment is not a payment to a person who has no legal title to the money. It is merely a payment

In order to overcome this situation the directors decided to close the Mills and on the 27th July, 1949, they gave notice of this decision to the workers. The Act was a piece of legislation which was enacted to provide for the control of production, supply and distribution of essential commodities and for the acquisition, holding and disposal of property and for the taking over of the control of such undertakings. 6304: The petitioners are engaged in the business of selling cinematographic films and other equipments like projectors, sound recording and reproducing equipment, industrial X ray films, graphic art films etc. in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The impugned sections are also violative of article 304 (b) of Constitution and are struck down. [709B C]

5104: The appellant was the owner of a building. The respondent landlord sought eviction of the tenant on the ground that the accommodation let for non residential purposes was required bonafide by the landlord for the purpose of building or rebuilding or making thereto any substantial additions or alterations and such additions or alterations cannot be carried out without the accommodation in the occupation of the tenant being vacated. The trial court as well as the appellate court held that the requirement of the landlord for reconstruction of the building was not bona fide. On appeal, the High Court held that the landlord had proved his need for reconstruction of a house and that the landlord was entitled to get possession of the premises vacated. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the landlord could seek eviction only if he required the premises for his own use and occupation and that the High Courts ' decision was erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court rightly held that the case fell under clause (g) which is similar to clause (f) of the instant case before us of Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. [13A] 2. The fact that the landlord intended to make alterations in the house either on account of his sweet will or on account of absolute necessity in view of the condition of the house, would not affect the question of his requiring the house bonafide and reasonably for his occupation when he had proved his requirement for occupying the house. [13B] 3. The fact of the landlord having proved his need of reconstruction of the house for the purpose for which it was let out does not affect the finding of the courts below that the landlord has proved his need. [13C] 4. The fact whether the landlord intended for reconstruction of his house or not is irrelevant. [13D] 5. The fact as to whether the landlord wanted the premises for the purpose mentioned in clause (h) of the proviso to section 12(1)(f) is irrelevant. The fact remains that the landlord did not want the premises for reconstruction. [13E] 6. The fact about the landlord having failed to prove his need for rebuilding the house does not affect his requirement for reconstruction. The fact regarding the landlord 's need for reconstruction is irrelevant
1597: The appellant company was a licensce for supplying electric energy to the public within the area of Akola. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was not unjustified in imposing on it the gratuity scheme at the time when it was closed. The scheme was intended to be implemented after the Company 's license expired. It is true that the Company had been taking over the business of the Company but the question was whether the Company was entitled to the benefit of the scheme. [817 D E] (ii)The Tribunal was right in imposing on its workmen the gratuity schemes at a time if they were not so much as to cover the case of the Company. [818 B C] (iii)In order to give effect to the scheme the Tribunal has to take into consideration the financial condition of the Company and the circumstances of the Company 'Suring the period subsequent to the date of the award. If the Company was in need of money the Tribunal would have taken into account the financial position of the Company, and would have given a direction to the Company to pay the amount due to the workmen. But the Tribunal did not do so. [819 G H; 820 A B]

Section 48 of the Act empowers the Central Government to make rules to carry out the purposes of the Act. Sub section 2 of section 48 provides that every rule made by the Central Government under this Act shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament while it is in session for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry o f the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid both Houses agree in making any modification in the rule or both Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the rule shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so however that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that rule.

5159: The respondents were manufacturing liquor in their own distillery. They were granted licences under the Madhya Pradesh Excise Act, 1915 for manufacture of liquor and for bottling liquor. The respondents challenged the validity of the aforesaid licences on the ground that they were not regulatory measures and were therefore ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed by the respondents holding that the State had no power to impose a tax or duty on liquor manufactured in its own distillery and that the State could not impose a tax on liquor manufactured outside the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State did not have the power to levy a tax or fee on the sale of intoxicants within the State and that the impugned provisions were violative of Article 301 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The State has no power to levy any kind of excise duty or fee. [839E] 2. The State can regulate the manufacture, sale, storage, export, import, transport, purchase and sale of liquor. It is also competent to the State to prohibit the consumption of intoxicating drinks or drugs which are not alcoholic liquors for human consumption. [840F] 3. The State cannot levy any kind or amount of excise duty on liquor sold in the State. [841A] 4. The State may regulate the manufacture or sale of liquor but such prohibition cannot be imposed except by law made by the State legislature. [842B] 5. The State Government has no power either to levy excise duty or to collect the same. [843C] 6. The State is empowered to legislate in respect of liquor. [844D] 7. The State does not have the right to trade or carry on business in liquor. It has no power whatsoever to levy any excise duty or fees. [845G] 8. The State Legislature has no power at all to levy excise duties or fees on liquor. [884H] 9. The State of Madhya Pradesh vs Shambhu Prasad Shukla, [1976] Suppl. SCR 496; M/s. 3065: The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 Indian Penal Code for causing the death of Madhandi Pidariammal. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses that the deceased purchased land from the accused for a sum of Rs. one thousand is not reliable. The evidence of P.W. 1, the Panchyatdars does not inspire confidence. The evidence given by them is not sufficient to prove that the accused had taken part in the commission of the crime. [326 F G] (2) The evidence given on behalf of the accused is not sufficient for convicting the accused. [327 A B] (3) The evidence regarding the fact that the deceased was attacked by the accused is also not reliable. 80: The plaintiffs were the owners of certain lands in the State of Bihar. They had a right to retain possession of the land and to get back the money paid by them. The defendants, who were the tenants, claimed that they were entitled to retain possession on the basis of the settlement made by the mortgagee, Lakhandeo Singh, who was represented by the defendants second party. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the defendants were not raiyats having acquired permanent occupancy rights in the lands as the result of the settlement by the mortgagee. On appeal the High Court held that the defendants could not be ejected on the ground that they were raiyats having been acquired permanent occupancy under section 3(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the High Court erred in law in holding that the respondents were raiyats and that the High Courts ' decision should have been reversed. HELD: (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the defendants had acquired any permanent occupancy rights. [875 C] (ii) The High Courts' decisions are based on the assumption that the defendants acquired permanent occupancy right under section 3 of the Bihar Tenancy Act. The presumption is that the defendants have acquired permanent occupancy. The presumption therefore is that the plaintiffs have acquired permanent ownership. [876 D] (iii) The High courts judgment does not give any indication that the defendants did acquire permanent occupancy. It merely says that the defendants would be entitled to retain the land if they were found to be raiyats having proprietary rights. [887 E] (iv) The High court has rightly held that the plaintiffs were not raiyat or raiyats having title to the land. [886 F] (v) The High 'Court was wrong in its view that the defendants being raiyats having no proprietary rights, the plaintiffs were entitled to remain in possession. [885 G]
4426: The appellant polled votes as against the votes polled by the respondent No. 1 in the election to the State Legislative Assembly. The respondent No.1 challenged the election of the appellant on several grounds including the allegation that he had filed a false return of the expenses and had incurred much more than the permissible limit which amounted to a contravention of section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court accepted the election petition only on one issue, viz., issue No. 4, which related to the corrupt practice as contemplated by section 123(6) of the Representation. of the People act, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the returned candidate had committed no corrupt practice under section 123(4) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts' power to declare an election void is circumscribed by the provisions contained in section 100(1)(b) of the 1951 Act. Section 100(1) (a) provides that if any person who has been elected to be or became subject to any disqualification mentioned in section 10A fails to get himself registered within the prescribed period, he shall be disqualified for being chosen as and for being a member of the House of the Legislature from the date of such election. [633C D] 2. The expression "candidate" in section 100 (1) (d) includes a candidate whose nomination paper has been found to be defective but the defect in the said form has not been cured. The word "codel" means a form of writing, i.e. whether it is used in relation to the form in which it is written or in other words, what it signifies. It does not mean anything more than that. [634E F] 3. The word 'codel ' in section 100 does not include a form of pleading. The word `codel' means a form or form of writing. A person may be qualified to vote at a general election if he is qualified to vote either for the whole constituency or for any part of it. [635F G]
1851: The appellant, a candidate of the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly from Hanumangarh constituency, filed an election petition under section 8 1 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, alleging that he had been guilty of corrupt practice under sub section (4) of section 123 of the Act in publishing a poster exhibit 3, which contained a statement of fact about the personal character and conduct of another candidate. The respondent was the returned candidate. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The burden is upon the person who alleges the corrupt practice to prove that such corrupt practice was committed by the respondent with his consent. The onus is not discharged merely because the respondent has not led evidence to show that the corrupt practices were committed by the appellant with his consent or knowledge. [901 E] (2) The burden of proof is always on the person who asserts the corrupt practice. The onus of proving the said corrupt practice is on the person making the allegation. If the allegations made are proved, the burden shifts on the person challenging the election to prove that there was no corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4). [902 F H] (3) The burden to prove that a particular corrupt practice was adopted by the respondent is on the respondent. He must discharge that burden. [903 A B]

4923: The appellants were the transferees of certain lands in their possession. They filed applications before the Collector under the Abolition Act for revision of the order of the Collector and the Board of Revenue, which upheld the orders of the Collector. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Revenue Officers while exercising powers under the Abolition Acts were not exercising the powers as revenue officers but as a persona designata under the Abolition act. HELD: (1) Under section 84 of the Abolition Act an appeal lay against all orders passed by the Collector or the Board of Revising Authority under the Code. The power conferred on the Commissioner is only a right of appeal provided under the Code and not a right of revision. [902 B] (2) Section 84 of the Act confers no power of revision on the Board of the Revenue. It merely provides that the Board may revise any order passed by the Revenue Officer under the provisions of the Act. The Board has no power to revise any order of the Revenue Officer. [903 C D] (3) The Board of Revenue under the Abolition law is a court within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Abolition law. The Board of Revise Authority is a creature of the statute and its decision cannot be reviewed by the Board of Revision. [904 E F]

The High Court of Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad and the High Court of Allahabad have been exercising their revisional jurisdiction under section 397 read with Section 401 Cr. P.C. in respect of the sentence awarded by the trial court. In exercise of its revisional power under Section 397 read with Sec. 401 Cr.P.C., the High Court has limited the scope of the revisional powers to the extent that it is permissible for the High Court to enhance the sentence without issuing notice to the appellant or affording him an opportunity of showing cause against such enhancement. This Court in Bachan Singh etc. vs State of Punjab, [1980] 1 SCR 645 while dealing with the revisional powers of the High Court under Section 397 Cr. P C. has ruled thus: "In view of the above discussion, we hold that the High Court was not competent to enhance the punishment without issuing notice and giving opportunity of hearing to the appellant. We accordingly set aside the conviction of the appellant under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC and the conviction of other two under Section 20 I.P.c. and enhanced the sentence to seven years rigorous imprisonment." The High Court did not issue any notice to the accused before enhancing the sentence. The High Court enjoys the power of revision under Section 397 r/w Section 401 Cr P C. In this appeal, on behalf of the appellants, it was contended that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to enhance the sentences without issuing notice. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The High Courts are empowered to exercise suo motu power of revision in appropriate cases where the sentence awarded is grossly inadequate or excessive. [704A] 1.2. The High courts have been invested with the power of a Court of Appeal under Section 386(c) of the Code. It is permissible for them to exercise the revisional power under section 397 r/ w Section 401 Cr, P C. [705B] 1.3. The High court exercises revisional jurisdiction under Section 397, Cr. PC. in case of an appeal by the State against the order of acquittal. [706D] 1.4. The High 'Court does not exercise the revisional jurisdiction under s. 397 read with section 401 Cr.

247: The appellants, who were the mortgagors of certain properties in West Bengal, filed a suit for rendition of accounts and for recovery of money due to them. The respondents contended that the decree was not executable as it was passed by a court having no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and that the decree had been obtained by fraud. Held, that the decree could be executed only by the Court having its own jurisdiction and not by the Court which passed it. The decree was not a nullity because it was passed on the basis of the consent of the parties. The consent of the decree holders was necessary before the execution of the decree. The consent order did not confer any title upon the respondents. The consent orders were binding on the respondents and they were not liable to be evicted from the properties purchased by the decree holders. The consent decrees were not voidable at the instance of the respondents. A compromise decree is a contract between the parties and the rights and obligations of the parties are governed by the terms thereof. The consent decree was not merely a formal expression of the rights of the parties but was intended to be a complete discharge of the decree debt. The consent terms were not binding on the parties when they entered into the compromise. The consent awards were not enforceable under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940, as the decree was a contract between two parties and the parties thereto. The consent award was not a decree within the meaning of section 2(2) of the Bengal Act. The consent judgment was therefore not a decree.

3195: The appellants, small manufacturers of matches, have been subjected to excise duty at the same onerus rate as has been applied to larger producers who are unequal in their economic capabilities in the matter of production and marketing a sort of traumatic egality. In the process of manufacture of matches the appellants have been subjected by the impugned notification to excise duty on matches which were not manufactured within the country. The appellants had been subjected to the same treatment as the other manufacturers of match manufacturers. The appellants contended that the classification made by the impugned notifications was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The classification is based on an intelligible differentia and it cannot be said that it is based on any discernible rational principle. [701 B] (ii)The classification must be founded on an intelligent differentia and the differentia must bear a just relation to the object sought to be achieved. It would not be open to the court to sit in appeal over the policy decision and examine whether the policy in its entirety is arbitrary or unreasonable. [702 C D]

5087: The appellant was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1967 68. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the delay in furnishing the return under section 208 was not due to any fault on the part of the appellant but due to the fact that the appellant had been informed by the Department that the return would be filed within three months from the date of receipt of the notice of demand. The appellant appealed against the order of the Appellate Assistant commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal holding that the delay was due to the appellant 's failure to furnish the return within the time prescribed and that there was no sufficient cause for condonation of delay. In the revision petitions filed by the appellant, the High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 215 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the delay in filing the return was due to circumstances beyond the control of the appellant; (ii) the delay was attributable to the appellant and therefore the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed in the petition; (iii) the delay should have been condoned by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner; and (iv) the appellant was estopped from challenging the validity of the notice issued by the Income Tax Officer. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The delay in filing a return is not due to the fault of the assessee but due to some other bona fide mistake or omission. [851C] 2.1. The delay can be condoned only if the assessee has shown sufficient cause for the delay in question. [852E] 3.1. It is open to the assessee to file a revised return after the expiry of the period of limitation provided under section 215(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961, and the assessee may claim the benefit of that provision. 1707: The appellant was declared elected to the State Assembly. He filed a petition under section 86(1) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for setting aside the election on the ground that there had been improper reception, refusal and rejection of votes at the time of counting. The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had not proved his case beyond reasonable doubt. On appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside the election as the appellant had failed to prove his case; (ii) the Tribunal could not have accepted the evidence of the appellant in regard to the allegations made against him; and (iii) the Tribunal having held that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice, the Tribunal should have given an opportunity to both the parties to inspect the ballot papers and other connected papers. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has power to examine the correctness or otherwise of the findings recorded by the Tribunal. [230 D] (a) The Tribunal is not entitled to go into the question whether the election was void because the election was not declared void but only voidable. It is open to the Tribunal to consider whether the election of the returned candidate is liable to be declared void if it finds that the result of the election has been materially affected. If the Tribunal finds that the election of a returned candidate is void, the Tribunal will give the returned candidate an opportunity to amend the petition and also to adduce additional evidence. [231 G H] (b) The Tribunal can decide whether the election is void because of the improper acceptance of any nomination or improper rejection of any vote or because the result of election has been affected. In such cases the Tribunal may proceed to examine the validity of the election on merits. [232 B C] (c) The Tribunal cannot go behind the original Form 20 and hold that the appellant has not proved his contention that he was not duly nominated as a candidate. [233 E] (d) The Tribunal must first decide whether the appellant has proved his election to the State Legislative Assembly. If the finding is that the appellant is not duly nominated, then the Tribunal would have to give an opportunity to the appellant to amend the Petition and adduce additional evidence in support of his case. The sales tax authorities held that the appellant was not entitled to exemption from inter State sales tax under section 5(2) (a)(iv) of the State Act. On appeal by special leave, HELD : The Explanation to section 8(2A) of the Central Act is as follows: "Explanation to section 8 (2A) (i) Where a sale or purchase of any goods has been exempted from tax generally or where such goods are sold to a registered dealer other than the Government, then, notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1A) of section 6 or sub section (I) or sub section

(2) of this section, the tax payable under this Act by a dealer on his turnover in so far as the turnover or any part thereof relates to the sale of any goods shall be calculated at the lower rate. " The Explanation to the said section does not say that the sale or purchase should be exempt only from payment of tax. It merely says that the sale of goods should be exempt from tax generally. In the present case, the appellant had no such exemption. [839 E F] The Explanation to s. 8(2 A) of the Act is not an exception to the general rule laid down in section 5(1) (a) of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1948. The Explanation to sub section (2A), however, lays down that the sale must be made to a registered person who is liable to pay tax under the Act. 544: The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple in the State of Madras, filed a suit for framing a scheme for this temple. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The right of a religious denomination to manage its own affairs in matters of religion guaranteed under article 26(b), is subject to, and can be controlled by, law which is protected by article 25(2)(b). [701 B C] (2) The right to manage its property is not subject to any restriction imposed by article 25 (2)(b) on the exercise of the right conferred by article 26(c). [702 D E] (3) The right conferred by Article 25(2) is subject to the restrictions contained in article 26(a) and (b) of the Constitution. The right to administer an institution is not subject either to the restrictions imposed by article 26 or article 27(b) of that article. [703 A B] (4) The right guaranteed by article 26 is subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the law made by Parliament under article 25(6) read with article 26(d) of the constitution. The restrictions imposed by section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure are reasonable restrictions within the meaning of article 25(5) of the Constitutent Assembly of India. [704 F G] (5) The right under article 26 is not subject only to the restrictions mentioned in article 25(1) but also to the restrictions specified in article 25 (4) and (5) of that Part. [705 H; 706 A] (6) The right is subject to restrictions imposed by articles 26 and 27 of the Constitution and is not subject merely to the restrictions referred to in article 26. [707 B C]
3983: The respondent was the plaintiff in a suit for partition and separate possession of certain properties. The appellant instituted a suit for a declaration that the dismissal of his application amounted to a decree for partition and for recovery of possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but dismissed it on the ground that the decree did not amount to a decree of partition. The High Court allowed the appeal, holding that the decree was a decree for specific performance of an agreement for sale of the property and that the decree could be enforced only against the purchaser. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The decree was a money decree as defined in section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The decree was therefore a money decree. [811 D] (2) The decree passed by the trial court was a money judgment. The decree did not become a money decree because the decree was not a money decree within the meaning of section 2(3). [812 E] (3) The decree did nothing more than a decree for a sum of money which had been paid into Court or which may have been received by the decree holder from the purchaser. [813 F] (4) The decree being a money decree, it was not a decree for money decree. It was merely a money decree and not a money judgment because the decree did nothing other than a money decree for the purpose of execution. [814 G] (5) The decree in question was a money suit. The decree in the present case was a money money decree. The decree passed in favour of the respondent was a money order. [815 B] (6) The decree, though it was a money award, was a money compromise decree. The respondent was entitled to recover possession of the land in execution of the decree. [916 C]
233: The Government of Madras issued a notification under section 14(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, appointing a Special Magistrate to try certain offences. The first petitioner was an Agricultural Demonstrator in the State of Madras and was employed as an Assistant Marketing Officer in Central Provinces and Berar for the purchase and movement of blackgram and other grains on behalf of the Madras Government. He was prosecuted by the Government of Madras for cheating, attempt to commit cheating, criminal breach of trust, criminal conspiracy, and criminal conspiracy. The second petitioner was convicted under section 420 read with section 120 B and section 409 I.P.C., and sentenced to one year rigorous imprisonment. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the sanction given by the Government was invalid because the order of the Government granting the sanction did not disclose that all the facts constituting the offence were placed before the sanctioning authority ; (ii) the sanction granted by the Government under section 197(1) Of the Criminal Procedure code was invalid because it had been obtained without the sanction of the Government; (iii) the sanction was bad since the Government had not applied its mind to the question whether the offence alleged against the first petitioner was committed by him or by some other person; and (iv) the sanction being valid was invalid because no sanction was necessary under section 197 of the Criminal procedure Code. HELD : (i) The sanction is valid even if it is not signed by the Government. [440 E] (ii) The sanction was valid when it was given. It could be withdrawn at any time before it was signed by the sanctioning authority. [442 F] (iii) The sanction given by Government was valid when the Government had applied its mind. [445 A] (iv) The sanction granted by Government was effective only after it was issued by the Government and it could not be withdrawn at a later stage. [446 D]
1250: The appellant company entered into a contract with the respondent for assembling and installation of machinery, plants and machinery. On December 19, 1953, the appellant entered into a Contract with the respondent. Under the terms of the contract, the appellant was to supply all materials and labour required for the execution of the works and that the performance was to be split up into two categories, the German section and the Indian section. The agreement provided that the appellant was liable to pay sales tax on the value of the materials used by them in the execution of works. The appellant 's case is that the work was completed in 1955 and the price paid was Rs. 2,31,50,000. The appellant contended that the contract was not a sale but only a transfer of property in goods involved in the execution thereof. Held, that the contract did not involve any transfer of property or right in goods within the meaning of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947, and the appellant was not entitled to claim that the transaction was a sale. The contract was one for the purpose of carrying out the works and the appellant had no right to ask for its performance. The contract did not create any title in the goods nor did it create any liability in respect of the price paid. The contract merely related to the delivery of the materials and not the completion of the works. The contract being one for the sale of goods, the sale was not a transfer of the property in the goods. The contract, therefore, did not amount to a sale.

707: The appellant, who was a candidate for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State of Madras from Alangulam Constituency in the District of Tirunelveli, filed nomination papers for election to Legislative Assembly of that State. He alleged that he was the Head Master of the National Training School, Tiruchendur and that he had been disqualified under section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 as holding an office of profit under the Government. The returning officer rejected the nomination paper on the ground that he was not qualified to be chosen as a candidate at the time of scrutiny. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was disqualified under sections 7(d), (e) and (f) of the Act as he was not a member of the Legislative Assembly at the time when his nomination was accepted; that the appellant could not be said to have ceased to be a member of a Legislative Assembly merely because he was interested as a partner in contracts for the execution of works for the Government and that the appellant had entered into an agreement with the District Board, Chittoor, for the execution and registration of works for Government. Held: (i) that the appellant is not disqualified under section 8(1)(a) of the , as he was neither a member of Legislative Assembly nor a member of any local authority within the meaning of section 3(2) of the . It was not necessary that he should have been a member of an association or body of persons which was not registered under the Act. The fact that he was a member of another association or body does not make him disqualified under section 9(1)(c). (ii)The appellant was not disqualified under sections 10(1)(b) and (d) of Act 43 of 1951 as he was a nonmember of the Legislative Council of the State. (iii)Section 10(3) of the Election Commission of India Act, 1950, provides that if a person has become subject to any disqualification mentioned in section 10(1) he shall cease to be a Member of Parliament.
40: The appellants were prosecuted for offences under sections 147, 148, 323, 324, 326 and 302/149 of the Indian Penal Code at the instance of one Polai Lal Biswas who was leading the mob. The prosecution case was that while the complainant was harvesting paddy crop on his field at about 10 a.m. on 29th November, 1949, a mob of about fifty persons came on to the field armed with ballams, lathis and other weapons and that the first appellant Logendra and others gave a stick blow to one of the labourers, Kangali, who fell down and died on the spot. The appellants pleaded not guilty contending inter alia that Mohender and Debender were not present in the village when the occurrence took place and that they had no motive to falsely implicate them. The Sessions Judge found that the existence of factions as alleged by the appellants was true. He also held that the plea of alibi was not satisfactorily made out. The High Court acquitted the appellants holding that the evidence showed that the appellants were not present at the time of the occurrence but were present at the scene of occurrence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence did not establish that the appellants had any intention to commit murder or that they knew that the deceased was likely to cause death. HELD : (1) There is nothing in the evidence to show that the appellants intended to kill the deceased. It is not suggested that the appellants wanted to take revenge from the deceased. [311 B] (2) The fact that the appellants did not know that the deceased would be killed does not mean that they intended to kill him. The fact that they did not know the names of the assailants does not lead to the inference that they intended the murder. [312 C D] (3) The appellants were entitled to acquittal because they did not offer any explanation for their presence at the scene. [313 E] (4) The appellants could not be convicted merely because they did know that the incident took place. [314 F]

1706: The appellants, who were the owners of certain lands belonging to them, filed applications under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act for referring the matter for a reference to the Court. 4714: The respondent, a workman in the appellant Corporation was discharged from service on account of unsatisfactory service. He filed an industrial dispute which was referred to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held that termination of service amounted to retrenchment and directed reinstatement with back wages. The employer Corporation challenged the decision before the High Court which upheld the decision of the Labour Court holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination of service of the respondent was not retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for non compliance with section 25F of the . Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service is not retrenchment. [880C] 2. The termination does not amount to retrenchment. It is only when the employee is retrenched. Section 2(oo)(c) of the defines retrenchment as meaning "termination of service by the employer on any ground other than misconduct". [880D] 3. The definition of retrenchment is not exhaustive but includes all circumstances or facts specified therein. It may be possible to contend that the termination is not retrenchment because the employee has been retrenched without complying with the provisions of section 25F. But the fact remains that the termination amounts to retrenchment. [881E F] 4. The termination is not termination simpliciter but is by way of punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. The termination can be said to be retrenchment if the conditions precedent are satisfied. [882G] 5. The termination by itself cannot be said to have been made in accordance with the provisions contained in section 25F, because the termination is by way or punishment inflicted by the nature of the job or employment. [883A B] 6. The termination will not amount to termination of service by way of penalty. [884B] 7. The termination must be in accordance with section 25FFF of the Act. [885C] 8. The termination would be by way of dismissal or removal from service. [886D]
1135: The respondent Sabha was the successor of the Mining Board exercising its powers under section 51 of the Madhya Pradesh Local Self Government Act, 1920. The respondent Sabha had issued notices against them calling upon them to pay coal tax for coal manufactured at the mines sold for export by rail within the territorial jurisdiction of the original Independent Mining Board. On March 12, 1935, the Mining Board notified the rules for the assessment and demand of the tax in question. On March 16, 1947, the Mining Boards exercising their powers under section 79 (1), clauses (xv), (xix) and (xxx) of the Act, resolved to levy coal tax and accordingly the first imposition made by it received the sanction of the local Government on December 16, 1935, as per Notification No. 8700 2253 D VIII, dated December 16, 1936, as amended by Notification No. 389/XV/XXXVI dated January 1, 1938. On March 17, 1948, the Mining board issued a notice to the respondent Sabha asking it to pay the coal tax levied under the Act. [748 E F] The notice is not bad because it does not state that the rate was increased from time-to time. The notification does not say that the rate should be increased from the date specified in the notification. The notification merely states that the rate shall be increased from lime to time. [749 C] The notice does not specify the date on which the tax was to be increased. The notice does neither state that the

[511C] (ii) The tenant was in occupation of a residential accommodation at M 18, Greasing Building, New Delhi, and the landlord had no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation. The landlord could have easily obtained the accommodation from the tenant if he
1056: The appellants were assessed to income tax for the year 1950 51 corresponding to the assessment year 1949 50. The Income Tax Officer passed on that return an order "no proceeding" and closed the assessment. For the assessment year 1951 52, the appellants filed their returns disclosing a total income of Rs. 1,37,000 odd as on March 31, 1950, which included the amount of Rs. 2,87,000 odds. The Income tax Officer held that the balance of Rs.1,87, 000 was not taxable in the assessment year 1950 51 but it should be taken into consideration while determining the net wealth of the appellants for the assessment year 1952 52. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the appeal. In further appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the appellants having failed to furnish the accounts of the previous years, the only course open to the Income Tax Officer was to take the financial year ending March 31,1950, as the previous year, and that the only course available to the Income tax Officer was to consider the credit in the assessment for the year corresponding to the year of assessment 1949 50 after giving opportunity to the appellants to show cause against the proposed action. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Income Tax officer did not act in accordance with the provisions of section 34(2)(a) of the Indian Income Tax Act. He merely acted as an agent of the assessee and he could not be said to have exercised his option under section 2(ii) of the Act. [550 C] (ii)The Income Tax Officer did not act according to law. [560 D] (iii)The Income tax officer did not exercise his power under section 22(2) of the Income Tax Act in respect of the assessment year 1948 50. The order of assessment was made by him on March 31. 1950. The Income 'tax Officer did not take into account the credit in respect of
6991: The respondent, while working as Income Tax Officer during the year 1982 83 completed certain assessments in the case of : (1) M/s Channaiah Automobiles, (2) N.S. Gupta Cotton Industries, (3) M/S Tilak Cotton Industries, and (4) M/ s Tilak Trading Co., was served with a charge memorandum dated 2.5.1989 alleging that he had failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty and exhibited a conduct unbecoming of a Govt. servant thereby violating provisions of Rules 3(1)(i), 3(1) (ii) and 3(1). The charges were denied by him. The respondent submitted his written statement of defence denying the charges levelled against him. The Inquiry Officer held the charges proved and imposed a penalty of reduction of pay by one stage for a period of three years without cumulative effect. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Appellate Authority which was rejected on 8.2.1991. Thereafter, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the inquiry conducted against the respondent was not fair and proper and quashed the orders of dismissal. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly held that the inquiry was vitiated because it did not follow the procedure prescribed under Rule 14 of the CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965. [306B] 2. The Tribunal was right in quashing the order of punishment. [307C] 3. The Tribunal committed an error in dismissing the application of the respondent. [308D] 4. The Tribunal could have remanded the matter back to the Disciplinary Authority to pass fresh orders after complying with the principles of natural justice. But the Tribunal has not done so. [309E] 5. The Tribunal should not have interfered with the findings of fact recorded by the Inquiry Officer or the disciplinary authority unless they are found to be perverse. [305F] 6. The Tribunal ought not to have interfered with only those findings. [304G]
2374: The appellant obtained an order for eviction from the respondent 's premises in execution of a decree passed by the Subordinate Judge. The respondent applied to execute the decree but the executing court rejected it on the ground that the application was barred by res judicata. The High Court held that the respondent had not obtained permission under section 19(1) of the Act and that the judgment debtors were not entitled to obtain stay of execution of the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the respondent could not be dispossessed without obtaining the permission of the Government. [501 B] (ii) The High Courts have been consistent with the view taken by the High Court that the respondent cannot be dispossessed except by recourse to the provisions of the Act. [502 C] (iii) The High courts are also consistent with the views expressed by the High Courts. [503 D] (iv) The High court has rightly held that the judgment debtor can not be dispossessed without obtaining the consent of the Government or the Court. [504 E]
4013: The appellant State Electricity Board and the Executive Engineer of the Rihand Power Station, hereinafter collectively referred to as the Board, entered into an agreement with the respondent State for supply of electrical energy for the production of aluminium. The metal is now produced by the modern electrolytic method under the influence of direct current. It takes about 10 kilo watt hours of electricity to produce a pound of aluminium, and the supply of cheap electric power is also an essential commodity under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951. The metal has many advantages and uses and has gained importance and has gnede ingots and other metals. The metal was produced by the new electric power plant which had been set up in the Riand Power Station. The metal had many advantages, uses and have gained importance that it is an essential commodity within the meaning of the Essential Commodities Act and its production is one of the scheduled industries under the Industries 'Development and Regulation Act. While the State feels aggrieved because the High Court had interfered with the Uttar Pradesh Electricity (Regulation of Supply, Distribution, Consumption and Use) Order, 1977, dated September 19, 1977, hereinafter referred to as 'the Order', which it made under section 22B of the Electricity Act, 1910, the Company contended that the High Court should not interfere with the Uttar Poornima Commission on the ground that the Commission had no jurisdiction to decide whether the supply of electrical goods was an essential commodity or not. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the Commission could not grant all the reliefs which it had claimed in its petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [719C] 1.2 The High Court has rightly held that the Commission can grant only such relief which it had prayed for in its petition. [720E] 1.3 The High Court cannot go behind the terms of the contract between the parties. The Commission has to be given a wider meaning than what it had originally given to it in its earlier order. [721D E] 1.4 The Commission has got the power to determine whether the supply is an essential activity or not. The Commission may give directions to the State
4687: The respondent was detained under section 3(1) of the (hereinafter called 'the Act') on the grounds that he and three others were found in a trawler containing eight packages with four packages with 4,645 contraband wrist watches valued at Rs. 10,48,700.00. The petitioner made a statement admitting that he was engaged as a member of the crew but denied any knowledge of the contraband goods. He stated that he was a member of crew but admitted that he was involved in smuggling activity. The detaining authority did not accept the plea of the petitioner and passed an order of detention against him. The High Court quashed the order of detention on the ground that the respondent had no "full knowledge" that the vessel was to be used for smuggling activities. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The satisfaction reached by the detaining authority cannot be said to be genuine on the material placed before the detaining authority. [847E] 2. The fact that the maximum penalty prescribed is five years imprisonment and fine would meet the ends of justice. [846A] 3. The satisfaction recorded by the detaining Authority cannot be said either to be genuine or bona fide on the material which was placed before the Detaining Authority. [849B] 4. The satisfaction must be based on some material placed before it. [850C] 5. In view of the fact that the minimum punishment prescribed is five year imprisonment and fine, the order of the detention cannot be sustained. [851D]
7115: The appellant company was ordered to be wound up on the ground that subscription of Rs. 10 crores and odd by the subscribers were not paid, as a body of creditors, within the time specified in the order dated September 30, 1984. The High Court directed the winding up order to be held in abeyance on condition that the holding company shall execute a security bond to cover subsidiary company 's liability to the extent of a sum of Rs.10.40 crores owed to its subscribers. The appellant company filed an application for extension of time to pay the amount due under the scheme of compromise and arrangement. The High court allowed the application and extended the time till October 31, 1985. On appeal by special leave, it was contended: (i) The High Court erred in directing payment of Rs. 2 crores towards the principal amount and Rs. 10.40 crores towards interest on the principal amount; (ii) The High court should have directed the holding company to deposit the amount in a separate bank account and the High Court should have directed that the holding Company should deposit the amount with the Registrar of Companies, Kerala, in a separate Bank Account; (iii) The High Courts direction to deposit the money in a separate account is contrary to law and cannot be sustained; (iv) The High courts direction to deposit Rs. 2 crore towards principal amount and interest on the amount of Rs. 1 crore from the date of the order of the High Court till the date of deposit is contrary to the directions of this Court in Ghanshamdas vs State of Bombay, ; and (v) The High Cour t should have directed payment of Rs, 2 crores towards principal amount, interest on the same amount from the date when the High Court ordered the winding up to be in abeyance. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court has committed an error in directing payment to the appellant of Rs.2 crores towards principal and interest on Rs.10 crores from the date the High Court passed the winding up orders. [907 E F] 1.2 The High Court could not have directed payment to the subscribers who had subscribed to the chit fund. The High Courts order was made without giving any opportunity to the subscribers to show cause why they should not be rest
3452: The appellant brought a suit in the court of the Assistant Collector, Baran for possession of land comprised in khasra Nos. 513 and 678 situate in village Balakhera under sections 180 and 183 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). By his judgment dated December 24, 1962, the 589 Assistant Collector dismissed the suit holding that Birdhi Lal was a trespasser. The appellant thereupon preferred an appeal to the Board of Revenue which was allowed by its order dated November 9, 1963. The Board of Revenue held that Birdi Lal being a trespasser was not liable to be ejected from the land. Aggrieved by the decision of the Board of Revising Authority and the Board of revenue, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the correctness of the decision of both the authorities. The High Court allowed the petition and held that Birdar was a trespassers and there was no error apparent on the face of the record. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'trespasser ' is defined in section 5(44) of the Act as follows: "5(44) Trespasser shall mean a person who takes or retains possession of land without authority or without permission of the owner." [580B] 1.2 The expression 'Tenant ' has been defined in section 2(6) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952 as follows: "(6) 'Landlord ' means a person who cultivates or holds land under another person and is or but for a special contract would be deemed to be a tenant;" [581C D] 1.3 The expression 'tenant ' is defined under section 2(4) of the Tenancy Act as follows:- "2(4) 'tenant ' means a tenant, other than a permanent tenant, who cultivates the land of himself, and whose rights are extinguished by the provisions of this Act, or any other law for the time being in force, and includes a person who, with the consent of the landlord, continues to cultivate the land after the tiller's day of the year, and also includes a sub-tenant who cultiv
3425: The respondent joined the Punjab Education Service (Class II) service by direct recruitment as senior lecturer in 1933. He was promoted to the post of Director of Public Instruction cum Secretary to Government, Punjab Education Department on October 1, 1949. He proceeded on leave preparatory to retirement on March 18, 1958. In June 1961 he received a copy of letter No. 5137 EDI 4(64) 65/22436 dated October 21, 1965 addressed by the Secretary to Government Punjab Education Department to the Director of Public Instructions and the Governor of Punjab Education Department intimating that his case had been examined with reference to rule 6.4 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules Vol. II read with para 9(1)(a) of the New Pension Rules, 1951. On January 28, 1962, the respondent submitted representations to the Chief Minister and Governor of Punjab against the aforesaid decision of the Government to apply 10% cut in his pension and gratuity. The Chief Minister and the Governor rejected the representation of the respondent. Thereafter, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order rejecting his claim for pension and death cum retiral gratuity. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the 10% cut under the new pension rules. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent is not entitled to any relief. [372B] 2. The respondent has no right to claim the benefit of pension or gratuity. The respondent cannot claim the benefit merely because he retired from service. [373C] 3. The respondent was entitled only to the benefit under the old rules. The respondent could not claim the benefit under those rules if he had retired prior to the date when the new rules came into force. [375E] 4. The respondent had no right to get the benefit of any particular rule. [376A] 5. The respondent having retired from service on March 18. 1958, he would be entitled to the benefits of the old rules which were applicable to him at the time of his retirement. [377F]
2200: The appellants purchased cotton from various dealers in Punjab and outside for the manufacture of yarn and cloth. Under the Act, the assessing authority imposed purchase tax on the goods purchased by them for the assessment year 1958 59 and 1959 60. The appellant filed petitions under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the orders of the assessing authorities and for restraining them from levying purchase tax on them. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeals to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions as the appellants were not dealers within the meaning of section 5(2) of the East Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948, and that the High Courts erred in holding that the appellants were dealers within the scope of section 5 (1) (b). HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in its view that the appellants could not be said to be dealers within the ambit of section 5 of the Act. [541 C] (ii)The High Court was right in holding that section 5(1)(b) was void because it did not provide for any exemption from sales tax. [542 D] (iii)Section 5(1) (a) provides that a dealer shall be liable to pay tax on the sale or purchase of goods if he is engaged in the business of selling or purchasing goods. Section 5(1), therefore, does not provide for exemption from payment of tax on the purchase of goods. [543 E]
1307: The appellant, a debtor in the second suit for enforcement of his mortgage, obtained a decree for payment of Rs. 2,000/ and interest and costs. In execution of that decree, the mortgaged property was sold for Rs. 4,160/ and an amount of Rs. 1,431/ was still due and payable under the mortgage decree. Out of the three parcels of land sold, three were purchased by Mondal and the remaining one was purchased by Mittra. Mondal applied for a personal decree under 0. 34, r. 6 of the Civil Procedure Code and obtained on September 7, 1940, a decree for Rs. 2.000/ and an order for rendition of the decree was made. Mondals applied for executing the decree. The Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit as it was barred by res judicata. In Second Appeal No. 1442 of 1942, the High Court set aside the decree of the Subordinate Judge and restored the decree of Mondal. In Second appeal No. 1443 of 1942, a single judge of the High Court held that the preliminary decree passed by the Subordinate Judge was not binding on the appellant and that the decree was not executable against him. In Second Appeals Nos. 1444 to 1445 of 1942, it was contended before this Court that the decree passed by a court in a suit for recovery of money is not binding on a party unless he has been impleaded in the suit or proceedings. HELD: (i) The decree passed by an inferior court in a proceeding for the recovery of money cannot be executed against a person who is not a party to the suit. [350 A] (ii) The decree is not executable as a decree passed by such inferior court. It is only a final judgment and not a decree passed in a suit. [302 B C] (iii) The decree does not operate as res judicata between the parties to the suit but it operates as a bar to the institution of any subsequent suit or proceeding after the decree in question. [305 D] (iv) The decree in the present case is not a final judgment. It is merely a final judgment because it is not a decree which can be executed either by the trial court or by the appellate court
2933: The respondent was carrying on business as a dealer in watches in Calcutta. In 1955, he used to have another business premises where he carried on the same business and seized watches of certain watches. On March 19, 1963, the Rummaging Officer seized the watches of the respondent under section 110(a) of the Customs Act, 1962. The Collector of Customs ordered confiscation of the watches and personal penalty. The respondent 's appeal to the Central Government failed. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Collector of Customs. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Collector had no power to extend the period for giving notice under section 124(a) to the owner of the watched property. Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: (1) The proviso to sub section (2) of section 110 of the Customs, Act, 1962 provides that no order confiscating any goods or imposing any penalty on any person shall be made if the owner of such goods furnishes a statement showing the value of the goods confiscated and the amount of penalty imposed. [683 F] (2) The proviso does not make it obligatory upon the Collector to give an opportunity to the owner to show cause why the order should not be passed. It is only when the Collector decides to exercise his discretion under sub section (4) of section 124 that he can pass an order confiscating the goods. [685 C D] (3) The proviso makes it clear that the Collector has no power to issue a notice under section 125(2). [686 E] (4) The Collector has no jurisdiction to pass an order of confiscation of the goods unless he has given an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken. [687 A B] (5) The proviso cannot be read as enabling the Collector to pass an ex parte order of confiscation without hearing the owner of goods. [690 G] (6) The Collector may proceed to take action under section 124A after the expiry of six months from the date of seizure of the watwar. [688 H]
6019: The appellants instituted a suit for declaration of their homestead right in the land and for confirmation of possession. The respondent claimed that the land formed part of the North Bhuggatdih Colliery which had vested in the Central Government under section 3 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The appellants contended that the disputed land formed part 's of the North Bhikhabhai Colliery which was vested in the State of Bihar by virtue of the notification issued under section 3(1) of the Bihar Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. The trial court rejected all the defences and decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court reversed the decree holding that the lease granted to the appellants in the instant case was an encumble with the mining lease and that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. In this appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the disputed lands formed part of North Bhuggata Colliery which vested in the Government under section 4 of the Act and that the vesting of the estate in the Central Govern ment did not take place as a result of any act or omission of the Central Government. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the disputed land forms part of the coal mine or not is a mixed question of law and fact. [311C] 2. The question of title cannot be decided in a proceeding under article 226 of the Constitution. [312D] 3. The High Court has rightly held that the suit filed by the appellants was barred by res judicata. [313E] 4. The High court was wrong in holding that the suit was barred by constructive res judicata. The question as to the nature of the suit is essentially a question of fact. It is open to the parties to adduce evidence in support of their respective cases. [314F] 5. The question about the nature of possession of the appellants does not arise at all because the appellants have not been able to establish that they are in possession of the disputed land. [315B C] 6. The question regarding the nature of title cannot also be decided in the present proceedings. [316A] 7. The question relating to the nature and extent of
975: The appellant was a non resident for the purposes of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. He did not submit returns of his income for those years and he did not submit any returns of his total income for those assessment years. In exercise of the powers under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922, the Income Tax Officer served notices on the appellant for assessment of tax in respect of those years. The appellant 's case was that the notices were invalid because they were issued after the period of limitation prescribed by section 34(2) of the Act. Held: (i) The proceedings for assessment were commenced within the period of eight years from the end of the year in which the notice was served on the appellant; (ii)The notices were valid in law; (iii)The assessments made in respect of the years in question were invalid in law; and (iv)the assessments could be completed only after the expiry of the period of four years from the date of service of the notices.
