The appellant filed an application for revocation of the authority of the arbitrator appointed under section 5 of the . The High Court dismissed the application on the ground that the only relief claimed by the respondents was the revocation of the power of the arbitrator under section 5. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Court was right in holding that the only remedy, among the many included in the petition, pressed at the hearing was leave to revoke the authority of an arbitrator under section 4(3)(a) of the . [959 E] (2) The High Courts were wrong in saying that the only reliefs claimed by the appellant were the revocation of authority of the Arbitrator under section 5, and that the High Court should have granted the relief sought by the appellant. [960 F G] (3) The High court was wrong in holding that there was no question of revoking the authority of a person who had entered into contract with the respondents. [961 A B] (4) The High 'Court was wrong in saying "that the only relief which could be granted is the revocation of an authority of the contractor". [962 C] (5) The High. Court was wrong in not granting the relief sought for by the appellant because the High Court did not grant the relief sought. [963 D] (6) The High, Court was wrong, in holding that it was not bound to grant the relief prayed for by the respondents. It was not correct to say that the High. Court should have given the relief sought in the application. [964 E] (7) The High: Court was wrong. in saying that it was bound to grant relief sought by a party. [965 H] (8) The High' Court was wrong when it held that the only prayer made by the appellant was the revocation. [966 D] (967 A) The High © Court was wrong if it held that there was nothing wrong in the order of the High Court. [968 E] (10) The High tion cannot be allowed to go
6596: The appellant, a Delhi Cloth & General Mills Limited, is the tenant of the building in question. Its claim for protection of the Act was disallowed by the courts below on the ground that clause (iii) of sub section (3) of Section 1 of the Jammu & Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, was attracted in respect of the appellant. The High Court upheld the validity of clause (iii). In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned clause does not take into account the nature of the premises or the income of the tenant but only the income of his spouse. [875C] 2. The appellant 's claim for protection under Article 14 of the Constitution is based on the basis of the agreement of lease executed between the parties. The agreement of lease provides that the rent payable by the tenant shall be inclusive of the increase in the cost of construction of the building and maintenance of the amenities provided therein. The increase in the rent is subject to the provisions of the Act and the Rules made thereunder. The appellant has no right to insist upon the continuance of the tenancy. [876D E] 3. The appellant cannot be said to have any vested right to continue to occupy the premises after the expiry of the lease period. The appellant had no right to continue in possession after the expiry thereof. The appellant could not be said to be entitled to continue in occupation after the expiry o f the lease period, even if he was not entitled to continue to remain in possession after expiry of the period of lease. [877E F] 4. The appellant is not entitled to the protection of the provisions of Article 14 of Constitution. [878A] 5. The appellant can be said to hold the property as a tenant on the terms and conditions of the agreement. [879B]
3375: The respondent was a carpenter for doing some ornamental work in a cinema hall of the appellant on July 6, 1968 when he fell down. He served a notice on the appellant demanding compensation as his regular employee. The appellant sent a reply dated August 21, 1968 stating that the respondent was a casual contractor and that the accident had taken place solely because of his own negligence. The Commissioner held that the injury had resulted in amputation of the left arm of the respondent above the elbow and directed payment of compensation to the extent of 50 percent and interest at 6 per cent per annum. The appellant 's appeal against this order was dismissed by the Commissioner. In the appeal before the High Court it was contended that the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to entertain and adjudicate on the claim under section 4A of the Act because the respondent was not a carpent or a carpentry but was a carpeter by profession and therefore the Commissioner could not have entertained the claim. HELD: (1) Section 4A of Act provides that the Commissioner may, suo motu or otherwise call upon any person who has been employed by him to appear before him or to act in such capacity under such person and if he is satisfied that the person so called upon is not a carpet labourer, he shall make an application to the Commissioner for compensation. [875 C] (2) The Commissioner can exercise the powers conferred on him under section 4 A of the Act only when there is a dispute between the employer and the workman regarding the quantum of compensation payable to the workman. The Commissioner cannot decide whether the workman should be awarded compensation under section 4(4). [876 D] (3) The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the workman is a carpen or carpenter by profession. The Commissioner has got jurisdiction to determine the amount of compensation payable under section 4B of the Act. [877 E]
1257: The appellant was married to the respondent. He was living with his wife and two children in a house at Ludhiana. On June 5, 1956, he went to the house of the respondent and demanded money for food. The respondent refused to give him money but told him that he would not be maltreated in future. The appellant and his mother went out of the house and tried their best to take her back to the house. She was kept locked inside a room and on June 16, 1956, she was kept locked in a room. On June 17, 1956, the respondent came down to Ludhiana and tried his best to take back his wife. Thereafter, he was kept locked outside a room and was beaten by all the three brothers of the appellant. The appellant was arrested and sent to the police station. The respondent made an application before the Magistrate under section 169 of the Code of Criminal Procedure praying that the case may be registered and investigated. The Magistrate rejected the application. The respondent filed a revision petition before the High Court which dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Magistrate had no jurisdiction to direct the registration of the case against the respondent. [880 A] (2) The Magistrate could not have directed the investigation to be done by the police. The Magistrate could only investigate the offence under section 307 of the Indian Penal Code. [881 D] (3) The Magistrate has no power to direct the investigation to the police. [882 E] (4) The Magistrate can order the investigation to proceed further if he thinks fit. If he is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for proceeding further, he cannot do so without registering the case and proceeding with the trial. [885 F] (5) The Magistrate is not bound to make a complaint under section 200 of the Code. It is open to the Magistrate to direct the police to register the case and investigate the same. But if he does not refuse to register the complaint or where he decides to proceed further in the matter, he is not obliged to forward the complaint to the police for investigation under section 156(3). [886 G H; 887 B] (6) The Magistrate should not act merely as a post office or a mouthpiece
932: The appellant was a member of the Harijan community in the State of Rajasthan. He was a resident of the village in which an additional police force was stationed. He was arrested on June 30, 1956 and released on bail on July 31, 1957. On August 1, 1957, he was served with a notice under section 15(1) of the . The appellant challenged his detention by a writ petition before the High Court on the ground that (i) the notification issued by the State Government under section 15 of the , did not apply to him as he had been detained for more than three months after the date of his arrest; (ii) the notification was invalid because it did not provide for the payment of cost of additional police force; and (iii) the notification did not take into account the fact that the area shown in the schedule annexed thereto was in a disturbed and dangerous state. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notification did contain a provision for payment of cost to the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notification does not purport to be a rule of evidence or a piece of evidence but merely provides for the payment to the appellant of cost of the additional police force. [224 D] (ii) The notification is not a mere notification but a declaration of the intention of the legislature to make the notification effective from April 1, 1957. It is only when the notification is issued under section 15 that the notification can be said to have been issued under section 3 of the Act. [225 E] (iii) The notification cannot be said to be a mere notification. It must be a notification of the nature specified in section 3 of Act 1 of 1951. [226 B C]
3105: The respondent Company is a fairly reputed concern. It has factories at various places in West Bengal, Faridabad and Mokamehghat in the State of West Bengal. It employs a very large number of workmen in its factory, administrative office and Central Repair shops in Calcutta and other places and a Purchasing Depot in Kerala. It had a large number of workers in its factory. The company entered into an agreement with the Union on August 30, 1962 for payment of bonus under the Act in addition to what was paid as per exhibit A.5. The company claimed that the employees were entitled to bonus under the agreement. The workmen refused to accede to the demand of the workmen. The company declined to accede the demand of workmen. The workmen filed a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the amount paid under the agreement was an ex gratia payment made out of charity and as such it was not an annual payment but was an incentive wages. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) The payment of bonus is an ad hoc or an ex graury wage. The payment of Bonus is an additional benefit to the workmen. [880C] (2) The payment is an incentive wage. The workmen accepted the position that the general bonus paid under the Agreement is neither customary nor a profit bonus. The workmen did not accept the position that bonus is an annual payment. The workmen were not entitled to any bonus under the Agreement. [881D E] (3) The payment under the agreement is an adhoc or an ex gratui tion payment. The payment under this agreement is an incentive wages and not a profit bonus or a bonus as an incentive wage; it is an incentive bonus and not a payment for the purpose of earning profits. [882F G] (4) The payment made under the agreement does not fall within the definition of "awarded ' in section 2(b) of the Act. The payment is not an ad hoc payment. The payments are not in the nature of a bonus. [883A B] (5) The payment in question is an incentive payment made out or received from the employer.
5898: The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in the Public Works Department of the State of Punjab. On various dates in the year 1980, he placed orders for the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforementioned orders. In the meantime, the respondent had retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The First Information Report was lodged against him under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 alleging that the respondent had committed offences punishable under section 161 IPC read with section 5(1)(d) of the Preventionof Corruption Act, 1988. The respondent filed a petition before the High Court praying for quashing of the First Information Report and for quashing of proceedings against him. The High Court relying on an earlier decision of that Court in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Punjab, quashed the First Information report. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the First Information Reports are not liable to be quashed on the ground that they have been lodged after the retirement of the respondent. [917B] 1.2 The respondent is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [918C D] 2.1 The respondent is not entitled to the protection of section 197 Cr. P.C. [919E] 3.1 The question whether or not the First Information Officer has jurisdiction to investigate into the offence alleged to have been committed by the respondent would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If it is found that the First information Report does not disclose any offence, the Magistrate can take cognizance of such offence and proceed further in the matter. [920D E]
1982: The appellant, a Private Limited Company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, was engaged in the production and sale of sugar. The Sugar Mills owned a sugar factory at Jaora within the premises of the Sugar Mills owned by it. The Sugar Mill was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The Sugar Factory was also situated in the State. The Sugar Industry was one of the industries specified in the Schedule to the Sugar (Control) Order, 1955 issued under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The Sugar Industries (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1958, was passed by the Central Legislature as amended from time to time. Section 3 of the Act provided for the levy of cess on the entry of cane into the premises of a factory for use or consumption therein. The appellant was assessed to pay the cess. The appellant challenged the validity of the said Act before the High Court which held that the Act had been validly enacted and that the appellant could not be asked to pay the amount of cess. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The provisions of the Act were validated by the Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Diamond Sugar Mills Ltd. vs State of Madhya Bharat and Ors.(1). It is well settled that the legislature can legislate on a topic within its competence but if there is a conflict between the two legislatures, the law made by Parliament and the law made under the Concurrent List must prevail. [430 E F] The Central Act was enacted by the Central Government in exercise of powers conferred by Entry 52 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The power to impose a cess is derived from Entry 52 of the Union List. The power of the State Legislature to enact a law with respect to the entry of sugarcane in the premises of any industry specified in the First Schedule to the Act is subject to the restrictions contained in the Second Schedule. The State Legislature has no power to legislate on a matter covered by the entries in the Concurrent List. [431 A C] The State Legislature can legislate on matters covered by the Entries in the State List. [442 D] The State of Madhya Pradeh vs The Union of India & Anr., ; , referred to.

(iii)The Act is not a legislation with respect to the matters enumerated in List I of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. Commissioner, it was invalid. On appeal the Additional District Judge confirmed the findings of the trial court and dismissed the suit. [1149 A B] (3) The object underlying section 149(1) is to prevent recovery of arrears by taking recourse to the procedure prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure for the recovery or adjustment of the arrears of revenue. [1150 D] (4) The object
5878: The respondent was a unit of metallic aluminium and was using the same type of steel as it used in the manufacture of steel ingots. 1785: The petitioner was selected by the Madras Public Service Commission as a Lower Division Clerk under the Madras Ministerial Service Rules, 1959. He was allotted to the Revenue Department and posted in South Kanara District. He was promoted as Upper Division Clerk with effect from April 2, 1956. According to the State, the petitioner should have been promoted much earlier than April 2, 1957 but he was not considered fit for inclusion in the eligibility list from 1955 onwards. In August 1957, the petitioner was considered and included in the eligibility List from 1955 onwards, but was not selected as he was not found fit. The State admits that he was considered and excluded in the eligibility lists from consideration. The petitioner contended that the Mysore Government had no power to alter the conditions of service of the petitioner so as to affect his seniority in the new department. Held: (i) Article 16(1) of the Constitution is not attracted in the case of the petitioner because the Mysore Government has no power to make any modification in the conditions of services of the petitioner. (ii)The Mysore Government had the power to alter or modify the conditions of appointment of the petitioner in the new Department. The Mysore Government had power to alter, modify or amend the conditions of recruitment of the petitioner and the petitioner could not be said to have been deprived of his right to continue in the new post.
351: The petitioners were tenants of certain villages in the State. They filed applications under article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of the Settlement Officer, and for a direction that the rent rates fixed by him should be revised. The High Court held that the petitioners had no locus standi to file petitions under article 226 of the Constitution. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief on the ground that they had been wrongly denied the right to move the High Court under article 226. The petitioners were not in any way prejudiced by the decision of the High Court. The petitioners did not come within the purview of article 226 of Constitution. The petitioners had no such right as was available to them under article 226 and the petition was liable to be dismissed on that ground alone. The petitioners could not invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under article 32 because they had not approached the High Court directly. The petitioners cannot claim the same relief as a matter of right. The petitioners have no vested right to ask for a writ under article 226, nor can it be claimed against the Government or the Board. The petitioners are not entitled to seek any relief from this Court. The petitions must fail.
44: The appellant was a salesman in a retail shop in Pulbazar in the district of Darjeeling. He sold a piece of cloth at a price in excess of the controlled price, and the appellant was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Supplies Act and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal to the Sessions Judge, the appellant was acquitted on two grounds, viz., (1) that no sanction was previously obtained for the prosecution as required by clause 36 of the Cotton Textiles Control Order, 1948, and (2) that the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, was not in force in the area on the date of the occurrence, and the conviction was set aside. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Act is not in force at the time of the alleged commission of the offence, but it is applicable only to an excluded area or a partially excluded area. [1021 D] (ii) The Act does not apply to an excluded territory. It applies to an excluded part of an excluded territory, and not to an excluded portion of an excluded part. The Act is intended to regulate the supply and distribution and the control of the production, supply, distribution and use of essential
1643: The appellant filed a petition under section 10(1)(a) of the , in the City Civil Court, Bombay, for judicial separation on the ground that she had "deserted" him for "a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of her petition". The respondent alleged that the wife had left the matrimonial home with the intention of permanently breaking it up and that such desertion continued during the requisite period of two years. The trial judge held that the wife 's case was that she had left the husband 's house with the intention to permanently break it up and therefore, the decree for judicial separation granted by the trial court as prayed for. The High Court reversed the decision of the trial judge and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The question whether the wife had established to the satisfaction of the Court that the respondent had an irrevocable determination to break up the matrimonial home when she left the matrimonial house is a mixed question of fact and law which cannot be decided without evidence. [839 B] (ii)The finding of the High Court that the wife has established to the reasonable satisfaction of the court that the respondent 's case is that she had 'an irrevocable determinatio n to break up her matrimonial home when he left the matrimonial place is a pure finding of fact and does not require any interference. [840 C D] (iii)The High Court was right in holding that the respondent could not prove that the wife left the matrimonial household when she left her matrimonial home. [841 E]
5256: The assessee carried on the business of manufacture and sale of woolen goods, cotton textiles and hides and leather products. For the as sessment year 1959 60, under the Income tax Act, 1922, the relev ant accounting was to be made by the assessee for the initial expenditure incurred by it for establishing its business. The assessee claimed a deduction in the computation of its profits and gains of business in respect of the expenditure in question not being in the nature of capital expenditure. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld that decision. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal made a reference to the High Court. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to claim deduction in the computing of its profits in respect of expenditure in question, not being in its nature of capital expend ss or revenue expenditure. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The assessee was bound under an agreement with Charles Walker & Co., London to pay the amount to Messrs Textile & General Supplies Pvt. Ltd. Bombay. The agreement provided that the assessee would permit use by the assessee of a number of registered trade marks specified in the agreement and further disclosed and make known to the approved officers of the assessee the technique, practices and application of the trade marks specified therein and further disclose and make known that the said mark would be used by the assessee at the time of the execution of the agreement. [639 E F] (2) The assessee had been carrying on the business in the name and style of M/s. Textiles & General Supplied Stores. The assessee had also been doing the business of manufacturing and selling woollen goods. The assessee was entitled, therefore, to a deduction in computing its profits and gain of business in the hands of the assessee. [640 G H]
1886: The appellant company entered into contracts with the respondent for purchase of plots in pursuance of which the respondent paid Rs. 2,000/ as earnest money and the balance of the consideration money was to be paid within one month from the date on which the respondent delivered possession of the plot. The respondent did not pay the balance of consideration money within the stipulated period but the appellant agreed to pay half of the price at the time of registration of the deeds and the balance within a year thereafter. The respondent failed to do so within the said period and the appellant forfeited the earnest money deposited by him under section 7(2) of the . The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of the amount due under the contract. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had committed breach of the terms of the contract and that the appellant was entitled to forfeit the earnest money. On appeal the High Court held that the forfeiture was illegal because the appellant had not complied with the provisions of section 7(1)(a) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the forfeiture could only be made after the expiry of the period of one month from date of delivery of possession of the land and that the forfeiture would have been effective only if the possession of the property was taken over by the Government. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no question of forfeiture of the earnest money by the appellant. [634 E] (ii) The High Courts were wrong in holding that even though the appellant had committed breach, the forfeiture was not automatic. It is well settled that where a person has committed breach of an agreement, he cannot take advantage of his own act or conduct. [635 F] (iii) The High courts were wrong in thinking that the forfeiture of the amount was not automatic and that the contract should be completed before the expiry of one month. [636 B C] (iv) The High court was wrong in holding the forfeiture was invalid because the appellant did not comply with the provisions contained in section 7(l)(a). [637 D]
5886: The petitioner and his wife filed objections to the proposed acquisition of their land under section 11 A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. After considering the objections the State Government published a declaration under section 6 of the Act on 19.1.1984. On 24.9.1984 the Land Acquisition Officer passed an award in respect of the land of the petitioner on 23.9.1986. The notice of the award was served on the petitioner on 30.9.86. The petitioner challenged the acquisition proceeding in a petition filed under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The Single Judge dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner 's objection was not maintainable as the award was made after the expiry of two years from the date of publication of the notification under section 4(1) of the Act. Aggrieved by the decision of the Division Bench the petitioner preferred a Letters Patent Appeal before the Division Bench which allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Single Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 11A of the Land Acquisi tion Act, 1894 is a procedural provision. It provides for the mode of taking possession of the land acquired under the Act. The Collector has to make an award within a period of two years after the publication of the declaration under section 9. The Collector must give notice of the Award to the persons interested. The person interested must also be heard before the Collector takes possession of the property. [650C D] PG NO 651 PG NO 652 PG NO 653 2. The provisions of section 11A are mandatory and non compliance thereof vitiates the acquisition proceedings. [652E F] 3. The provisions contained in sections 11A and 11B are mandatory. The Collector is required to take possession of the acquired land before the expiry of the period specified in section 11A. The Collector cannot wait till the award is pronounced. He can only proceed with the acquisition proceedings if he finds that there is some delay in making the award. The Collector may, therefore, resort to the procedure prescribed by section 11A for determining the compensation. [653F G] 4. The provisions relating to the determination of compensation are mandatory. They do not confer any right upon
4732: The appellant was a manufacturer of spare parts and accessories of various aircrafts. The appellant manufactured spare parts and components thereof for the manufacture of the same. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on the turnover attributable to the said goods sold by the appellant. The appellant contended that the turnover apportioned from the job works undertaken by it related to the sale of materials by the appellant to the Indian Air Force or other private parties, as the case may be, and as such, the turnover apportioned to the appellant was taxable as held by the Sales Tax authorities. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions filed by the appellant holding that the turnover allocated to the appellant in the second appeal was not assessable to sales tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a manufacturer of a spare part and accessories of different aircrafts and has established facilities for assembling, servicing, repairing, overhauling of aircrafts, their instruments and accessories which were sent to the appellant for the aforesaid purposes during the relevant years in question. At the instance of the appellant, the main job done was assembled, servicing and overhauling. The appellant had no concern with the said process of assembling, assembling, repairing and overhaul of the aircrafts which were supplied to the Indian air force. [693C D] 2. The appellant cannot escape the liability to pay tax on the entire turnover of the job work undertaken by it. [694E] 3. The appellant has been able to establish that the turnover allocable to it under the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, was not liable to tax. [695F] 4. The appellant was entitled to exemption from payment of sales tax on its turnover relating to the sales made in the canteen of the appellant. [696G] 5. The appellant could not claim that the turnover attributed to the job work done by it was not taxable. [697A]

3092: The respondents, who were partners of a firm carrying on business in the State of Madhya Pradesh, imported tendu leaves from outside the State. The Act does no doubt require the importer to obtain permission from the State Government for the transport of the tendu leaves but it does not prohibit such transport. [881 D E] (3) The Act has been enacted to provide for the regulation of transport of tendu trees and for matters connected therewith. The object of the Act is to regulate the transport of tendures and tendu leaves. The Act is intended to regulate the movement of tendu plants from one place to another. The Act provides for the regulation and control of transport of such tendu plants. The Act
6094: The appellants manufacture and sellers of beer. They are manufacturers of or dealers in beer. They sell the goods at the rate specified in the Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 on the basis of a declaration made by them under section 5(2) of the Act. The appellants contend that the declaration is not correct inasmuch as the declaration was made after the amendment of the Act by the Finance Act, 1983. The appellants also contend that the levy of sales tax on the turnover of goods at the rates specified in the Act is ultra vires the Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The declaration made by the appellants is not correct. [311C] 2. The declaration is not only in respect of goods mentioned in the Schedule but also in respect of other goods which are subject to tax at the point of first sale in the State. [312D] 3. The declaration does not amount to an exemption from payment of sales tax. It is only when the goods are subjected to tax at different points of sale in the same State that the declaration would be effective. [313E] 4. The declaration in the present case is not one of the conditions precedent for the applicability of the exemption notification. The declaration must be made before the goods are sold. [314F] 5. The declaration can be made only if the goods are liable to tax at a particular point of sale in a State. [304G]
7035: The appellant was charged with an offence under section 302 IPC for the murder of one Trinayan Chandra Baruah. 2097: The appellant firm was carrying on the business of selling vegetable ghee. HELD: (i) The notification does not apply to a case where the goods are sold in the course of interState trade or commerce. 2932: The respondent was a member of the Indian Police Service appointed on 25th January, 1937 and at the material time he was holding the substantive rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police in Bihar. He was also reported to have contravened certain provisions of the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1954; and that disciplinary proceedings in respect of these matters were contemplated against him. The respondent filed his memorial to the Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs on 24th August 1964 complaining against the order of suspension passed by the Chief Secretary on 7th July 1964. The respondent was placed under suspension with immediate effect until further orders. The respondent received a memorandum dated 27th August 1964 from the Chief Secretary to the Governor of Bihar stating that the charges against him had been dropped and that he should be suspended for a period not exceeding 90 days. On receipt of this memorandum the respondent made an application to the Secretary, Home Department, Government of Bihar, requesting that the order of the Chief Secretary be withdrawn. The Secretary, Home, Department, Government rejected the said request. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the order was valid and quashed the order of punishment. The appellant contended before this Court that the order having been passed after the enquiry into the allegations against the respondent was invalid because it was not made in accordance with the rules governing the service conditions of the respondent. HELD : (i) The order of suspension is not a punishment but only an administrative order. It does not amount to punishment. [718 E F] (ii) The order is not a mere formality or routine order. It must be passed in conformity with the rules. The order has to be passed after complying with the requirements of natural justice. [719 C D] (iii) The order cannot be challenged on the ground that it was passed without giving an opportunity to the respondent to defend himself. [720 B] (iv) The order being purely administrative one, it could not be interfered with by the court

1611: The respondent was convicted under section 323 and section 324 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code. HELD : (i) The rule providing for conditional release of a person who is already in custody does not apply to cases where the accused has already been arrested and is likely to be enlarged on bail. [186 D E] (ii) The rule does not apply if the accused is already in jail and is likely again to be released. If the accused is not in jail then the rule will have no application. [187 F] (iii) The rule is applicable only where the accused is in jail and not where the accused was in jail. [188 A B] (iv) The rule applies only where the person is already under detention and is likely first to be released and not where he is already in Jail. [189 C] (v) The rule cannot apply where the accused had already been arrested. [185 D] (vi) The rule can apply only where the arrested person is already on bail and is likely immediately to be released from custody. [184 H]

1604: The appellant, who was the first defendant in the suit for possession of certain properties, filed a suit for possession against the first respondent and his two sons. [881 C] (3) The appellant did not claim any right in the properties which belonged to him. The appellant was merely claiming possession of the property which was joint family property. 4667: The detenu was detained under section 3 (2) read with section 3 (3) of the . The order of detention was challenged on the ground that if the detaining authority does not specify in the order of detention as to which particular supply and/or service he had in mind while making it, the order of preventive detention would be vitiated. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive custody is a sine qua non for passing an order of detention. [959 E] 2. The expression "acting in any manner prejudicial to maintenance of public order" has been defined in section 2(a) of the , to mean "acting prejudicial to the security of the State or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community". The expression "law and order", therefore, means "order, public or private"; it includes all orders passed by administrative authorities; "public order" is synonymous with public order. It is difficult to define what are meant by "public order". The expression 'law and order' is not confined to the words "in any manner prejudicial" only. It covers acts done in the execution of the duties or functions entrusted to them. In the present case, the District Magistrate did not specify in his order of detention either the nature of the activities which were prejudicial to the maintenance of public Order or the nature of those which were prejudicial. He merely stated that the detenu had been supplied with the grounds of detention. The High Court was right in quashing the order of the District Magistrate. [960 G H; 961 A B] 3. The expression 'acting in ' in section 3(2) of the Act must be construed in its popular sense meaning that the act complained of must have some connection with the purpose of the Act or the object sought to be achieved. If the object of the Act is to prevent the breach of public order or to regulate the conduct of the business of the Government, then the Act will come into play. But if the object of a law is to prevent a person from doing anything which is likely to cause harm to himself or others, then such a law will come into operation even though the act may be done in the discharge of official duty. [962 D E
710: The Uttar Pradesh Transport Service (Development) Act, 1955, was enacted by the U.P. Legislature in exercise of its powers under article 246 read with entry 5 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and it received the assent of the President on December 14, 1955. Section 3(1)(c) of the Act provided that all laws in force immediately before the commencement of the Act in any State immediately before such commencement shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. Section 11(5) of the U. P. Act provided for the payment of adequate compensation. The U. P Act was passed in 1956 and came into force on January 1, 1956. The U P Act was repealed by the Central Act, 1951, which was replaced by the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1956. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act saved the provisions of the Central Act as from the date of repeal of the Act. The U, P Act was thus repealed by the U P Act. The petitioners who were the appellants before us challenged the validity of the U P. Act on the ground that it violated articles 31(2), 19(1)(f) and 31(1) of the Constitution. Held: (i) that the U.p. Act did not infringe the fundamental rights guaranteed by article 31(2) of the constitution and was therefore void under article 254(2). (ii)that the U. p. Act did neither offend article 31(1), nor does it violate article 13(2) Of the Constitution. (iii)that the provisions of section 6 of the Act were validated by the U, P. Act by the Central Amendment Act, 1956, and the U. '. Act was validated by section 4 of the Act, which was validated only by section 4A of the Act and section 6 of Act was valid. (iv) that the provisions of sections 7 and 8 of the Act are validated by sections 9 and 10 of the Act because they are validated under section 4 of Act. (v) that the Act is validated by Sections 9 and 10 and section 11(5), as amended by Act No. 1 of 1956.

1892: The respondent was a firm owning a cinema house. The appellant Corporation had fixed the scale of fees on the basis of annual valuation of the cinema houses made by a method which does not appear on the record. The respondent 's cinema house had seats and under the changed method it became liable to pay a fee of Rs. 6,000 per year. In the result it became liable for a fee of 5 per show. In the hearing before the High Court the respondent contended that the new method was so high as to make it impossible for the respondent to carry on its business. The High Court rejected this contention. It held that the levy amounted to expropriation and was therefore invalid as violating cls. (f) and (g) of sub article (1) of article 19. Held, that the levy was not ultra vires the Act. The High Courts in India have consistently taken the view that the levy is not confiscatory but is merely compensatory. The imposition of tax is not punitive or penal. The imposition is not punishing the person who has committed an offence. The imposition may be harsh or disproportionate to the gravity of the offence. The classification of the premises into different categories is not arbitrary. The classification must be based on rational basis and the differentia between the premises and the premises which are used for the purpose of keeping a place open for public amusement cannot be said to be arbitrary. The distinction between the premises which were used for the purposes of keeping a particular place for public amusement and those which were used in the other premises cannot be said that the classification is unreasonable. The classification is not discriminatory nor can it be said that it is discriminatory. The classification may be founded on some differentia having a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. But the differentia must have a rational relation with the object of the statute in order to attract the application of Article 14. The classification need not be reasonable in the sense of imprecise or imperilful. It must also be based on some rational nexus with the object to be achieved. If the classification is found to be clearly unreasonable then it would be unreasonable to say that the levy of the tax is not justified because the Legislature intended to pass a law imposing a tax

3768: The respondent was the owner of a house in which she had a limited interest. She executed a will on October 10, 1956 bequeathing her entire property to her. Sub section (1) of section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 provided that where a female has a limited estate under an instrument which is not restricted by the instrument, sub section (2) would apply and the restrictions imposed by the instrument would be applicable only if the property was given to her in lieu of maintenance or in lieu of any other mode of maintenance. The appellant filed a suit for partition claiming a share in the property contending that the will was invalid as it did not confer upon her a life interest in the property and that the High Court should have held that the will in question was invalid. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the will had been validly executed and that the appellant could not claim any right in the property. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the High 'Court erred in holding that the test laid down by the Privy Council in the case of Mst. Khatoon v. Mst. Bibi, (1948) L.R. 74 I.A. 298, applied. The test laid down in the case was that the test must be satisfied that the property was intended to be given to the daughter in lieu of her maintenance and that the will created no interest in the properties in favour of the daughter. The test therefore was whether the property was really intended to be transferred to the daughter by the father. The test was whether the intention of the father was to give the property to his daughter in lieu Of maintenance. The test is not whether the property is intended to be so transferred but whether the intention is to create an interest in the income of the property. The test may be different from the test laid in the case. In the present case, the test laid by the Privy council was not satisfied because the test laid was not satisfied. The test being that the property should be deemed to be given in lieu of the maintenance, the test was not fulfilled.
2331: The appellants were charged with offences under sections 120B, 420, 467 and 468 read with section 471 of the Indian Penal Code as also under section 380 of the Indian. Indian Penal Code for having committed theft of postal orders and cheques. The trial court convicted them under sections 120 B, 420, 465 and 468 read along with section 471 I.P.C., but acquitted them on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (i) the charge against the appellants was not one of conspiracy but only of cheating and forgery; (ii) the evidence in support of the allegation was insufficient to establish the charge; (iii) the evidence was insufficient to prove the charge; and (iv) the conviction was bad because the evidence was not sufficient to establish the charges. HELD : (1) The charge against the appellant was not one which could be established by direct evidence. It was open to the prosecution to adduce evidence to show that the accused had conspired or abetted the commission of a particular offence. [430 F] (2) The evidence in support thereof must relate to the offence charged and the facts alleged must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. [431 A C] (3) The evidence led by the prosecution did not disclose any offence under section 120 B, IPC. The evidence showed that the accused were in possession of the postal order and cheques at the time of their delivery. There was no evidence to show how they received those post orders. [432 D E] (4) The evidence was not enough to establish the offence. [441 G] (5) The evidence of the witnesses examined by the prosecution was not sufficient for establishing the charge. [433 D] (6) The evidence showed clearly that the accused knew that the post orders were forged and that they had dishonestly induced the postal authorities to deliver them to the addressee. 2165: The respondents filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of possession of the plaint schedule land and mesne profits. The trial court held that the respondents were the khatedars of the suit land and that they had been in possession thereof in that capacity. The appellate court confirmed the finding on the question of title but dismissed the second appeal. The High Court, in second appeal, held that the suit was maintainable in a civil court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision of the revenue court on the question whether the respondents were tenants or not was vitiated by an error of law by the courts below because the said decision was based upon the evidence adduced before them and was binding on the parties. HELD: (1) The decision of the Revenue Court on the question as to title is not conclusive on the point under consideration. [839 E] (2) It is well settled that the jurisdiction of a civil court is limited to ascertaining whether a particular person has been in actual possession of the property in dispute or not. The jurisdiction of a Civil Court is confined only to seeing whether the officer who passed the order had a hostile or adverse interest in the property in question. If he acts in good faith in entering into the witness box and producing the document in his defence, the Civil Court will be entitled to see whether the officer has acted with material irregularity in passing the order. [840 F G] (3) The decision in the case of the Collector of the District of Bhopal vs Mst. Saiyadanan, A.I.R. 1958 Madhya Pradesh, 279, referred to.
435: The workmen of the Calcutta Tramway Company (hereinafter referred to as 'the Company ') were employed by the Calcutta Trombay Tramways Co. Ltd., and the employees of the Calcutta Transport Company, who were employed by it. The company claimed that the dearness allowance should be on the basis of the cost of living index of the workmen class at 370 points in the pay ranges below Rs. 50 and up to the pay range of Rs. 250 and by a flat rate of Rs. 5 in the higher pay range, taking the cost of live index of the workman class at 370 point. The Tribunal allowed the claim for the higher pay scale but reduced the amount awarded by the company to Rs. 47/8/ for the lower pay scale. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Tribunal had erred in reducing the dearness allowance to Rs. 7/8/ and that the Tribunal was not justified in reducing the same from Rs. 51 to Rs. 100. HELD: (i) The Tribunal has given good reasons for its decision. It is true that the Tribunal has given very cogent reasons for its conclusion. But it cannot be said that the Tribunal did not give any reason for its decision in arriving at its finding. [701 B C] (ii) The Tribunal had given a very reasonable and satisfactory explanation for the increase in the dearness allowance. The Tribunal had also given some justification for the increase. The Tribunal could have easily taken into account the fact that the company had been paying the dearness allowance at the rate of Rs, 51 per month. [702 D E] (iii) The Tribunal was right in holding that the dearness allowances should be on a uniform basis irrespective of the number of workmen employed in the company. [703 F]
6500: The appellant, a State Government Undertaking, filed a suit against the Union of India and the Government of the Union Territory of Himachal Pradesh for a declaration that he was the owner of the land in dispute. He claimed ownership in respect of the said land on the basis of a registered deed dated 14th October, 1964 executed by his father in favour of the appellant. The suit was decreed by the trial court. On appeal, the High Court affirmed the decree. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation as the appellant had not been impleaded as a party to the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit is barred under section 27 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953. [732C] 2. The suit has been filed within three years from the date of the alleged dispossession. The suit having been instituted after the expiry of three years from 6th April, 1970, the suit is clearly barred by limitation. [733D E] 3. The suit must be held to have been filed beyond the period of limitation prescribed under section 27. [734E] 4. The suit should have been dismissed as barred by limitation because the appellant did not file any application for impleadment within the time prescribed. [735F] 5. The suit cannot be said to be barred by limitation since the appellant had failed to make an application within the prescribed period. [736A] 6. The suit being barred by limitation, the same was liable to be dismissed. [737B]
992: The appellant was a shopkeeper in the shop of the respondent. He had been carrying on business as a commission agent and had been selling articles to customers. The Inspector of Shops and Commercial Establishments, Ferozepore Circle, visited the appellant 's shop on Friday, and found that the shop closed on the day of the week on which his shop would remain closed. The Inspector seized the articles and sent them to the prescribed authority for examination. The Inspector submitted a report to the prescribed Authority stating that the goods were not sold by him but were sold by the appellant to other persons. The Inspector also stated that he had no intention to sell the goods at all. The appellant pleaded that the Act would not apply to his shop because the entire work in the shop was being done by himself and by the members of his family and that to hold that section 7(1) of the Act would apply to his shops would be unconstitutional as violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 14, 19(1)(f) and (g). The Additional District Magistrate rejected the plea raised by the appellant regarding the constitutionality of section 7(I) of the Punjab Trade Employees Act, 1940. Section 3 of the Act provides that the State Government may appoint one or more shops or establishments for the purposes of this Act. Section 4 provides that the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for regulating the conditions of service of persons appointed to shops or establishments. Under section 5 the State Government has power to make rules for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The Act does nothing more than
1049: The petitioners, who were the owners of a bull or bullock in their respective villages, were slaughtered on the ground that they had been carrying on business as bulls and bullocks. They applied for a certificate under section 3(1) of the U.P. Prevention of Cow Slaughter (Amendment) Act, 1958, which was granted by the State Government. The petitioners contended that the provisions of the Act were ultra vires the Constitution and should be struck down as unconstitutional. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief. The petitioners did not carry on business as cows or bulls within the meaning of section 3(2)(b) of the Act. The petitioners were not carrying on business at all. The petitioners could not claim any right to carry on business in bulls and cows. The petitioners had no right to carry out their business. The petitioners ' contention that the provisions contained in section 3(3) of the amending Act were invalid was rejected.
2728: The appellant was a tenant of a shop in the Dispensary Road, Dehra Dun. He applied to the R.C. & E. Officer for an order in ejectment on the plea that he had not vacated the shop and that he had let it out to one Alladia. The Rent Control & Eviction Officer declared that the shop was vacant. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that he was an allottee and a tenant of the shop. The Trial Court held that Gokal Chand had at no time vacated the shop. He accordingly made an order declaring that Goklal was an allottee. The District Magistrate set aside the order. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the order of the civil court was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Civil Court is without jurisdiction. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 194 7, imposes certain restrictions on eviction of tenants. By section 7(1)(a) it is provided that every landlord shall, within days after an accommodation becomes vacant by his ceasing to occupy it or by termination of a tenancy or by release from requisition or in any other manner whatsoever, give notice of the vacancy in Writing to the District Magistrate. The District magistrate has power under section 7(3) to direct the landlord to let or not to let the premises. [366D E] 2. Section 7(3), which provides that if the landlord does not vacate the premises within 15 days after the accommodation became vacant, the Rent Controller may pass an order directing the landlord to evict the tenant. The order passed by the District Magistrate is not without jurisdiction. [365F] 3. The order is without jurisdiction and is liable to be quashed. [367G] 4. The order under section 7A(2) is without jurisdiction as the landlord has not given notice of the vacation of the premises. The District Judge has jurisdiction to pass an order under section 8(4). [368B C] 5. The order dated March 31, 1969 is without jurisdiction because the order is without authority. [369E] 6. The order was without jurisdiction and was bad in law. [370
2302: The petitioners challenged the validity of the Taxation Laws (Extension to Union Territories) Regulation No. 3 of 1963, on the ground that the President had no power to promulgate the Regulation under article 240 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the impugned Act was not legally extended to Pondicherry and that the impugned Regulation was ultra vires the powers of Parliament as well as of the State Legislatures. Held, that the impugned provisions were not validly enacted in exercise of the powers conferred by article 240 of Constitution. The power to make laws for the peace, order or good government of India exercised by the President under article 240(1)(a) of the Constitution is a legislative power and cannot be delegated by the President to any other authority. The power of making laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India is a legislative function. The power conferred by article 246(4) of the Government of India Act, 1935, is subject to the provisions of the Constitution and the power of the Parliament to legislate with respect to matters enumerated in List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution does not extend to matters which are exclusively within the exclusive domain of the Parliament. The power given to the Parliament to enact a law with respect to taxes on income is not an independent power but a power coupled with a duty. The power is not necessarily confined to the subjects covered by the entries in Lists I and II of the Seventh schedule. The power can be exercised only in relation to those subjects enumerated in List III. The power cannot be exercised in relation to matters which fall outside the legislative competence of the Parliament and which are not enumerated in List II.
5329: The appellant was a manufacturer of motor vehicles. He was granted exemption from duty under the Notification dated August 1, 1974. The Notification exempted certain goods from the duty of excise leviable thereon. The appellant claimed that the said goods were not excisable goods and therefore, they could not be subjected to duty under the Act. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the Notification did not apply to the facts of the case. On appeal, the Collector held that the Notification applied only to those goods which were produced in the factory of manufacture and not to other goods. The Tribunal allowed the appeal holding that the Notification had no application to the facts before it. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Notification applies only to those specified goods which are produced or manufactured in the factory. [203B] (2) The Notification does not apply to all the specified goods. It is applicable only to those notified goods which are actually produced or manufactured. [204C] (3) The Notification has no application to any specified goods. [205D] (4) The Notification is not applicable to the facts in this case. [206E] (5) The Notification cannot apply to the goods produced or manufactured by the appellant. [207F] (6) The Notification must be read as a whole. [208G]
6504: The respondent was promoted from Class 'B ' to the post of Assistant Military Estates Officer (AMEOT) in 1962 and thereafter he was promoted as Assistant Military Estates Officers (AMEIOT). In 1964, the appellant was promoted as Deputy Military Estates Officer. In 1968, the respondent was promoted as AMEO Grade B. In 1969, the respondent filed a petition before the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging his promotion on the ground that the order promoting him was illegal because it was made without giving him an opportunity of being heard. The Tribunal allowed the application holding that the respondent was entitled to be considered for promotion to the post. On appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The respondent was not entitled to be appointed to the post as he had been promoted earlier than the respondent. [607C] 2. The Tribunal has rightly held that the respondent is entitled to be promoted to the post which he was holding prior to the promotion of the respondent. The Tribunal was right in its conclusion that the respondent could not have been promoted to the higher post. [608D] 3. The Tribunal erred in directing the appellant to promote the respondent to the post in question. [609A] 4. The Tribunal committed an error in dismissing the application of the respondent under section 19(3)(a) of the Act. [610F] 5. The Tribunal should have directed the appellant to consider the respondent for promotion to this post. [608G]
4772: The appellant was a candidate for election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly. He secured 30350 votes as against 30327 votes secured by the first respondent. The result of the election was announced on May 20, 1982 in which the first respondent was declared elected having secured 30450 votes as well as 11268 votes as against 30210 votes secured by him. Thus, the first respondent secured 30450 and 11268 votes respectively. The appellant challenged the validity of voting by machine and held that the respondent was duly elected to the Assembly seat. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 324 does not confer any power on the Commission to make laws or rules in respect of matters relating to or in connection with the elections to the Parliament or State Legislatures. [902B] 2. The Election Commission is a creature of the Constitution itself, its plenary powers flowing directly from article 324 and if there is any legislation laying down the procedure for holding elections, it has to follow the same. [903C D] 3. The Commission being a creature, its plener is bound to act within the limits prescribed by the Constitution and cannot act arbitrarily without following the procedure prescribed by law. [904E F] 4. The Commission is a constitutional body constituted under the Constitution and it is entrusted with the task of conducting elections to the Houses of Parliament and the States. It is an independent body. It is not required to perform any function which is quasi judicial in nature. It is expected to act fairly and reasonably. [905F G] 5. The Commission has to act within certain limits. It is also expected to act judicially. [906A]
3978: The appellant, a brilliant and a young man of about 25 years age, was convicted for the murder of his wife, aged about 20 years, by the Sessions Court. He was sentenced to death under section 302 I.P.C., and to imprisonment for life under section 376 I.P., Penal Code. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the sentence of death should be commuted to one of transportation for life, and (2) the sentence should not be converted into imprisonment for life. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sentence of death is not only excessive but also harsh. [801B] 2. The sentence should have been commuted to life imprisonment. [802A] 3. The sentence must be reduced to the period already undergone. [803E] 4. The sentence shall run concurrently. [804F] 5. The sentence is to be modified accordingly. [805G]
1018: The respondent was a constable in the U.P. Police Force and was promoted to the rank of head constable and posted as officer incharge of police station, Intiathok, District Gonda. Complaints were received by the District Magistrate to the effect that the respondent was receiving bribes in the discharge of his duties. On November 3, 1952, the District Magistrate sent an endorsement to the Superintendent of Police to the effect "A strong officer with plenty of push in him and met with a strong opposition in this new charge". On December 17, 1952, he was forced to go on leave for two months. Before the expiry of his leave, he was reverted to his substantive post of head constable. On February 27, 1953, he was again placed under suspension and on February 27,1953, he was transferred to Sitapur. On February 28, 1953, the Superintendent of police made the following endorsement in his character roll: "A strong Officer with pl deprivation of his work and reputation for integrity is not good but that his transfer should be after some time and that in the meantime his work might be closely watched." On March 30, 1954, the respondent was dismissed from service. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the order of termination of service was punitive and that it was passed without complying with the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. It held that the order was punitive because the respondent had been given ample opportunity to defend himself and there was no violation of principles of natural justice. Held, that the order dismissing the respondent was punitive. The fact that the respondent did not give any explanation for his conduct would not make the order punitive. There must be something more than mere failure to furnish the particulars of the allegations which may or may not be vague. If the facts stated in the report are such that one could say that the charges against the respondent were not specific and definite, then the order cannot be said to have been passed in colourable exercise of power.

927: The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and had been dismissed from service by an order dated August 18, 1950. He challenged his dismissal on the ground that he was not entitled to continue in service after the date of his retirement as he had not been removed from service within the meaning of article 311(2) of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant was not entitled under article 311(1) of the constitution to continue in office until he attained the age of superannuation. The order of August 18,1950, which was passed by the Rajpramukh of the State in exercise of powers conferred by article 311(3) of theConstitution, did not amount to removal or dismissal within the meaning Of article 311(4). The order of the Rajpuramukh of the Punjab State was not in accordance with article 311(5) of the, Constitution. The order was not invalid because it was made without complying with the provisions of article 311 (2) of. the Constitution. The appellant was not a member of a civil service of the State and could not be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed. The order did not amount either to removal or reduction in rank but amounted to removal. The order therefore did not fall within article 311(6) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The order must be held to have been made in compliance with the provisions contained in article 311(7) of the Constitu tion and the appellant was rightly dismissed from service.
3187: The State of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification under section 68D(2) of the , in respect of the proposed scheme for providing State road transport services on the route or portions thereof. The appellants, who were operating their private operators, challenged the validity of the said notification and the High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the notification dated February 20, 1963 was not valid as it did not specify the routes which should be included in the scheme; that the notification merely stated that the scheme would be implemented after the approval of the Central Government had been obtained; that the scheme was not intended to provide any road transport service on the route and that the notification was only an intimation to the State Transport Undertaking that the scheme had been approved by the State Government. HELD: (1) The notification does not purport to give any power to the State Government to issue a direction to the State transport undertaking to implement the scheme. It merely gives the State Transport undertaking the right to provide road transport services. [173C] (a) The notification merely states that the scheme has been approved by a State Government. It does not say that the scheme is to be implemented after approval of the State Government, nor does it say that the State Transport Undertakings are to be given any directions to implement the schemes. [174E] (b) The notification clearly indicates that the scheme will be implemented after its approval by the State Transport Authority. The notification merely makes it clear that the scheme shall be implemented after it has been approved. The notification also does not indicate that the scheme should be implemented after such approval. [175B C] (c) The notification simply says that the scheme may be implemented after a decision has been taken by the State. It does nothing more than make it clear that it is intended to operate after the approval by the Central Government. [176F] (d) The notification cannot be construed to mean that the scheme must be implemented after all the approvals have been accorded by the State Governments. [177G]
3306: The appellant was a young boy of about seventeen years and three months. He was convicted under section 379 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for snatching two sarees from one Govind, while he was carrying them from the show of his master to that of a dyer. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant under section 379, but the High Court maintained the sentence of imprisonment imposed on him. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since he was a young person aged about seventary years and three month old at the date of the offence and the offence was not punishable with imprisonment for life, the Court, in spite of the fact that he was a youthful offender, could not have applied its mind to those provisions and imposed the sentence of fine. HELD : (i) The appellant had no reason to think that the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act should be applied in the case. [646 C] (ii)The appellant was a youthly offender and was not a fit person to be sent back to prison. It is only when he was a child below the age of seventeen or three months that he would be able to make an attempt to commit such offences. [647 D]
5056: The respondent company was granted a patent under the Patent. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the appellate court confirmed the decree. In second appeal, the High Court held that the appellant 's patent was not in accordance with the provisions of section 9 (1) (b). The High Court also held that the respondent 's patent could be said to have been in accordance with section 9(2)(c) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. It means that the patent has been issued by the Government or any other authority specified in the Act and it is not necessary that the patent should be in accordance with law. [640B] 3. The word "in accordance" is not used in the Act but in the context of the Act itself. The word 'in accordance' is not used either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. [641C] 4. The word in accordance is not used as a technical term in the Act, but in the sense of a legal term. The word is used in the context in which it occurs. [642D] 5. The word has to be construed in its popular sense and in the sense in which it is understood in common parlance. The word must be given its ordinary meaning. [643F] 6. The word as used in section 9(l)(a) is not intended to refer to the actual words of the statute. It refers to the words of the law. [664G] 6. Section 9 (1)(a), therefore, cannot be read in isolation from section 9(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [665A]

2711: The route involved in this case was the one between Meerut and Dankaur which had no direct passenger bus. The R.T.A., followed the procedure laid down in section 57 of the , and granted permits to the appellants and others, who were operating on the routes. The RTC applied for permits to operate a direct service from Meerut to Dankaur. This was not a case where the R.T..A. had already decided upon opening the new route fixed the number of permits necessary for such a route and then invited applications from operators. The RT.A. followed the procedure prescribed in section 57, and rejected the application of the appellants. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that (i) the R. T. A. had no jurisdiction to grant or refuse permit to any applicant; (ii) the RTC did not have the power to grant or refused the permit; (iii) the RT. A. was entitled to issue a notification under section 57(3), and (iv) the RTA could not be said to have acted arbitrarily in refusing to grant the permit. HELD : (1) The R. T., was not competent to grant the permits. [880 E] (2) The RTC was not entitled to grant the same. [881 C] (a) The RT was not competent merely because the R.TC had already decided to open the new route. It is only the R. V. T.A. who can be said to be interested in the route. [882 B] (b) The RTO has no authority to grant or not to grant permit to any individual applicant. The RTO is not bound to grant permit if there are more than one route. [887 G] (c) The RTA has no authority either to grant or to refuse permit to an applicant. The Regional Transport Authority has no authority whatsoever to grant or refuses permit to an operator. [886 H] (d) The RTR does not confer any right on the applicant to get a permit. [885 F] (e) The RTU is not a statutory body. It is a statutory body and its decision must be based on the relevant provisions of
2950: The appellant, a partner of a firm, was prosecuted for having committed offences under section 120B read with section 420 and section 465 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court convicted him under section 420 read with section 465. On appeal by special leave it was contended that (1) the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; (2) the evidence showed that the accused were running a business in partnership with the firm and that the firm had issued policies and printed pamphlets and handbills representing that it was a Government of India 's Registered Firm No. 1468. HELD : (i) The prosecution has failed to prove its case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. [146 D] (ii) The prosecution case was based on circumstantial evidence. There is no reason why the prosecution should be disbelieved merely because the circumstances are such as to exclude the possibility of any other person being guilty of the offence. [144 E] (iii) The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused persons formed an unlawful assembly and the common object of the unlawful assembly was to commit the offence. It is necessary to establish that the accused did some act which amounted to criminal conspiracy. [145 F] (iv) The prosecution could not prove beyond reasonable doubts that the accused had conspired or had a common intention to commit the crime. [143 G] (v) The prosecution cannot fail on the ground that the accused have been acquitted by the trial court. [144 H] (vi) The prosecution can prove the existence of a conspiracy even though the same may not be proved. [144 C] (vii) The prosecution is not bound to prove the existence or absence of a conspiracy. [144 D] (viii) The prosecution would be justified in bringing home the charge of conspiracy only if the ingredients of the offence are satisfied. [145 E] (ix) In the present case, the prosecution has failed in proving the existence of the conspiracy. [144 F] (x) The prosecution was entitled to bring home the charge that the accused conspired or abetted the commission of the crime. The prosecution has also failed to prove the ingredients of section 120 B read with section 415 I.P.
1429: The appellant company was a small scale industry. It had a large number of industries controlled by the respondent company. The respondent company claimed that the chemical works should be treated as an integral part of the respondent 's industry and that the wage structure etc. fixed on the basis of the financial position of each unit should be taken into account. The Industrial Tribunal held that the chemical work was an integral part and that the workers in the respondent factory were entitled to the benefit of the wage structure, dearness allowance and gratuity. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the chemicalwork was one unit of a large number industries controlled by a company and that the workmen in the respondent Factory were entitled to be paid the same wages as are being paid to the workmen in other concerns in Delhi. Held: (i) The chemical works is an integral part, of the respondent factory and its employees cannot claim the benefit of this wage structure or the dearness allowance fixed on the wage structure. (ii)The workmen in the appellant factory were not entitled to the benefits of the wage scheme, gratuity and provident fund, but they were entitled to certain benefits under the wage scheme. (iii)The workmen were not entitled, as a matter of course, to any particular pay scale or allowances. (iv)The workmen must have been employed in the respondent factories and their conditions of service could not be altered without the consent of the employer.
3051: The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Martin & Co., and was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of aluminium products. In the year 1950, the appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent for the supply of certain goods to the respondent. The respondent agreed to purchase the said goods from the appellant for a period of 999 years. The appellant paid Rs. 10,000 as advance and the balance of Rs. 1,00,000 was payable within one month from the date of the agreement. The respondent also paid Rs. 1 lac towards the price of the goods. On the expiry of the period of the agreement the appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of the amount due under the agreement. It was contended that the agreement was not binding on the respondent and that the appellant had no right to recover the amount under the agreement and that the respondent was entitled to recover the entire amount under the contract. Held: (i) The agreement was not voidable at the instance of the respondent but only voidable at his instance. (ii)The agreement was not enforceable because it was not binding upon the respondent. (iii)The agreement did not create any interest in the property in favour of the respondent. [345 D] (iv)The agreement is not voidable under section 23 of the Contract Act. (v)The agreement does not create any title or interest in immovable property. The agreement is not a mere transaction of lease but a licence. [346 B C] (vi)The agreement being voidable at will, the respondent cannot claim any benefit out of it. [347 E] (vii)The agreement between the parties was not binding because it was voidable at its instance. [348 F] (viii)The agreement in question was not binding under section 23. The agreement was voidable under the provisions of section 23 of Act. [349 A B]
