1506: The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge for offences under section 302/149 I.P.C. and section 302/34 I.P,C. The trial judge held that the charges under section 302 /34 had not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt and so, according to him, the prosecution case under section 148 was not proved beyond a reasonably doubt and so acquitted them of the said offence. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the convictions and sentences imposed on the appellants. In regard to the four other accused persons, it was contended before this Court that the charge under section 302 I.P.,C. was not proved against them as they were acquitted by the trial court and that the acquittal of the appellant Gurcharan Singh was not justified in law. HELD : (i) The charge under section 149 I.P,.C. is not proved beyond any reasonable doubt. [880 D] (ii) The evidence of the eye witnesses does not show that the appellants had taken part in the assault on the deceased. It is true that the appellants did not take part in the attack but they took part in the incident. But the fact that the appellants were armed with deadly weapons cannot be used against them because they were not armed with deadxious weapons. [881 E] (iii) There is no reason why the appellants should have been convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P..C. [882 F]

1187: The petitioners and the respondents were migrants from Pakistan. They had become evacuees and their shares in the properties could be properly declared evacuee property under section 11 of the Act. The petitioners challenged the order dated August 14, 1952, made under section 11 on the ground that it was a nullity as the notice under section 7 of the Act was not issued to them and they were not contesting the validity of the order. Held, that the order is a nullity for the reason that it was passed by the Custodian of Evacuee Property who had no jurisdiction to pass the same. The order does not affect the rights of the petitioners to hold property in the properties which are sought to be declared evacuee property. The order merely declares the properties to be evacuee property. It does not purport to affect the rights or interests of the petitioners in those properties. The order is a mere administrative order and does not affect any rights of the parties. The order cannot be said to have been made in breach of the provisions of the Act or the rules framed thereunder.
862: The appellant, a Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh, was a factory in Bombay. It had been set up by the Textile Mills Association of India (hereinafter called 'the Association) and other companies owning cotton textile mills specified in the annexure to the Special Leave Petition. The mill was closed on one day and the workers were compelled to reduce their consumption of electricity during the period between November 1, 1951 and July 13, 1952. The workers claimed that they should be paid compensation for loss of wages and dearness allowance due to the short working or closure of the mill at 8 hours per week as before. The Industrial Court held that the workers were entitled to compensation for loss in respect of the closure of the mills and directed payment of compensation accordingly. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal was erroneous because the provisions of Standing Orders and 17 were not applicable to the case of the appellant as the workers were not covered by Standing Orders and the workmen were not entitled to compensation under section 73 of the Bombay Electricity Act, 1948. Held, that the decision in the case of Rashtriyas was correct and the appeal must fail. The provisions of Standing Order No. 17 are not applicable to a case where the workers have been permitted to work for more than 48 hours in a week. The provisions are not applicable if the workers are required to work for less than 48 hours. The provisions do not apply when the workers are allowed to work for 48 hours in any week. The workers are not entitled to claim compensation for loss caused to them due to the closure of their mills. The provisions in the Standing Orders and in the order of the Bombay Government are not applicable. The provisions relating to the payment of compensation are not applicable in the present case because the workers were allowed to work only for 48 hours.
1045: The appellant was a commission agent and pucca aratiya. He had been acting as such for the respondent since November 7, 1951, in the course of which various contracts were made between them in Greater Bombay. On February 26, 1952, two of these contracts were outstanding, one of which was in respect of groundnuts and was a forward contract. In March 1952, disputes arose between the parties as to whether the forward contracts in groundnuts were illegal as the making of such contracts was prohibited by the Oilseeds (Forward Contract Prohibition) Order, 1943, issued under the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, and hence the arbitration clause contained in it was null and void. The appellant made an application to the Bombay City Civil Court for setting aside the award on the ground that forward contracts in groundsnuts were not illegal as the make of such contracts were prohibited by the Act. The respondent contended that forward contracts were illegal as they were not in terms of the Act and therefore the award in terms of arbitration clause contained therein was a nullity. Held, that the appellant 's application was competent under section 34 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, and the High Court was right in its view that the arbitration clause in the forward contract in groundnut and groundnut oil entered into by the respondent with the appellant was invalid. The words "in accordance with" occurring in the arbitration clause are clear from the words "for the purpose of securing the payment of money due or otherwise". The words "for any other purpose" mean that the object of the arbitration clause is to secure the payment of the money due or to be received by the claimant. The words 'for any other purposes' mean that the purpose must be fulfilled before the arbitration clause can operate. The words used in the arbitration agreement are "for any purpose other than those for which the same may be expressed". The words 'or otherwise ' do not refer to the main purpose of the arbitration agreement. The words are not to be construed strictly but are to be construed in their natural and ordinary sense.
